movements.name: There Is a Court
movements.desc: Before anything else, Scripture seats a Judge and opens a bench. The book takes place in a courtroom.

movements.name: The Court Runs on One Code
movements.desc: The standard on that bench is the Torah — the covenant terms, sworn and binding, not private feeling.

movements.name: You Are Named on the Docket
movements.desc: You are not watching the trial. You are a party to it, entered by name, with standing and an estate.

movements.name: The Acquittal
movements.desc: Charged and unable to pay, you are cleared at the tree — the Father laid the account on the Lamb He provided. Entry by blood.

movements.name: Your Life Is the Testing
movements.desc: Now cleared, you walk. Every day is conduct weighed against the code — the testing of the delivered. Walk by the Bread.

movements.name: It Is All Entered as Evidence
movements.desc: Word, deed, and blood — every step of the walk is deposed and filed. Nothing falls off the record.

movements.name: The Bench Convenes
movements.desc: The ruling is read, and each party is paid exactly what the record assigns.

roadNote: The road runs one direction, start to finish: the court, its law, your name entered, the acquittal at the tree, the walk that follows, the record of that walk, and the verdict. Entry is by blood (IV); the walk that proves it is by the Bread (V); the verdict is still ahead (VII).

5.lead: To condemn is the opposite ruling to acquittal — guilty, liable, sentenced. The word is built from kata, ‘down,’ and krino, ‘to judge’: to judge down against a defendant. Every use assumes a fixed standard the accused has been measured against and failed. “There is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Messiah Yahushua” (Romans 8:1) is precious precisely because condemnation was real, filed, and deserved. Take away the standard and the good news collapses — a man cannot be spared a sentence that was never on the books.

root.sense: to give judgment against, to condemn; kata (down) + krino (judge)

5.courtroomWord: A verdict term — the ruling of guilt and the sentence that follows.
5.itsRole: Condemnation is the guilty verdict — the court measuring a defendant against the standard and finding him short. It presupposes the law it judges by; without a standard there is nothing to condemn under. This is why deliverance is framed as ‘no condemnation’: the sentence was real and deserved, and it is lifted — not because the law vanished, but because the account was answered.

proofTexts.text: No condemnation to them which are in Messiah Yahushua.
proofTexts.note: The sentence lifted, not the law removed.

proofTexts.text: He that believeth not is condemned already.
proofTexts.note: The standing verdict on the unanswered.

proofTexts.text: The judgment was by one to condemnation.
By thy words thou shalt be condemned.
proofTexts.note: The verdict weighed on the evidence.

plainTerms: To condemn is to rule someone guilty and sentence him — the opposite of acquittal. It only means something against a standard the person broke. ‘No condemnation’ is good news because the guilty verdict was real and deserved, and it has been lifted.
bringItHome: A judge measures the defendant against the law and rules: guilty. That is condemnation — a real verdict with a real sentence. ‘No condemnation in Messiah’ is the sentence lifted off a guilty man — which only means anything because the law he broke is still the law.

courtroomRoles.does: renders the verdict of guilt, or clears it.
measured against the standard, condemned or acquitted.
the measure the verdict is rendered by.

9.lead: An advocate is defense counsel — one called alongside to plead your case before the bench. “If any man sin, we have an advocate with the Father, Yahushua Messiah the righteous” (1 John 2:1). This is no vague comforter; it is an attorney standing before the court on the defendant’s behalf. The office only functions inside a live trial where charges can still be filed. To have an advocate is to admit there is a court, a prosecutor, and a case — and then to find that competent counsel has already taken the brief.

root.sense: one called alongside; an advocate, counsel for the defense

9.courtroomWord: A counsel term — the one who pleads the defendant’s case before the bench.
9.itsRole: When the accuser files, the advocate answers. Yahushua stands before the Father as counsel for the accused, pleading a settled account against every charge. He does not deny that a case exists; He answers it with the price paid. The advocate is why the indictment does not stand.

proofTexts.text: We have an advocate with the Father, Yahushua Messiah the righteous.
proofTexts.note: Counsel for the accused, standing with the Father.

proofTexts.text: Who also maketh intercession for us.
He ever liveth to make intercession for them.
Now to appear in the presence of Yahuah for us.

plainTerms: An advocate is your defense lawyer before Yahuah. When the accuser charges you, Yahushua pleads your case — not by denying the court, but by answering it with the paid account.
bringItHome: The prosecutor finishes his charges and the accused has no words. Then counsel rises — not to argue the man is innocent, but to lay a paid receipt on the bench. Charge answered. That is the advocate: Yahushua before the Father, pleading a settled account.

courtroomRoles.does: pleads the case before the Father — counsel with Him, not a second self-standing judge.
before whom counsel appears.
represented, and cleared.

10.lead: The accuser is the adversary who stands to prosecute — not a folk-tale imp but the party who brings the charge. In Zechariah 3:1 the satan stands at the right hand of the high priest “to resist him,” to accuse him before the court; in Job he presses his case before the bench of heaven. The role is legal: he files, he indicts, he demands the guilt of the accused. And it presupposes a law to accuse under. Revelation names him the accuser of the brethren, then announces he is cast down.

root.sense: adversary, one who opposes or accuses; the prosecuting party

10.courtroomWord: A prosecution party — the adversary who brings and presses the charge.
10.itsRole: In the true court the accuser’s charge is tested and, if unanswered, stands. Against the covered it does not stand: the account is paid, an Advocate pleads, and the accuser is thrown out of court. His whole standing depends on an open charge — close the account and his office collapses.

proofTexts.text: Satan standing at his right hand to resist him.
proofTexts.note: The accuser positioned to prosecute the priest.

proofTexts.text: Doth Job fear Elohim for nought?
proofTexts.note: The adversary pressing his case before the court.

proofTexts.text: The accuser of our brethren is cast down.
Your adversary the devil... seeking whom he may devour.
proofTexts.note: The accuser at work against the saints.

plainTerms: The accuser is the prosecutor — the one who brings charges against you before Yahuah. His power is only in an open case. When the account is paid, he is cast down.
bringItHome: Picture the prosecutor who never sits — day and night lodging charges against the accused. That is the accuser. But once the debt is paid and counsel pleads it, the judge clears the docket and the prosecutor is put out. He had nothing left to charge.

courtroomRoles.does: brings and presses the charge.
hears, and casts the accuser down.
cleared by the paid account.

16.lead: The church pictures forgiveness as a change of feeling — letting go of a grudge. But nasa means to lift, to carry, to bear away: the legal removal of a charge from the account. To forgive iniquity is to pick the liability up off the record and haul it elsewhere. “Blessed is he whose transgression is forgiven” — lifted — (Psalm 32:1) describes a debt physically removed from the ledger, not an emotion softened. What gets lifted is something the law had entered in the first place. No entry, nothing to lift; no debt, nothing to forgive.

root.sense: to lift, to carry, to bear, to take away; to bear off a charge

sharesRoot.note: One verb, four legal motions: to lift a charge away (Forgive), to bear the liability of a charge (Bear Iniquity), to lift a face in partiality (Lift the face), and to lift an empty report and carry it (False Report).

16.courtroomWord: A removal term — the lifting of a charge off the record.
16.itsRole: Forgiveness is not the softening of a feeling but the lifting of a liability — the charge carried off the account so the ledger clears. Because nasa means to bear, the charge lifted from the guilty must be borne by another; the same verb runs through the Servant who bare the sin of many. To forgive is to remove the entry — which presupposes an entry the law had made.

proofTexts.text: Blessed is he whose transgression is forgiven.
proofTexts.note: The charge lifted from the record.

proofTexts.text: Forgiving iniquity and transgression and sin.
He bare the sin of many.
proofTexts.note: The charge lifted from the guilty, borne by the Servant.

proofTexts.text: That pardoneth iniquity... he retaineth not his anger.
proofTexts.note: The debt removed, not merely overlooked.

plainTerms: To forgive is to lift a charge off the record — to carry the liability away — not just to feel better about a wrong. And because the word means ‘bear,’ what is lifted from the guilty is carried by another. No charge on the books, nothing to forgive.
bringItHome: Forgiveness is not shrugging off a feeling; it is lifting a debt off the ledger and carrying it away. And the same word says who carries it: the Servant who bare the sin of many. The charge does not vanish — it is lifted from you and borne by Him.

courtroomRoles.does: lifts the charge from the record.
the Servant who bears the sin lifted from the guilty.
whose liability is carried away.

17.lead: “Forgive us our debts” (Matthew 6:12) is bookkeeping, not metaphor. An opheilema is a binding obligation owed and enforceable at law — the exact word a creditor would use for a sum on the books. The model prayer casts sin as an outstanding balance and forgiveness as its cancellation. A debt does not appear from nowhere; it is incurred when an obligation fixed by agreement goes unmet. Which means every prayer for forgiveness quietly concedes the standard: one cannot owe a debt under a law that does not exist, and one cannot ask the cancellation of a debt one denies was ever owed.

root.sense: that which is owed, a debt; a legal obligation

17.courtroomWord: A ledger term — a binding obligation owed and enforceable, entered on the books.
17.itsRole: A debt is a balance the law recognizes and a creditor can enforce. Sin, in the prayer’s own accounting, is such a balance — incurred by breaking an obligation, cancelled only by a lawful discharge. The whole logic of forgiveness runs on it: there must be a real debt, under a real standard, for its cancellation to mean anything. This is why the certificate of debt could be cancelled while the law stood.

proofTexts.text: Forgive us our debts, as we forgive our debtors.
The lord... forgave him the debt.
proofTexts.note: The balance cancelled by the creditor.

proofTexts.text: The reward... reckoned... of debt.
proofTexts.note: The accounting language of debt and credit.

proofTexts.text: He frankly forgave them both.

plainTerms: A debt is a real balance you owe that the law can enforce. The Lord’s Prayer treats sin as exactly that — a debt to be cancelled. And you cannot owe a debt where there is no law, or ask forgiveness for one you say was never owed.
bringItHome: ‘Forgive us our debts’ is ledger language, not poetry. Sin runs up a balance on the books, and forgiveness is the creditor striking it off. But a struck debt proves there was a debt — and a debt proves there was a standard that fixed what was owed.

courtroomRoles.does: carries the balance incurred by breaking the obligation.
holds the debt, and may cancel it.
the obligation entered on the books.

18.lead: The master legal instrument of Scripture, and the word the modern church most sentimentalizes into ‘relationship.’ A berith is a binding treaty between a sovereign and a people, complete with named parties, stipulations, witnesses, sworn ratification, and sanctions for breach — the ancient suzerain treaty in its bones. Every ‘spiritual’ bond with Yahuah is, underneath, a ratified contract with terms. This is why the Scriptures divide into an old and a renewed covenant rather than an old and a new mood. To be in covenant is not merely to be loved; it is to be legally bound, with everything that binding entails.

root.sense: a covenant, treaty, binding compact; cut and ratified between parties

18.courtroomWord: The master instrument — the binding treaty that governs the whole relationship.
18.itsRole: A covenant is the legal frame everything else hangs on: parties, terms, witnesses, ratification, sanctions. It is not a warm bond but a contract, and every other legal word in Scripture operates inside it. To enter covenant is to accept its terms and come under its sanctions; to be in Messiah is to stand within a ratified compact, not merely to feel near.

proofTexts.text: Behold the blood of the covenant, which Yahuah hath made with you.
In the same day Yahuah made a covenant with Abram.
proofTexts.note: The covenant cut between the parties.

proofTexts.text: I will make a new covenant with the house of Israel.
A testament is of force after men are dead.

plainTerms: A covenant is a binding treaty — named parties, terms, witnesses, and penalties for breach. It is the master contract every other legal word in Scripture works inside. To be in covenant is to be legally bound, not just fondly attached.
bringItHome: A covenant is not a friendship; it is a signed treaty with clauses and consequences. When Yahuah enters covenant with a people, He is binding Himself and them by terms — witnessed, ratified, enforceable. Everything else in the courtroom — the charges, the pardons, the verdicts — happens inside that contract.

courtroomRoles.does: sets the terms and binds Himself to them.
bound to the stipulations and sanctions.
the binding treaty that frames all the rest.

20.lead: The devotional reading softens atonement into ‘at-one-ment,’ a restored closeness. But kaphar means to cover, to satisfy, to wipe the charge so the account balances — the legal settlement of guilt. On Yom Kippur the blood was applied to answer a claim the law had filed against the people, not to warm the national mood. Atonement is what closes the case: the debt covered, the ledger squared, the docket cleared. It is transactional by nature — an outstanding liability lawfully discharged, and the price for it provided by Yahuah Himself.

root.sense: to cover, to purge, to make atonement; to satisfy a claim

sharesRoot.note: Kaphar (atonement, the covering) and kopher (ransom, the price of a life) share the k-p-r root: atonement covers the charge, the ransom pays the price that covers it.

20.courtroomWord: A settlement term — the covering of guilt that closes the case and clears the account.
20.itsRole: A filed charge must be answered before the account can close. Atonement answers it — the blood applied, the claim covered, the ledger squared. It is not a change of feeling but a discharge of liability, and in the true court the price that covers is the one Yahuah provided, not one the guilty could pay.

proofTexts.text: It is the blood that maketh an atonement for the soul.
proofTexts.note: The covering that answers the claim.

proofTexts.text: On that day shall the priest make an atonement for you, to cleanse you.
proofTexts.note: The docket cleared on Yom Kippur.

proofTexts.text: By whom we have now received the atonement.
The chastisement of our peace was upon him.
proofTexts.note: The price of the covering, laid on the Lamb by the Father.

plainTerms: Atonement means to cover a charge and settle the account — to wipe the debt so the books balance. It is not a warm feeling of closeness; it is a legal discharge of guilt, paid with a price Yahuah provided.
bringItHome: A debt is filed against you, and someone lays a covering over it that answers it in full — the account reads zero. That is atonement: not the case forgotten, the case closed. And the covering was provided by the Judge Himself, at His own cost.

courtroomRoles.does: provides the covering that settles the claim.
the Lamb on whom the price was laid.
whose charge is covered and account cleared.

28.lead: To render the legal due — good for good, ill for ill — as the case requires. “To me belongeth vengeance, and recompence” (Deuteronomy 32:35) is a court reserving to itself the right to settle every outstanding account, favorable and unfavorable alike. Recompense is not spite when the ledger runs against a man, nor mere generosity when it runs for him; it is the verdict paid out in full. The same word that guarantees the faithful their wage guarantees the guilty their sentence. To recompense is to close the account by giving each party exactly what the record assigns.

root.sense: to make whole, to pay in full, to render what is owed
to deal out, to bring a matter to its due return

sharesRoot.note: One root, three faces of a single legal idea: peace is the account paid (Shalom), the wrong repaid (Restitution), the verdict paid out (Recompense). The same shalam is why Isaiah can say the chastisement of our peace was upon Him — the recompense that makes us whole and the peace it buys are the same word.

28.courtroomWord: A settlement verb — the paying-out term of the court. It does not weigh guilt or innocence; that is already decided. Recompense is the act that comes after the finding: the debt settled, the wage paid.
28.itsRole: Recompense is the payout. The pay that sin earns is death (Romans 6:23) — a real debt the court will collect. But at the tree the Father stepped in and laid that payment on the Lamb He provided. The recompense did not fall on us; it fell on the Son. The right to settle the account belongs to Yahuah alone, and He commits the settling to His Son (John 5:22) — the Son who bore it once will render it at the end.

proofTexts.text: The wages of sin is death.
proofTexts.note: The debt on the books — the pay sin earns.

proofTexts.text: The chastisement of our peace was upon him.
proofTexts.note: The Father lays the payment on the Son; the recompense that makes us whole falls on the Lamb.

proofTexts.text: To me belongeth vengeance, and recompence.
proofTexts.note: The right to settle the account is reserved to Yahuah's court.

proofTexts.text: The Father… hath committed all judgment unto the Son.
proofTexts.note: The payout is handed to the Son — an office given, not seized.

proofTexts.text: He shall reward every man according to his works.
proofTexts.note: The same Son delivers the final payout at the bench.

plainTerms: Recompense means being paid back exactly what is coming to you — good or bad — because the record says so. It is not revenge, and it is not a gift. It is the account settled down to the last line.
Here is the turn: the pay that sin earned was death, and it did not land on you. Yahuah laid it on the Lamb He provided. The payment that should have made you pay is the payment that makes you whole.
bringItHome: Picture a debt so large it costs a life. The court will be paid — that part is certain. But the Father steps in and lays the payment on the Son He provided. Isaiah saw it a thousand years early: “the chastisement of our peace was upon him.” The recompense that makes us whole fell on the Lamb, not on us. The Father rendered it; the Son bore it. That is the tree.
The Father did the appointing; the Son did the bearing. Neither is the other, and the Son does not step forward on His own — He is the Lamb the Father provided and laid the account upon.
28.bringItHomeForward: And the same Son the Father laid the payment on is the One to whom the Father hands the final payout: “he shall reward every man according to his works.” What He bore at the tree, He delivers at the bench (Movement VII). Tree to throne — the Father appointing, the Son carrying it out.

courtroomRoles.does: reserves the right to settle every account, and lays the payment where He wills.
the Lamb the Father provided, on whom the recompense fell.
the one whose wage was death — the debt that had to be paid.
fixes exactly what each party is owed, to the last line.

31.lead: A book, in Scripture, is a legal register, not a storybook. A sefer was the document of record — a deed, a certificate, a roll. When Jeremiah buys a field, the purchase is written in a sefer, witnessed, and sealed (Jeremiah 32:10-12). So “the book of life” is a citizenship roll, an official register of those enrolled, and to be blotted out of it is a legal removal from the record (Exodus 32:33). To be written in the book is not to be remembered fondly; it is to be entered, by name, on the standing legal record of the kingdom.

root.sense: a writing, document, scroll; a legal register or deed

31.courtroomWord: A register term — the official document of record on which names and deeds are entered.
31.itsRole: The court keeps records, and the book is the record. Deeds are written in it, names are enrolled in it, and removal from it is a legal act. The book of life functions as a citizenship roll: to be in it is to hold standing in the kingdom; to be blotted from it is to lose that standing. It is documentary, not sentimental.

proofTexts.text: Whosoever hath sinned against me, him will I blot out of my book.
proofTexts.note: The register, and legal removal from it.

proofTexts.text: I subscribed the evidence, and sealed it.
proofTexts.note: The deed written in a sefer.

proofTexts.text: The books were opened... and another book... the book of life.
proofTexts.note: The records read at the bench.

proofTexts.text: A book of remembrance was written before him.
proofTexts.note: The record kept before the court.

plainTerms: A book in Scripture is an official record — a deed, a roll, a register — not a story. The book of life is a citizenship list; being written in it means you are on the record, and being blotted out is a legal removal.
bringItHome: Think less ‘novel,’ more ‘county deed book.’ When Jeremiah bought his field, the sale went into a sealed document — a sefer. The book of life is that kind of record: your name entered on the official roll of the kingdom. To be in it is to have standing; to be struck from it is to lose it.

courtroomRoles.does: keeps the book; enrolls and blots names.
entered by name on the record.
the official document read at the bench.

39.lead: People treat it as a verbal period at the end of a prayer. It is actually a legal signature. In Deuteronomy 27 the people stand and answer “Amen” to each pronounced curse — sworn, on-the-record assent to the covenant’s penalty clauses. To say Amen is to affirm at law: let it stand, hold me to it, so be it by my own word. It binds the speaker. Every time a believer closes a prayer with “amen,” he notarizes it — putting his name to the document — usually without the faintest idea he has just signed something.

root.sense: firm, established, sure; a sworn affirmation — ‘let it stand’

39.courtroomWord: A signature term — sworn assent that binds the one who speaks it.
39.itsRole: A covenant requires the parties’ assent on the record. Amen is that assent — the people’s signature under the terms, penalties and all. It is not a pious flourish but a binding affirmation, and it commits the speaker to what he has just agreed.

proofTexts.text: And all the people shall say, Amen.
proofTexts.note: Sworn assent to the covenant’s clauses.

proofTexts.text: And the woman shall say, Amen, amen.
proofTexts.note: The oath sealed by the word.

proofTexts.text: These things saith the Amen, the faithful and true witness.
proofTexts.note: The word as a title of the trustworthy witness.

proofTexts.text: In him Amen, unto the glory of Yahuah.

plainTerms: Amen is not a period on a prayer — it is a signature. It means ‘let it stand, hold me to it.’ When you say it, you are putting your name to what was said and binding yourself to it.
bringItHome: A contract is read aloud, clause by clause, and at each one the party says the ancient equivalent of ‘agreed — hold me to it.’ That word is Amen. It is a signature spoken. Every prayer you close with it, you have just signed.

courtroomRoles.does: binds himself on the record.
to whom the assent is given.
signed by the word.

41.lead: In Hebrew, covenants are not ‘made’ — they are cut. To karat a covenant is to ratify it by cutting animals in two and passing between the pieces, invoking the same fate upon whoever breaks the terms (Genesis 15:10, 17-18; Jeremiah 34:18). The verb is the act of legal ratification, a self-maledictory oath enacted in blood: let it be done to me as to these beasts if I break faith. When Yahuah alone passes between the pieces before Abraham, He binds Himself under that sanction. Every covenant in Scripture is, at its root, something cut — sworn under penalty, not merely agreed.

root.sense: to cut; to cut a covenant by passing between severed pieces; also to cut off

sharesRoot.note: One root, three cuttings: the covenant cut (karat), the sinner cut off (karet, Karath), and the marriage bond cut (kriythuth, Divorce).

41.courtroomWord: A ratification term — the cutting that binds a covenant under a self-maledictory oath.
41.itsRole: A covenant is enacted by cutting — the parties pass between severed pieces, binding themselves to the fate of the animals if they break the terms. This is the most solemn form of legal ratification: an oath in blood. That Yahuah alone passes between the pieces in Genesis 15 means He takes the covenant’s sanction on Himself. To cut a covenant is to bind it beyond retraction.

proofTexts.text: In that day Yahuah made a covenant with Abram.
Which cut the calf in twain, and passed between the parts thereof.
A burning lamp that passed between those pieces.
proofTexts.note: Yahuah binding Himself under the sanction.

proofTexts.text: The blood of the covenant.

plainTerms: In Hebrew you don’t ‘make’ a covenant — you cut one. The parties passed between cut animals, swearing, ‘let this happen to me if I break the terms.’ It is an oath in blood. To cut a covenant is to bind it beyond taking back.
bringItHome: Two parties walk a path lined with the halves of slaughtered animals and swear: let me become like these if I break faith. That is cutting a covenant — the most binding oath there is. And in Genesis 15, Yahuah walks it alone, taking the whole sanction on Himself.

courtroomRoles.does: cuts the covenant, and takes its sanction on Himself.
sworn under the same penalty.
the fate invoked on a covenant-breaker.

46.lead: To hear, in Torah, is to heed and comply — hearing that carries obedience as its legal freight. “Hear, O Israel” (Deuteronomy 6:4) does not request attention; it summons a people to obey the terms about to be read. Shama is the vassal’s response to the suzerain’s stipulations: to hear is to submit to the ruling. This is why hearing is never passive in Scripture but the beginning of allegiance. The one who truly hears is the one who does; the one who hears and refuses to comply is, in the law’s own reckoning, one who has not heard at all.

root.sense: to hear, to listen, to heed, to obey

46.courtroomWord: A compliance term — hearing that carries obedience to the terms read.
46.itsRole: In covenant, to hear is to submit — the response of a party to the stipulations set before it. ‘Hear, O Israel’ summons obedience, not attention. Shama binds hearing and doing together: to hear the terms is to come under them. This is why the disobedient are said not to have heard — in the law’s reckoning, hearing that does not comply is not hearing at all.

proofTexts.text: Hear, O Israel: Yahuah our Elohim is one Yahuah.
proofTexts.note: The summons to obey the terms.

proofTexts.text: All that Yahuah hath said will we do, and be obedient.
To obey is better than sacrifice.
Be ye doers of the word, and not hearers only.
proofTexts.note: Hearing that does not comply is empty.

plainTerms: In Torah, to hear means to heed and obey — not just to listen. ‘Hear, O Israel’ is a call to comply with the terms, not to pay attention. Hearing and doing are one: if you hear and don’t obey, Scripture says you haven’t really heard.
bringItHome: When a lord read his terms to those under him, ‘hear’ meant ‘submit to this’ — not merely ‘notice it.’ That is shama. ‘Hear, O Israel’ calls a people to come under the covenant, and the proof of hearing is doing. Hearing without obeying, in the law’s own accounting, is not hearing.

courtroomRoles.does: sets the terms to be heard and heeded.
hear, and by hearing come under the terms.
read to be obeyed, not merely noted.

49.lead: To confess is a legal admission — to say the same thing the record says. To confess sin is to agree with the charge rather than contest it, entering a plea that matches the evidence; to confess the Name is to make a binding public declaration of allegiance. “Whosoever therefore shall confess me before men” (Matthew 10:32) is on-the-record testimony that binds the one who gives it. Confession, in either direction, is testimony entered about oneself: agreement with the indictment, or a sworn declaration of loyalty. It is not merely admitting a feeling; it is going on the record before the court.

root.sense: to acknowledge, to confess, to give thanks openly
to say the same thing, to profess or confess openly

49.courtroomWord: An admission term — testimony entered about oneself, agreeing with the record.
49.itsRole: A court runs on testimony, and confession is testimony a party gives about himself. To confess sin is to plead in agreement with the charge — the admission that opens the way to its being lifted. To confess the Name is to declare allegiance on the record, a binding profession. Either way, confession is not private feeling but entered testimony, spoken before the court.

proofTexts.text: If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us.
proofTexts.note: Admission agreeing with the charge, met with lawful pardon.

proofTexts.text: Whosoever shall confess me before men, him will I confess.
If thou shalt confess with thy mouth... thou shalt be saved.
Whoso confesseth and forsaketh them shall have mercy.

plainTerms: To confess is to go on the record — either agreeing with the charge against you (confessing sin) or declaring your allegiance (confessing the Name). It is testimony about yourself, not a private feeling.
bringItHome: In court, a defendant can contest the charge or agree with it. To confess sin is to agree — ‘the record is right about me’ — which is the plea that opens the way to pardon. To confess the Name is the other kind: standing up and declaring, on the record, whose side you are on.

courtroomRoles.does: agrees with the charge, or declares allegiance.
before whom the confession is entered; who pardons or receives it.
which the confession agrees with.

50.lead: To deny is legal repudiation — the disowning of a bond or a party on the record. “Whosoever shall deny me before men, him will I also deny before my Father” (Matthew 10:33) frames denial as a courtroom act with a matching courtroom consequence: repudiation answered by repudiation. To deny is the reverse of confession — testimony withdrawn, a covenant tie publicly disavowed. Peter’s threefold denial is precisely this: standing before accusers and repudiating his bond to the accused. Denial is not a mood of distance; it is a legal act of disowning, entered before witnesses, with standing consequences on both sides of the bench.

root.sense: to deny, disown, repudiate; to refuse to acknowledge

50.courtroomWord: A repudiation term — the disowning of a bond or party, entered on the record.
50.itsRole: If confession is testimony that binds, denial is testimony withdrawn. To deny the Name before men is to repudiate one’s covenant tie publicly — a legal act with a legal answer: him will I also deny. It is the reverse motion of confession, and it carries standing consequences before both courts, the earthly and the heavenly.

proofTexts.text: Whosoever shall deny me before men, him will I also deny before my Father.
If we deny him, he also will deny us.
Thou shalt deny me thrice.
In works they deny him.
proofTexts.note: Denial entered by deeds, not only words.

plainTerms: To deny is to disown — publicly repudiating your bond to someone, on the record. It is the opposite of confession. And Scripture makes the consequence match: deny Him before men, and He denies you before the Father.
bringItHome: Peter stood before accusers and said, in effect, ‘I have no bond with that man’ — three times, on the record. That is denial: not distance in feeling, but a covenant tie publicly disowned. And the court answers in kind.

courtroomRoles.does: repudiates the bond on the record.
whom the denial repudiates, and who answers in kind before the Father.
before whom the repudiation is entered.

52.lead: An heir is one with legal standing to receive an estate — not a beggar hoping for kindness, but a party holding a recognized claim the law will enforce. “If children, then heirs; heirs of Yahuah” (Romans 8:17) confers legal status, not merely affection. An heir’s expectation is guaranteed by his position: the estate is coming to him by right of standing. This is the dignity buried in the word — to be made an heir of Yahuah is to be granted enforceable title to an inheritance, entered on the estate as one legally entitled to receive.

root.sense: an heir; one who receives an allotted inheritance

sharesRoot.note: All from the kleron- root: the heir (kleronomos) receives the inheritance (kleronomia) by inheriting (kleronomeo).

52.courtroomWord: A standing term — one with the legal right to receive an estate.
52.itsRole: An heir is defined by standing, not hope: the estate is his by right, and the law will enforce the claim. To be made an heir of Yahuah is to be granted that standing — an enforceable title to the inheritance, entered on the estate. It is why the believer’s expectation is secure: not a wish for kindness, but a recognized legal claim guaranteed by his position as son.

proofTexts.text: If children, then heirs; heirs of Yahuah, and joint-heirs with Messiah.
No more a servant, but a son; and if a son, then an heir.
proofTexts.note: The status that carries the estate.

proofTexts.text: Heirs according to the hope of eternal life.
Whom he hath appointed heir of all things.
proofTexts.note: The Son appointed heir by the Father.

plainTerms: An heir is someone with the legal right to receive an estate — not begging for a gift, but holding a claim the law will enforce. To be an heir of Yahuah is to be granted that standing: the inheritance is yours by right, secured by your position as a son.
bringItHome: An heir does not hope the family might be generous — he holds a legal claim on the estate, and the law backs it. That is what it means to be made an heir of Yahuah: not a beggar at the door, but a son with enforceable title to the inheritance.

courtroomRoles.does: confers the standing of heir.
holds enforceable title to the estate.
heir of all things by the Father’s appointment, with whom the sons are joint-heirs.

58.lead: To buy is to acquire by paying the market price and thereby transfer ownership from seller to buyer. “Ye are not your own... ye are bought with a price” (1 Corinthians 6:19-20) states a completed purchase with a change of owner: the believer is property lawfully acquired at cost. The verb is commercial and legal, not romantic. To be bought is to have a new owner with the owner’s rights over the thing purchased. This is why the redeemed are called servants and the price is named blood — the transaction moved title, and title carries authority.

root.sense: to buy in the marketplace; to acquire by paying a price

sharesRoot.note: The act and its completion: to buy (agorazo) and to have been bought. The price moves the title.

58.courtroomWord: A purchase term — the acquisition of ownership by a price paid.
58.itsRole: A purchase transfers title. To buy is to move ownership from one hand to another, and the price is what establishes the new claim. In redemption the price is blood and the title moves to Yahuah — the redeemed acquired, owned, and thereby secured and answerable. Buying is the mechanism; ownership is the result.

proofTexts.text: Ye are bought with a price.
Hast redeemed us to Yahuah by thy blood.
Sold all that he had, and bought it.
proofTexts.note: The pearl acquired at full cost.

proofTexts.text: The assembly... which he hath purchased with his own blood.

plainTerms: To buy is to pay the price and take ownership — title moves to the buyer. In redemption the price is blood and the buyer is Yahuah: the redeemed are acquired, owned, and secured.
bringItHome: A purchase is simple — you pay the price, and the thing is now yours, with every right an owner has. Redemption is that transaction at the highest cost: the price is blood, and the title moves. The redeemed are bought — owned, and safe in the Owner’s hand.

courtroomRoles.does: acquires the redeemed by the price.
the blood that makes the purchase.
title moved, now owned.

59.lead: Bought is the purchase completed and on the record. “Thou wast slain, and hast redeemed us to Yahuah by thy blood” (Revelation 5:9) — the redeemed are owned property, lawfully acquired, and the price paid establishes the claim. Ownership carries the owner’s rights: the bought belong to the buyer and are answerable to him. Far from diminishing the believer, this is the ground of his security — a lawful owner defends his property and honors the price he paid. To have been bought is to have been legally claimed, the transaction closed, the title transferred, the receipt written in blood.

root.sense: to buy in the market, to purchase; egorasthete, ‘ye were bought’

sharesRoot.note: The same verb, two aspects: to buy (the act) and to have been bought (the completed purchase). Title moved; the receipt is the price.

59.courtroomWord: A completed-purchase term — ownership transferred by a price paid.
59.itsRole: A purchase moves title, and the price establishes the claim. To be bought is to have a new owner with the owner’s rights — and, for the redeemed, an Owner who defends what He paid for. The transaction is closed and recorded; the believer is no longer his own but lawfully held, the receipt written in the price.

proofTexts.text: Hast redeemed us to Yahuah by thy blood.
Ye are bought with a price.
Ye are bought with a price; be not ye the servants of men.
proofTexts.note: One Owner, His rights over the bought.

proofTexts.text: Denying the Lord that bought them.
proofTexts.note: The purchase real even where denied.

plainTerms: To be bought means the purchase is done and title has moved — you belong to the buyer, and the price paid proves the claim. For the redeemed, that is security: the Owner defends what He paid for.
bringItHome: A sale closes when the price is paid and the title changes hands — the thing bought now belongs to the buyer, with all an owner’s rights. That is the redeemed: bought, title transferred, receipt written in blood. Not diminished by it — secured by it, because the Owner protects what cost Him so much.

courtroomRoles.does: acquires the redeemed by the price; holds and defends them.
the blood by which the purchase was made.
lawfully claimed, answerable to the Owner.

60.lead: The birthright is the firstborn’s legal privilege — a double portion of the estate and the headship of the family. It was a real, transferable legal asset: Esau “sold his birthright unto Jacob” (Genesis 25:33) in a binding exchange he could not later undo (Hebrews 12:16-17). The bekorah was inheritance-law attached to birth order, conferring rank and a larger share of the property. This is why despising it was so grave — it was the squandering of a legal entitlement for a bowl of stew. To hold the birthright is to hold the firstborn’s documented claim on the estate.

root.sense: the right of the firstborn; a double portion and headship

60.courtroomWord: An estate term — the firstborn’s legal claim to rank and a double share.
60.itsRole: Inheritance in Torah runs by law, and the firstborn’s claim is fixed by it. The birthright is that claim — documented, transferable, binding once exchanged. It confers headship and a double portion, and its sale or forfeit is a legal act with legal consequence. The believer’s calling as firstborn is estate language: a claim on the inheritance, held by right.

proofTexts.text: Esau sold his birthright unto Jacob.
By giving him a double portion of all that he hath.
proofTexts.note: The firstborn’s share fixed at law.

proofTexts.text: Esau, who for one morsel of meat sold his birthright.
The firstborn of every creature.
proofTexts.note: The rank and inheritance of the firstborn borne by the Messiah.

plainTerms: The birthright was the firstborn’s legal privilege — a double share of the estate and headship of the family. It was real property you could sell, and Esau did, for a bowl of stew. To hold it is to hold a documented claim on the inheritance.
bringItHome: The oldest son held a paper worth double everyone else’s — rank, headship, a double portion. Esau traded that paper for a single meal, and could not get it back. That is the birthright: a legal entitlement, as real as a deed, and as losable as one.

courtroomRoles.does: holds the double portion and headship by right.
divided by the law of the birthright.
fixes the firstborn’s claim.

61.lead: Adoption is a formal legal act that places a person into a family as son, with the full inheritance rights of one born to it. It is a courtroom placement, not a change of biology: “ye have received the Spirit of adoption” (Romans 8:15). Under the law an adopted son’s former debts were cancelled and his new standing was fixed and irreversible. To be adopted by Yahuah is to be legally installed as son and heir, granted a standing and an estate one was never born to — the old account wiped, the new status entered on the record.

root.sense: the placing as a son; adoption, a legal act conferring sonship

61.courtroomWord: A status act — the legal placement of a person as son, conferring an heir’s rights.
61.itsRole: Standing in the household is conferred by decree, not earned by birth. Adoption enters a new party on the estate with full rights of inheritance and cancels what stood against him. It is why the believer can be called heir: the placement is legal and secured, not a sentiment of belonging.

proofTexts.text: Ye have received the Spirit of adoption, whereby we cry, Abba, Father.
That we might receive the adoption of sons.
Having predestinated us unto the adoption of children.
proofTexts.note: The placement purposed from the first.

proofTexts.text: If children, then heirs.

plainTerms: Adoption is a legal act that makes you a son with full rights — not by birth, by decree. The old debts are cancelled and the new standing is permanent. It makes you an heir.
bringItHome: A judge signs the order and a child who was outside the family is now a son — same room, new standing, full claim on the estate, old record wiped. That is adoption. Yahuah does it by decree: not born to it, placed into it, and made heir.

courtroomRoles.does: decrees the placement.
granted standing and estate.
wiped at the placement.

64.lead: Free is manumitted status — the standing of one released from legal bondage, entered on the record. Freedom in Scripture is a change of legal position, from bound to loosed, not merely a feeling of ease: “stand fast therefore in the liberty wherewith Messiah hath made us free” (Galatians 5:1). The freedman held documented standing that could be defended. This is why liberty must be ‘stood fast’ in — it is a legal status one can be argued back out of. To be made free is to have one’s bondage lawfully ended and one’s release certified, a new standing granted by an authority competent to grant it.

root.sense: free, freeborn or freed; not under bondage

64.courtroomWord: A status term — the standing of one legally released from bondage.
64.itsRole: Freedom is a legal position, not a mood — the released bondman holds a new standing on the record. It can be defended, and it can be forfeited, which is why Scripture commands standing fast in it. To be made free is to have an authority competent to release you certify your release: the bondage lawfully ended, the new status entered. Liberty is enacted and recorded, not merely felt.

proofTexts.text: Stand fast therefore in the liberty wherewith Messiah hath made us free.
proofTexts.note: A status to be held, defensible.

proofTexts.text: If the Son therefore shall make you free, ye shall be free indeed.
Being then made free from sin.
Is Messiah’s freeman.

plainTerms: Free is a legal status — released from bondage and certified as such — not just a feeling of ease. It can be defended and it can be lost, which is why Scripture says to stand fast in it. To be made free is to have your release granted by one with the authority to grant it.
bringItHome: A freed slave did not just feel different — he held papers, a new legal standing that a court would recognize and defend. That is freedom in Scripture: bondage lawfully ended, release certified. And because a status can be argued away, we are told to stand fast in it.

courtroomRoles.does: releases the bound by competent authority.
granted a new, defensible standing.
lawfully ended and recorded.

67.lead: Clean means legally admissible — fit to approach the sanctuary and enter the assembly. Cleanness is a status determined by law, not a comment on hygiene: the priest examines and pronounces a person or thing tahor the way a judge issues a finding of standing (Leviticus 13). To be clean is to be ruled eligible to draw near. This is why cleanness can be lost and restored by prescribed legal process rather than by washing alone. The categories clean and unclean are courtroom findings about who may lawfully approach — determinations of standing, entered by an authorized officer.

root.sense: clean, pure; legally admissible to approach the holy

67.courtroomWord: A status finding — the ruling that a person or thing is admissible to approach.
67.itsRole: Approach to the sanctuary is regulated, and cleanness is the standing that permits it. The priest does not wash the leper clean; he examines and pronounces — a legal finding. Cleanness can be lost and restored only by the prescribed process, because it is a status under law, not a state of hygiene. To be clean is to be ruled fit to draw near.

proofTexts.text: The priest shall pronounce him clean.
proofTexts.note: A legal finding, not a wash.

proofTexts.text: Put difference between... unclean and clean.
To make a difference between the unclean and the clean.
proofTexts.note: The standing categories set at law.

proofTexts.text: Who shall ascend... He that hath clean hands, and a pure heart.
proofTexts.note: Cleanness as the standing to approach.

plainTerms: Clean is a legal status — fit to come near the holy — not a statement about dirt. The priest pronounces it, the way a judge rules on standing. It can be lost and restored only by the prescribed process.
bringItHome: A man could be freshly washed and still ruled unclean, or restored to clean only by a set process — because cleanness was never about soap. It was a legal finding: are you admissible to approach? The priest examined and pronounced, and the ruling set your standing before the sanctuary.

courtroomRoles.does: examines and pronounces clean or unclean.
ruled admissible or barred.
sets the categories of approach.

71.lead: To anoint is investiture into office — the formal act that installs a priest, king, or prophet and confers the authority of the post. The oil is the legal ceremony of appointment, and it changes standing: from the day Samuel anointed David, “the Spirit of Yahuah came upon David” and the office was his (1 Samuel 16:13), though years passed before the throne. To be anointed is to be commissioned, vested with authority to act — not merely honored. The anointing is the appointment made official, effective from the moment the oil is poured.

root.sense: to smear, to anoint; to consecrate into office

sharesRoot.note: Mashiach — ‘the Anointed One’ — is the same root: the act of anointing (mashach) and the office-holder it produces. The Messiah bears the title because Yahuah invested Him with the office.

71.courtroomWord: An investiture term — the formal act that installs a person into office with its authority.
71.itsRole: Authority to serve as priest, king, or prophet is conferred, not assumed. The anointing is the transfer of office onto the one designated, witnessed and effective. This is why the Messiah is ‘the Anointed’ — He holds the office because Yahuah invested Him with it, a warrant received, not seized.

proofTexts.text: Samuel took the horn of oil, and anointed him... and the Spirit of Yahuah came upon David.
Thou shalt anoint Aaron and his sons, and consecrate them.
Yahuah hath anointed me to preach good tidings.
Against Yahuah, and against his anointed.
proofTexts.note: The appointed one, set by the Appointer.

plainTerms: To anoint is to appoint someone into office — priest, king, or prophet — and hand them its authority. The oil is the ceremony. It is why the Messiah is ‘the Anointed’: the office was given to Him by Yahuah.
bringItHome: The oil is poured, and a shepherd boy is now the anointed king — the office is his from that moment, even before the crown. That is anointing: not honor, appointment. And it is why the Messiah bears the title — the office was conferred on Him by the One who anoints.

courtroomRoles.does: confers the office by the anointing.
vested with authority to act.
the ceremony that makes the appointment official.

76.lead: A crown is two legal things at once — sovereignty conferred, and the honor awarded to the faithful at the verdict. A crown marks the right to rule, and it is also the prize adjudged at the end: “there is laid up for me a crown of righteousness, which the Lord, the righteous judge, shall give me at that day” (2 Timothy 4:8). Note who awards it — the righteous judge, at the appointed day, as a verdict. The crown is either authority worn on the head or the sentence of commendation handed down from the bench. Both senses are legal: delegated rule, or the court’s favorable ruling made permanent.

root.sense: a crown, wreath, diadem
a victor’s or honor’s crown

76.courtroomWord: A sovereignty-or-award term — the sign of the right to rule, or the prize adjudged at the verdict.
76.itsRole: A crown either confers authority or records a verdict. Worn by a king, it marks delegated rule; awarded to the faithful, it is the court’s commendation made permanent, given at that day by the righteous judge. Both are legal: the crown is rule granted or judgment rendered, not mere ornament.

proofTexts.text: A crown of righteousness, which the Lord, the righteous judge, shall give me at that day.
proofTexts.note: The prize adjudged from the bench.

proofTexts.text: He shall receive the crown of life.
proofTexts.note: The award to the one who endures.

proofTexts.text: Be thou faithful unto death, and I will give thee a crown of life.
Thou settest a crown of pure gold on his head.

plainTerms: A crown is either the sign of the right to rule or the prize handed down at the end by the Judge. When it is a reward, note who gives it and when: the righteous Judge, at that day. It is a verdict worn on the head.
bringItHome: A crown sits on a king’s head as the mark of his authority — or it is placed on the faithful as the court’s final commendation, made permanent. Either way it is a legal act: rule conferred, or a verdict rendered and worn.

courtroomRoles.does: confers rule, and awards the crown at the verdict.
granted authority, or commended at that day.
rule conferred or judgment rendered.

78.lead: An elder is a judicial officer who sat in the gate to hear cases and issue rulings — a seat on the local bench. When a matter arose, “then shall his father and his mother... bring him out unto the elders of his city... unto the gate” (Deuteronomy 21:19). Boaz convenes ten elders to witness and legalize a land transaction (Ruth 4:2). The word carries office and jurisdiction, not merely advanced age. To appoint elders in the assemblies was to establish a governing and adjudicating authority. An elder is a magistrate: one seated to weigh disputes and pronounce the community’s binding decisions.

root.sense: old, an elder; a magistrate seated in the gate

78.courtroomWord: An office term — the magistrate seated to hear cases and render the community’s rulings.
78.itsRole: Local justice ran through the elders — they sat in the gate, heard disputes, witnessed transactions, and pronounced binding decisions. The office is judicial, not merely a matter of age. When elders are appointed in the assemblies, a governing and adjudicating authority is established. To sit as an elder is to hold a seat on the bench.

proofTexts.text: Bring him out unto the elders of his city, and unto the gate.
proofTexts.note: The elders as the local court.

proofTexts.text: He took ten men of the elders of the city.
proofTexts.note: Elders convened to legalize a transaction.

proofTexts.text: Let them judge the people at all seasons.
Let the elders that rule well be counted worthy of double honour.
proofTexts.note: The governing office in the assembly.

plainTerms: An elder was a local magistrate — one who sat in the city gate to hear cases, witness contracts, and hand down binding rulings. The word means office and jurisdiction, not just old age. Appointing elders set up a governing, judging authority.
bringItHome: When two neighbors had a dispute, they went to the gate, where the elders sat — and those men heard the case and ruled, and their word was binding. That is an elder: a judge on the local bench. The title is about the seat, not the years.

courtroomRoles.does: hear cases and render binding rulings.
brought before the elders for judgment.
the court where the elders sit.

79.lead: The gate was the courthouse of the ancient city — the place where elders convened, contracts were witnessed, and cases were tried. “Then shall the elders of that city... say” (Deuteronomy 21:20); Boaz conducts his legal business ‘up to the gate’ (Ruth 4:1). To seek judgment ‘in the gate’ (Amos 5:15) was to seek it in court. The gate was the civic and legal center, the venue of law. This gives depth to ‘the gates of hell shall not prevail’ — a contest of authorities, court against court. The gate is where standing was established and verdicts were rendered.

root.sense: a gate; the city gate, the seat of law and judgment

79.courtroomWord: A venue term — the courthouse of the city, where cases were tried.
79.itsRole: Justice had a place, and it was the gate — where elders sat, witnesses gathered, contracts were sealed, and verdicts were pronounced. To take a matter to the gate was to take it to court. The gate is the venue of law, and the imagery of contending gates is a contest of jurisdictions. Where the gate is, judgment is rendered.

proofTexts.text: Then went Boaz up to the gate, and sat him down.
proofTexts.note: Legal business transacted at the gate.

proofTexts.text: Unto the elders of his city, and unto the gate.
Establish judgment in the gate.
proofTexts.note: Justice done in the venue of law.

proofTexts.text: Her husband is known in the gates, when he sitteth among the elders.
proofTexts.note: The gate as the seat of the magistrates.

plainTerms: The gate was the city’s courthouse — where elders judged cases, witnesses gathered, and contracts were sealed. ‘Judgment in the gate’ means justice done in court. It was the legal center of the town.
bringItHome: When a dispute needed settling in an ancient city, everyone went to the gate — the elders sat there, cases were heard there, deals were witnessed there. It was the courthouse. So ‘judgment in the gate’ is simply ‘justice in court,’ and warring gates are warring authorities.

courtroomRoles.does: sit in the gate to judge.
bring their case to the gate.
the court where standing is set and verdicts rendered.

81.lead: The hand is power, custody, and jurisdiction. To be ‘delivered into the hand’ of an enemy is to pass under legal control (Judges 2:14); to be redeemed ‘out of the hand’ is release from custody (Exodus 6:6). The hand is the reach of authority, the sphere in which one holds jurisdiction over persons and property. This is why placing a matter ‘in the hand’ of a mediator, or a life ‘in thy hand,’ is entrusting it to that party’s legal power. The body’s hand becomes the law’s shorthand for who holds control — whose jurisdiction a person or a thing currently falls under.

root.sense: hand; power, control, custody, jurisdiction

81.courtroomWord: A jurisdiction term — the reach of authority; whose control a person or thing is under.
81.itsRole: Custody and control are spoken as ‘the hand.’ To fall into a hand is to pass under jurisdiction; to be redeemed from a hand is to be released from it. The hand marks who holds legal power over a person or property at any moment. To commit something into the hand of another is to transfer it to that party’s authority. It is the law’s shorthand for control.

proofTexts.text: He delivered them into the hands of spoilers.
I will rid you out of their bondage... and I will redeem you.
proofTexts.note: Release from the hand of the oppressor.

proofTexts.text: Neither is there any that can deliver out of my hand.
Into thine hand I commit my spirit.
proofTexts.note: Committing a matter to another’s authority.

plainTerms: The hand, in Scripture, means power and control — whose custody you are in. Delivered ‘into the hand’ of an enemy means under their control; redeemed ‘out of the hand’ means released. To put something ‘in the hand’ of another is to give them authority over it.
bringItHome: ‘In the hand of’ is simply ‘under the control of.’ To be in an enemy’s hand is to be in his custody; to be pulled out of his hand is to be freed. And to commit your spirit into Yahuah’s hand is to place yourself under His authority — the safest custody there is.

courtroomRoles.does: out of whose hand none can deliver; into whose hand one commits himself.
whose hand holds control for a time.
under whichever jurisdiction currently holds it.

83.lead: In Scripture the face is presence before authority — the standing to appear. To ‘seek the face’ of Yahuah is to petition the court for audience; to have Him ‘hide his face’ is to be denied a hearing (Psalm 27:9). To appear ‘before the face’ is a legal presentation, an entrance into the presence of the one who decides. This is why the priests bore the tribes’ names before Yahuah and the bread of the Presence sat before His face — the language is of parties represented in court. The blessing “Yahuah make his face shine upon thee” (Numbers 6:25) is a plea for favorable audience before the bench.

root.sense: face, presence; the front, the standing to appear before

sharesRoot.note: Nasa panim — ‘to lift the face’ — shares panim: appearing before the face (audience) and lifting the face (partiality) are two courtroom uses of the same word.

83.courtroomWord: A presence term — the standing to appear before the one who decides.
83.itsRole: To come before the face is to be granted audience by the court; to be shut from it is to be denied a hearing. Presence before Yahuah is a legal presentation, not a mood of closeness. The priest represents the tribes before the face; the petitioner seeks the face; the blessing asks the face to shine — favorable audience granted. The face is where standing to appear is exercised.

proofTexts.text: Yahuah make his face shine upon thee.
Hide not thy face far from me.
proofTexts.note: The fear of being denied a hearing.

proofTexts.text: Thou canst not see my face... and live.
proofTexts.note: The weight of standing before the Presence.

proofTexts.text: That seek thy face, O Elohim of Jacob.

plainTerms: The face, in Scripture, is presence and audience — the standing to appear before Yahuah. To seek His face is to ask for a hearing; to have Him hide it is to be denied one. It is courtroom language, not romance.
bringItHome: To come ‘before the face’ of a king was to be granted an audience — admitted into his presence to make your case. That is what seeking Yahuah’s face means: the standing to appear before the Judge. And when the blessing asks His face to shine on you, it asks for a favorable hearing.

courtroomRoles.role: the One before whom one appears
courtroomRoles.does: grants or hides audience.
seeks the face, exercises standing to appear.
bears the people’s names before the face.

85.lead: The footstool is dominion and subjugation — the defeated placed lawfully under the ruler’s feet. “Until I make thine enemies thy footstool” (Psalm 110:1) is a declaration of total jurisdiction: the conquered reduced to the ruler’s possession, under his authority in the most literal posture. The earth called Yahuah’s footstool (Isaiah 66:1) declares His dominion over it. The image is legal as much as martial — conquest converted into settled, rightful rule. To be made a footstool is to be brought fully under another’s lawful authority, the contest ended and the jurisdiction absolute.

root.sense: a footstool; that placed under the feet

85.courtroomWord: A dominion term — the subjugated placed under the ruler’s lawful authority.
85.itsRole: When a contest for authority ends, the loser is placed under the victor’s feet — not merely defeated but brought under jurisdiction. The footstool marks that settled dominion. ‘Sit at my right hand until I make thine enemies thy footstool’ hands the enthroned One total authority over every rival, the subjugation lawful and complete. To be a footstool is to be under absolute, rightful rule.

proofTexts.text: Until I make thine enemies thy footstool.
The earth is my footstool.
Till he hath put all enemies under his feet.
Till his enemies be made his footstool.

plainTerms: A footstool is what is placed under the ruler’s feet — the defeated brought fully under his authority. ‘Enemies made a footstool’ means total, settled dominion, not just a won battle. The earth as Yahuah’s footstool declares He rules it all.
bringItHome: An ancient king would rest his feet on the necks of the conquered — the picture of a contest ended and authority made absolute. That is the footstool: not just defeat, but subjugation under lawful rule. ‘Enemies made thy footstool’ hands the King total jurisdiction.

courtroomRoles.does: places every rival under lawful dominion.
given total jurisdiction over His enemies.
brought fully under rightful authority.

89.lead: Not a mood, not a metaphor — a plaintiff. The first time blood appears as a wrong, Yahuah tells Cain, “the voice of thy brother’s blood crieth unto me from the ground” (Genesis 4:10). Blood has a voice, and that voice files a case demanding justice. That is why innocent blood and the avenger of blood sit at the heart of Torah’s justice system — spilled blood is a legal claim the court must answer. Hold that against Hebrews 12:24, where Yahushua’s blood “speaketh better things than that of Abel.” Abel’s blood cried for judgment; this blood is the price Yahuah Himself provided to answer the court — the claim met, the docket cleared. Even the tree is filed under evidence.

root.sense: blood; the life, and the legal claim that shed blood makes

89.courtroomWord: A plaintiff — shed blood is a legal claim that cries for justice and must be answered.
89.itsRole: In Torah, blood is not symbol but standing: it cries, it accuses, it demands satisfaction, and the court is bound to answer it. The whole apparatus of innocent blood, the avenger, and the cities of refuge exists because blood files a case. At the tree the claim is answered not by the guilty but by the price Yahuah provided — a blood that speaks better things, satisfying the court and clearing the docket.

proofTexts.text: The voice of thy brother’s blood crieth unto me from the ground.
proofTexts.note: Blood as a plaintiff filing a case.

proofTexts.text: The blood... that speaketh better things than that of Abel.
proofTexts.note: A blood that answers rather than accuses.

proofTexts.text: It is the blood that maketh an atonement for the soul.
Blood... defileth the land... it cannot be cleansed... but by the blood of him that shed it.
proofTexts.note: The legal weight of shed blood.

plainTerms: Blood in Scripture is a plaintiff, not a picture. Shed blood cries out and demands justice; the court has to answer it.
At the tree, the claim was answered by the price Yahuah provided — a blood that speaks something better than Abel’s: satisfaction, not accusation.
bringItHome: Abel’s blood cried from the ground for justice, and the court heard it. Every drop of innocent blood since has filed the same case. Then a blood is offered that does not cry for judgment but answers it — the price the Judge Himself provided. The docket clears. Even the tree, in this reading, is filed under evidence.

courtroomRoles.does: cries for justice and files the case.
provides the price that answers the claim.
whose blood speaks better things than Abel’s.

90.lead: A cry is the legal appeal of the oppressed to a higher court. The cry of the wronged is not merely emotional noise; it is a petition Yahuah’s court is bound to hear: “if thou afflict them in any wise, and they cry at all unto me, I will surely hear their cry” (Exodus 22:23). Abel’s blood cries; Sodom’s victims cry; the laborer’s withheld wages cry (James 5:4). A cry is a case lodged with the highest bench, and the response is judicial: the court takes it up and acts. To cry out is to file an appeal that cannot be ignored.

root.sense: to cry out, to call for help; to lodge an appeal against wrong

90.courtroomWord: An appeal term — the petition of the wronged that the court is bound to hear.
90.itsRole: The oppressed have recourse: the cry. It is not venting but filing — a legal appeal that reaches the highest bench and obligates it to respond. Yahuah binds Himself to hear the cry of the afflicted; the shed blood, the defrauded laborer, the wronged widow all cry, and the court acts. A cry is an appeal that cannot be dismissed.

proofTexts.text: If they cry at all unto me, I will surely hear their cry.
proofTexts.note: The appeal the court must answer.

proofTexts.text: The voice of thy brother’s blood crieth unto me.
The cry of Sodom and Gomorrah is great.
proofTexts.note: The cry of the wronged reaching the bench.

proofTexts.text: The cries of them which have reaped are entered into the ears of the Lord.

plainTerms: A cry, in Scripture, is a legal appeal — the wronged calling to a higher court. Yahuah binds Himself to hear it. It is not just emotion; it is a case filed that the court must answer.
bringItHome: When the powerless have nowhere else to turn, they cry out — and that cry is not lost in the air. It is an appeal lodged with the highest court, and the Judge has bound Himself to hear it. Abel’s blood, the cheated worker, the afflicted widow — each cry is a case, and the court acts.

courtroomRoles.does: lodges the cry against the wrong.
bound to hear the cry and act.
the injustice the cry brings to the bench.

91.lead: Betrothal is a binding legal contract preceding the wedding — so firm that breaking it required a formal bill of divorce, and violating a betrothed woman carried the penalty of adultery (Deuteronomy 22:23-24). It was covenant, not courtship. This is why Yahuah says to Israel, “I will betroth thee unto me for ever... in righteousness, and in judgment” (Hosea 2:19) — the vocabulary of a ratified engagement with legal force, sworn in the language of the court. To be betrothed is to be legally bound before the union is consummated, held to the contract from the moment it is cut.

root.sense: to betroth, to engage by binding contract

91.courtroomWord: A contract term — the binding engagement that precedes and secures the marriage.
91.itsRole: A covenant is often bound before it is consummated, and betrothal is that binding — the contract cut, the parties held to it, the penalties already in force. Yahuah’s betrothal of His people is spoken in exactly these legal terms: a pledge in righteousness and judgment, secured before the wedding. To be betrothed is already to belong, under contract.

proofTexts.text: I will betroth thee unto me for ever... in righteousness, and in judgment.
proofTexts.note: The binding pledge in legal terms.

proofTexts.text: The damsel, because... a betrothed wife.
proofTexts.note: The contract’s force before the wedding — its violation judged as adultery.

proofTexts.text: What man is there that hath betrothed a wife, and hath not taken her?
proofTexts.note: The betrothed bond recognized at law.

proofTexts.text: I have espoused you to one husband.
proofTexts.note: The assembly betrothed to the Messiah.

plainTerms: Betrothal was a binding engagement — a real contract before the wedding, so serious that breaking it took a divorce. Yahuah ‘betroths’ His people in the language of law: bound to Him before the union is complete.
bringItHome: In that world the contract was signed long before the wedding day — and from that moment the two belonged to each other, held to every term. That is betrothal: not a promise to maybe marry, but a binding bond already in force. Yahuah pledges His people exactly so — already His, under contract.

courtroomRoles.does: pledges the bond in righteousness and judgment.
bound from the moment the contract is cut.
in force before the wedding, penalties attached.

92.lead: A bride is a covenant party bound by the marriage contract — holding the rights and duties the covenant assigns, not merely a beloved figure. The assembly pictured as bride is a legal spouse under a ratified bond (Revelation 21:2, 9). The term fixes standing: a bride has claims on her husband and obligations to him, secured by the marriage covenant. This is why the marriage imagery is never merely sentimental in Scripture — it invokes a contract with terms, fidelity clauses, and consequences for breach. To be the bride is to be a party to the covenant, with everything a covenant confers and requires.

root.sense: bride, daughter-in-law; a party to the marriage covenant

92.courtroomWord: A covenant-party term — the bound spouse holding the marriage covenant’s rights and duties.
92.itsRole: Marriage is a covenant, and the bride is a party to it — with enforceable claims and binding obligations. When the assembly is called the bride, it is placed under a ratified bond, not merely admired. The status carries rights (the husband’s provision and protection) and duties (fidelity to the bond), and the covenant defines both.

proofTexts.text: The bride, the Lamb’s wife.
As the bridegroom rejoiceth over the bride, so shall thy Elohim rejoice over thee.
proofTexts.note: The covenant bond in marriage terms.

proofTexts.text: The love of thine espousals, when thou wentest after me.
This is a great mystery... concerning Messiah and the assembly.
proofTexts.note: The marriage covenant as the pattern.

plainTerms: A bride is a party to the marriage covenant — with real claims on her husband and real duties to him. When Scripture calls the assembly the bride, it is naming a legal bond with terms, not just a warm relationship.
bringItHome: A bride is not merely beloved — she is a party to a contract, with rights she can claim and duties she owes, all secured by the covenant. That is the assembly as bride: bound to the Messiah by a ratified bond, provided for and answerable, under terms.

courtroomRoles.does: holds the marriage covenant’s rights and duties.
owes provision and protection under the bond.
defines the claims and obligations of both.

94.lead: Adultery is covenant infidelity — a breach of the marriage contract carrying legal penalty. The prophets charge Israel’s idolatry as adultery precisely because it violates a ratified bond: “thou hast played the whore with many lovers” (Jeremiah 3:1). The word names contract-breaking, not merely lust. To commit adultery is to violate the exclusivity clause of a covenant, and Torah treats it as an offense against the bond itself — tried, in the prophets, as a case in the covenant court.

root.sense: to commit adultery; to break the marriage covenant

94.courtroomWord: A breach term — the violation of the marriage covenant’s exclusivity clause.
94.itsRole: A covenant carries terms, and marriage carries the term of exclusivity. Adultery is its breach — actionable, penalized, and in the prophets, prosecuted. When Scripture calls idolatry adultery, it is not a loose metaphor; it is a charge of covenant-breaking brought against a bound party.

proofTexts.text: Thou shalt not commit adultery.
I had put her away, and given her a bill of divorce.
proofTexts.note: The breach answered by legal dissolution.

proofTexts.text: As a wife that committeth adultery, which taketh strangers instead of her husband.
Let her put away her whoredoms.

plainTerms: Adultery is breaking the marriage covenant — violating the promise to belong to one. Scripture calls idolatry adultery because it breaks the same kind of bond with Yahuah. It is contract-breaking, and it is actionable.
bringItHome: A signed marriage covenant has one non-negotiable clause: no other. Break it and you have not merely wandered in feeling — you have breached a contract, and the court can act. Israel’s idols were charged exactly so: not a mood, a breach.

courtroomRoles.does: the covenant party whose exclusivity is breached.
charged with covenant-breaking.
the bond whose clause is violated.

95.lead: Divorce is the formal legal dissolution of the marriage covenant by written instrument — the ‘bill of divorcement,’ a document that severs a contract (Deuteronomy 24:1). Divorce in Scripture is paperwork, a legal act with a legal record, not a mere parting. Yahuah frames His judgment on Israel in exactly these terms: “I had put her away, and given her a bill of divorce” (Jeremiah 3:8). The covenant, being a legal bond, could only be dissolved by a legal act. This is why the word carries such weight — it marks the official termination of a ratified relationship, entered by document, with standing consequences for both parties.

root.sense: a cutting off, i.e. divorce; the bill of divorcement, from karath (H3772), to cut

sharesRoot.note: Kriythuth is a ‘cutting,’ from the same root H3772: the covenant cut (Cut), the sinner cut off (Karath), and here the marriage bond cut.

95.courtroomWord: A dissolution term — the written instrument that legally severs the marriage covenant.
95.itsRole: A covenant made by a legal act can be ended only by a legal act, and divorce is that act for marriage: a written bill that severs the bond and records the severance. It is not walking away but filing — a document with standing consequences. Yahuah’s dealing with unfaithful Israel is cast in exactly this legal register: a bill of divorce issued for covenant-breaking.

proofTexts.text: Then let him write her a bill of divorcement.
I had put her away, and given her a bill of divorce.
proofTexts.note: The covenant dissolved by legal act.

proofTexts.text: Where is the bill of your mother’s divorcement?
proofTexts.note: The document as the proof of severance.

proofTexts.text: Yahuah... saith that he hateth putting away.

plainTerms: Divorce is the legal end of a marriage covenant — by a written bill, not just by leaving. It is paperwork that severs a contract. Even Yahuah’s judgment on unfaithful Israel is described as issuing a bill of divorce.
bringItHome: A marriage covenant, being a legal bond, could not just be abandoned — it had to be cut by a document, the bill of divorcement, filed and recorded. That is divorce: the official severing of a ratified bond. The same ‘cutting’ root runs through covenant, being cut off, and this.

courtroomRoles.does: severs the bond by written instrument.
released and recorded as such.
the document that dissolves the covenant.

98.lead: Chesed is the covenant obligation of steadfast kindness owed between bound parties — loyalty a covenant partner is duty-bound to show, not random benevolence. Chesed is the faithfulness that keeps covenant even when it costs, the kindness that flows from obligation rather than mood. “That I may shew him kindness for Jonathan’s sake” (2 Samuel 9:1) is David honoring a covenant already sworn. When Scripture says Yahuah’s chesed endures forever, it declares His covenant loyalty unbreakable. It is a legal-relational term: the reliable, obligated faithfulness a bond requires of the parties within it.

root.sense: covenant loyalty, steadfast love, obligated kindness

98.courtroomWord: A covenant-duty term — the loyal kindness bound parties owe each other.
98.itsRole: A covenant creates obligations, and chesed is the obligation of loyal kindness within it. It is not sentiment but duty — the faithfulness a party is bound to show because the bond requires it. Yahuah’s chesed is His covenant-keeping, reliable and enduring; the believer’s chesed is the loyalty owed back. It is love as covenant fidelity, expected the way faithfulness to a bond is expected.

proofTexts.text: That I may shew him kindness for Jonathan’s sake.
proofTexts.note: Chesed rendered on a sworn covenant.

proofTexts.text: To love mercy, and to walk humbly with thy Elohim.
His mercy endureth for ever.
I desired mercy, and not sacrifice.

plainTerms: Chesed is covenant loyalty — the steadfast kindness bound parties owe each other. It is not a random nice feeling; it is faithfulness you are duty-bound to show because of the bond. Yahuah’s chesed is His covenant-keeping, and it never fails.
bringItHome: Two people swear a covenant, and years later one keeps it at cost to himself — not because he feels like it, but because he is bound. That is chesed: loyalty that holds because the bond holds. Yahuah’s toward His people never runs out.

courtroomRoles.does: shows chesed as unbreakable covenant loyalty.
owes chesed back within the bond.
the ground that makes the kindness an obligation.

99.lead: Favor is a favorable disposition or ruling extended toward one who holds no claim to it. To ‘find favor in the eyes’ of a king or a judge is to receive what could not be demanded — an outcome granted from above, not owed from below (Esther 5:2; Genesis 6:8). Favor is unearned standing bestowed by one with the authority to bestow it. This is the clean Hebrew sense underneath the softer modern word: not a warm feeling, but a ruling in one’s favor that the recipient could not have compelled. Favor is the court inclining toward a party out of the judge’s own good will, apart from merit.

root.sense: favor, grace, acceptance; a favorable disposition granted

99.courtroomWord: A disposition term — a favorable inclination or ruling granted apart from merit.
99.itsRole: Some outcomes cannot be demanded, only granted — and favor is the granting. To find favor is to receive a favorable ruling one had no standing to require, extended by an authority free to extend it. Noah found favor; Esther obtained favor; the recipient contributes nothing but the finding. Favor is the court’s own goodwill, inclining toward a party who could not compel it.

proofTexts.text: But Noah found grace in the eyes of Yahuah.
She obtained favour in his sight.
proofTexts.note: The favorable disposition of the one in authority.

proofTexts.text: Thou hast found grace in my sight.
