So shalt thou find favour... in the sight of Elohim and man.

plainTerms: Favor is a favorable ruling you could not demand — granted from above out of the giver’s goodwill, not owed to you. It is the clean sense under the softer word ‘grace’: not a feeling, but the court inclining toward you apart from what you earned.
bringItHome: Esther could not demand the king’s welcome — she could only find favor, and he extended the scepter. That is favor: a favorable ruling granted by one free to grant it, to someone with no claim to require it. Noah found it in Yahuah’s eyes the same way.

courtroomRoles.does: extends favor out of His own goodwill.
granted standing he could not demand.
the favorable ruling, unearned.

100.lead: Faithful means fidelity to the terms of the bond — reliability that holds under testing, the trait a court can count on. A faithful party keeps covenant when keeping it is costly; emunah is steadfastness proven, not merely intended. “Know therefore that Yahuah thy Elohim... keepeth covenant and mercy” (Deuteronomy 7:9) grounds His faithfulness in covenant-keeping. To be faithful is to be contractually dependable — to render what one is bound to render, consistently, so the other party may rely on it. This is why the faithful are commended and the unfaithful charged: fidelity to the bond is the very thing the covenant measures.

root.sense: firmness, steadfastness, fidelity; faithfulness that can be relied upon

100.courtroomWord: A fidelity term — proven reliability in keeping the terms of the bond.
100.itsRole: A covenant is only as good as the parties’ faithfulness to it, and emunah is that faithfulness — tested, proven, dependable. Yahuah’s faithfulness is His covenant-keeping; the believer’s is the loyalty the bond requires in return. It is measured by conduct under pressure, which is why the walk is where faithfulness is shown. The faithful are those the court can rely on to keep terms.

proofTexts.text: The faithful Elohim, which keepeth covenant.
Great is thy faithfulness.
He that is faithful in that which is least is faithful also in much.
Be thou faithful unto death.

plainTerms: Faithful means reliable to the bond — keeping the terms even when it costs. Yahuah’s faithfulness is His covenant-keeping; ours is the loyalty owed back. It shows up in conduct under pressure, which is why the walk is where it is proven.
bringItHome: A faithful party is one you can count on when it is hard — who keeps the agreement when breaking it would be easier. That is emunah. Yahuah is faithful in exactly that way: He keeps covenant. And the walk of this life is where our own faithfulness is tested and shown.

courtroomRoles.does: keeps covenant, reliable without fail.
owes faithfulness back, proven in the walk.
the terms faithfulness keeps.

102.lead: An account is two things at once — the record kept and the reckoning demanded for it. “Every one of us shall give account of himself to Yahuah” (Romans 14:12) summons each party to answer for the ledger that bears his name. The unprofitable steward is told, “give an account of thy stewardship” (Luke 16:2) — produce the books, answer for the balance. In the court of heaven the entries are real and the audit is coming; an account is a balance owed and examined, not a vague impression of a life.

root.sense: a word, reckoning, account; the statement rendered and the reckoning required

102.courtroomWord: A ledger term — the record of a matter and the formal answer required for it.
102.itsRole: The books are open, and every party is called to answer for his own. An account is not settled by sentiment; it is audited entry by entry. The sober weight of the word is that a day is appointed when each gives account — the record read back, the balance addressed.

proofTexts.text: Every one of us shall give account of himself to Yahuah.
proofTexts.note: Each answers for his own ledger.

proofTexts.text: Give an account of thy stewardship.
proofTexts.note: Produce the books; answer for the balance.

proofTexts.text: All things are naked and opened unto the eyes of him with whom we have to do.
They shall give account thereof in the day of judgment.

plainTerms: An account is both the record and the answer you give for it. The books are open, and a day is set when each person answers for his own — entry by entry, not in general.
bringItHome: A steward runs the estate all year, then the owner returns and says: bring the books. Not “tell me how it felt” — bring the books. That is an account: the record laid open and answered for. The court of heaven keeps one for every life.

courtroomRoles.does: before whom each gives account of himself.
answerable for the balance on the books.
read back, entry by entry.

114.lead: The avenger of blood is the executor of the court’s sentence — the kinsman charged to require shed blood once guilt had been lawfully established. He was no vigilante: he could act only after the congregation judged, and only against one found guilty of intentional killing (Numbers 35:19-24). The same law that empowered him restrained him, hedging his role with the cities of refuge and the requirement of trial. The goel ha-dam shows that even the requiring of blood was legally regulated — justice executed, not private revenge, by the party the law appointed.

root.sense: kinsman-redeemer, one with the right to act for a relative
blood; the life that cries for justice

114.courtroomWord: An executor term — the officer who carries out the blood-sentence, within the law’s limits.
114.itsRole: A verdict must be executed, and the law appointed who executes the blood-sentence — the kinsman, but only after judgment and only against established guilt. The cities of refuge stand as the check: the accused is protected until tried. The avenger is thus an officer of the court, not a free hand — his power defined and fenced by the same statute that grants it.

proofTexts.text: The revenger of blood himself shall slay the murderer.
That the manslayer die not, until he stand before the congregation in judgment.
Then the congregation shall judge between the slayer and the revenger of blood.
proofTexts.note: The court, not the kinsman, decides guilt.

proofTexts.text: Lest the avenger of the blood pursue... while his heart is hot.

plainTerms: The avenger of blood carried out the death-sentence for murder — but only the kinsman, only after a real trial, and only against proven intentional killing. The cities of refuge kept him from acting on his own. He was an officer of the law, not a vigilante.
bringItHome: A man is killed, and the nearest kinsman has a duty — but not a free hand. He cannot strike until the assembly has judged and guilt is proven; until then the accused sits safe in a city of refuge. That is the avenger of blood: even vengeance was put under law, executed by an officer, not a mob.

courtroomRoles.does: carries out the blood-sentence, within limits.
judges guilt before any execution.
protected in refuge until tried.
both empowers and restrains the avenger.

116.lead: A cause is the legal case itself — the matter in dispute before the court. “Judge me, O Yahuah... plead my cause” (Psalm 43:1) asks the bench to rule on a filed claim, not to console a feeling. A rib is a controversy formally lodged, awaiting adjudication. This is why Yahuah is repeatedly asked to “maintain the cause” of the afflicted and the poor (Psalm 140:12) — to take their case and see it justly decided. The cause is the substance of the suit, the thing the court exists to settle.

root.sense: a dispute, controversy, legal case; the matter contended before the court

sharesRoot.note: The case and the arguing of it share the root: the cause (rib, the matter) and to plead (rib, to contend it before the bench).

116.courtroomWord: A case term — the controversy formally lodged for the court to decide.
116.itsRole: A court exists to settle causes — real disputes brought for judgment. To have a cause is to have a claim on the docket; to have it maintained is to have the court take it up and rule. The afflicted appeal to Yahuah to judge their cause because the case is real and the bench is just. The cause is what the trial is about.

proofTexts.text: Judge me, O Yahuah... and plead my cause.
proofTexts.note: The case brought for a ruling.

proofTexts.text: Yahuah will maintain the cause of the afflicted.
proofTexts.note: The court taking up the case.

proofTexts.text: He shall plead my cause, and execute judgment for me.
proofTexts.note: The cause argued to a verdict.

proofTexts.text: Yahuah will plead their cause.
proofTexts.note: The poor’s case taken by the bench.

plainTerms: A cause is the actual case before the court — the dispute to be decided. To ask Yahuah to ‘judge my cause’ is to ask Him to rule on a real claim, not to soothe a feeling.
bringItHome: Every trial is about something — a specific dispute lodged for decision. That is the cause. When the afflicted cry ‘judge my cause,’ they are not asking for comfort; they are asking the Judge to take their case and rule. And He does.

courtroomRoles.does: brings the cause for judgment.
maintains and decides the cause.
the dispute the court exists to settle.

117.lead: To accuse is to file the formal indictment — to name the charge and open the trial. It is the prosecutor’s act, not the gossip’s: kategoreo lodges a case before the bench. Scripture shows the accuser at work “before our Elohim day and night” (Revelation 12:10), pressing the guilt of the brethren without rest. Accusation presupposes a law to accuse under; strike the standard and the charge has nothing to name. And the good news sits in the same verse — the accuser is cast down, the indictment thrown out.

root.sense: to speak against, to bring a charge, to accuse formally in court

sharesRoot.note: The verb and the party who does it share the kateg- root: to accuse (kategoreo) and the accuser (kategoros) who files the charge.

117.courtroomWord: An indictment term — the formal lodging of a charge that opens the trial.
117.itsRole: A lawful accusation names a real breach under a real law and submits it to be tested. In the court of heaven the accuser files without rest, but the charge stands only if it can be proved and left unanswered. Against the believer it is answered — an Advocate pleads, the account is paid, and the indictment is dismissed.

proofTexts.text: The accuser of our brethren... accused them before our Elohim day and night.
There is one that accuseth you, even Moses.
proofTexts.note: The law itself accuses where it is broken.

proofTexts.text: Who shall lay any thing to the charge of Yahuah’s elect?
proofTexts.note: The challenge to any accuser of the acquitted.

proofTexts.text: They began to accuse him.
proofTexts.note: The formal charge lodged against Yahushua.

plainTerms: To accuse is to file a charge in court and open a case — not just to complain. Every accusation assumes a law that was broken. Against the delivered, the charge is answered and dropped.
bringItHome: A prosecutor stands and reads the indictment — count by count, all night, every night. That is the accuser of the brethren. But defense counsel rises with a paid receipt, and the judge strikes the charge. Accusation only wins where the account is still open.

courtroomRoles.does: files the charge and presses the case.
answers the charge for the accused.
before whom it is lodged, and who dismisses it.

119.lead: Guilty means liable — owing restitution, under the court’s finding of fault. Asham names both the guilt incurred and the offering that answers it: the trespass that creates a debt and the sacrifice that discharges it (Leviticus 5:6). To be guilty is not merely to feel bad but to carry a liability the law has assessed, a balance owed to the offended party or to Yahuah. This is why the guilt-offering involved restitution plus a fifth (Leviticus 6:5) — guilt is a measurable legal debt. To be found asham is to stand adjudged in the wrong, owing what the law requires until the debt is lawfully settled.

root.sense: guilt, guiltiness; also the guilt-offering that answers it

119.courtroomWord: A liability term — the finding of fault and the debt it creates.
119.itsRole: Guilt is not a feeling but a legal status: fault found, liability assessed, a debt owed until settled. Remarkably, the same word names the guilt and the offering that clears it — guilt is measurable, and it has a remedy. The guilty owe restitution, sometimes with a fifth added; the account must be squared. To be guilty is to stand adjudged liable, awaiting lawful discharge.

proofTexts.text: He shall bring his trespass offering.
proofTexts.note: The guilt, and the offering that answers it.

proofTexts.text: He shall... restore it... and shall add the fifth part more thereto.
Recompense his trespass with the principal thereof.
He is guilty of all.
proofTexts.note: The finding of fault under the whole standard.

plainTerms: Guilty means legally liable — found at fault and owing a debt, not just feeling bad. The same Hebrew word means both the guilt and the offering that clears it, because guilt is measurable and has a remedy. The guilty owe restitution until the account is squared.
bringItHome: To be found guilty is to be handed a bill — the fault assessed, the debt fixed, sometimes with a penalty added. It is not a mood; it is a liability. And the mercy is that the same word points to the remedy: the offering that answers the guilt and clears the account.

courtroomRoles.does: found liable, owing the debt.
assesses the fault and requires the settlement.
the sacrifice that answers the liability.

123.lead: Eretz gezerah is the decreed land of cutting-off — the ‘land not inhabited’ to which the scapegoat was sent on Yom Kippur, “bearing upon him all their iniquities unto a land not inhabited” (Leviticus 16:22). Gezerah comes from a root meaning to cut, to decree, to separate; eretz is land. Together they name a place fixed by decree as the destination of what is cut off — a legal banishment, sin carried out of the camp to a severed place. It is the executed sentence of separation, the removal of guilt to a land set apart for it by the court’s decree.

root.sense: land, earth, country
a cutting off, a decreed separation; from gazar, to cut, to decree

123.courtroomWord: A banishment term — the decreed place to which what is cut off is removed.
123.itsRole: A sentence of separation needs a destination, and eretz gezerah is it: the decreed land where the cut-off is sent. On Yom Kippur the scapegoat carries the iniquities out to this severed place — guilt removed from the camp by decree, not merely forgotten. It pictures the executed sentence of separation: the charge carried away to a land fixed for it, out of the presence of the holy.

proofTexts.text: The goat shall bear upon him all their iniquities unto a land not inhabited.
To let him go for a scapegoat into the wilderness.
So far hath he removed our transgressions from us.
proofTexts.note: Guilt removed to a severed distance.

proofTexts.text: Thou wilt cast all their sins into the depths of the sea.

plainTerms: Eretz gezerah is the ‘cut-off land’ — the uninhabited place the scapegoat was sent to on Yom Kippur, carrying the people’s sins away. It pictures guilt removed by decree, carried out of the camp to a place set apart for it. It is a sentence of separation, executed.
bringItHome: On the Day of Atonement one goat did not die — it was sent away, carrying the nation’s guilt out to a barren, decreed land, never to return. That is eretz gezerah: the place of cutting-off, where what is condemned is carried and left. Sin is not merely pardoned in the camp; it is removed to a severed place by decree.

courtroomRoles.does: decrees the separation and the place of removal.
carries the iniquities to the cut-off land.
removed from the camp to the decreed place.

127.lead: Din is the Aramaic word for the court session and the verdict it issues — judgment as both the proceeding and its ruling. In Daniel’s vision, “the judgment was set” (Daniel 7:10) uses this legal register: the court convened, the case heard, the sentence handed down. Din is not a private opinion or a mood of disapproval; it is the formal act of a bench in session. When the Ancient of Days sits, the din begins, and from it dominion is given and taken. It is the courtroom itself, named.

root.sense: judgment; the court and its verdict (Aramaic)

127.courtroomWord: A court term — the session convened and the verdict it renders.
127.itsRole: A trial is a proceeding that ends in a ruling, and din names both. When din is set, the bench is in session and a verdict is coming. In Daniel 7 the din is the hinge of the whole vision: the court sits, the books open, judgment is rendered, and the contested kingdoms are decided. Din is the formal machinery of judgment, not a feeling about right and wrong.

proofTexts.text: The judgment was set, and the books were opened.
Judgment was given to the saints of the most High.
proofTexts.note: The verdict rendered for His people.

proofTexts.text: The judgment shall sit, and they shall take away his dominion.
proofTexts.note: The ruling that strips the usurper.

proofTexts.text: Let judgment be executed speedily upon him.

plainTerms: Din is the Aramaic word for the court itself — the session and the verdict together. When Daniel says ‘the judgment was set,’ he means the bench convened and a ruling was coming. It is the courtroom in session, not a private opinion.
bringItHome: In Daniel 7 the whole scene turns on one moment: the court sits. That is the din — the session opened, the books read, the verdict handed down. From that bench, kingdoms are decided and dominion changes hands. It is judgment as a formal act, not a feeling.

courtroomRoles.does: convenes the din and renders the verdict.
for whom judgment is given.
whose dominion the din takes away.

129.lead: In Daniel's court the verdict does not merely punish — it strips. Sholtan is jurisdiction, the legal right to rule; heedayah is its removal, the bench recalling an authority that was seized or expired. “The judgment shall sit, and they shall take away his dominion, to consume and to destroy it unto the end” (Daniel 7:26). This is not conquest by force but a ruling from the seat: the right to govern, revoked. Every power that reigns does so on a lease, and the Ancient of Days holds the deed.

root.sense: to pass over, remove, take away (Aramaic)
dominion, jurisdiction, the right to rule (Aramaic)

129.courtroomWord: A jurisdiction term — the court's power to revoke the right to rule. Not violence; a ruling that cancels a mandate.
129.itsRole: In the true court all dominion is granted and revocable. Heedayah sholtan is the moment the bench recalls it — the horn that had made war with the saints (Daniel 7:21) has its jurisdiction consumed when the court sits. The counterfeit runs the other way: a power strips a standing it was never given the right to strip, and seats itself. The true revoking is the answer to the false seizing.

proofTexts.text: The judgment shall sit, and they shall take away his dominion.
proofTexts.note: Jurisdiction revoked from the bench, not the battlefield.

proofTexts.text: They had their dominion taken away, yet their lives were prolonged.
proofTexts.note: The right to rule removed while the party remains.

proofTexts.text: There was given him dominion... an everlasting dominion.
proofTexts.note: The true grant — given to the Son of man by the Ancient of Days, received, not seized.

proofTexts.text: The kingdom is departed from thee.
proofTexts.note: Jurisdiction pulled from a ruler who called it his own.

plainTerms: Dominion is the right to rule, and it is always on loan. Heedayah sholtan is the day the loan is called in — the court taking back the authority a power thought it owned. No army does it; a verdict does.
bringItHome: A steward runs the estate for years and starts calling it his own. Then the owner returns, opens the books, and revokes his authority with a word — not a brawl, a ruling. That is heedayah sholtan: every throne that forgot it was leased has its lease canceled the moment the true Owner sits.

courtroomRoles.role: the Judge, the Ancient of Days
courtroomRoles.does: grants dominion, and revokes it from the seat.
ruled by seized authority; its jurisdiction consumed when the court sits.
the One to whom the true, everlasting dominion is given by the Ancient of Days.

130.lead: Daniel names the signature crime of the counterfeit power in two words: “he shall think to change times and laws” (Daniel 7:25). Zeman is the appointed time — the set seasons Yahuah fixed in the lights of heaven (Genesis 1:14); dath is the statute, the decree with binding force. To alter either is not reform; it is forgery. The horn does not abolish the law in the open — it edits it, moves the appointed times, rewrites the statute, and keeps the form while changing the substance. It is legislation by a power that was never the Lawgiver.

root.sense: appointed time, set season (Aramaic)
decree, edict, law with binding force (Aramaic)

130.courtroomWord: A tampering term — the unlawful editing of the statute and the calendar by a party with no authority to legislate.
130.itsRole: Only the Lawgiver may set the times and fix the law. In the break the counterfeit thinks to change them, assuming the Lawgiver's chair. The tell is subtle: not “the law is abolished” but “the law is amended” — the seventh day moved, the appointed feasts replaced, the reckoning of time reset. The court's answer stands in the same passage: the dominion of the one who changed the times is taken away (Daniel 7:26).

proofTexts.text: He shall think to change times and laws.
proofTexts.note: The counterfeit's signature — edit, do not openly abolish.

proofTexts.text: Let them be for signs, and for seasons.
proofTexts.note: The times fixed by Yahuah in sun and moon, not by man.

proofTexts.text: Ye shall not add unto the word... neither shall ye diminish.
proofTexts.note: The standing prohibition the horn violates.

proofTexts.text: The judgment shall sit, and they shall take away his dominion.
proofTexts.note: The tampering answered from the bench.

plainTerms: Zeman is Yahuah's calendar — His appointed times, set in the sun and moon. Dath is His law. To change either is not to update it; it is to counterfeit it.
The break's move is quiet: keep the religion, move the days, rewrite the rule, and few notice the signature was forged.
bringItHome: A forger does not tear up the contract — that would be caught. He changes a date, alters a clause, and passes it off as the original. Daniel's horn does exactly that with Yahuah's law: not abolished, just amended — the seventh day slid to another, the feasts swapped, the calendar reset. Same-looking document, different terms. And the court that sits in Daniel 7 revokes the forger's authority for it.

courtroomRoles.does: alone fixes the appointed times and the statute.
thinks to change what he had no right to touch.
sits, and takes the forger's dominion away.

131.lead: Attiq Yomin — the Ancient of Days — is the title of the presiding Judge, and in it seniority itself is standing. When Daniel’s court convenes, “the Ancient of days did sit... the judgment was set, and the books were opened” (Daniel 7:9-10). The name is not merely poetic age; it is jurisdictional. The One who was before every power that rose and will remain after every power falls holds the highest bench by right of being first and last. Every lesser throne is measured against His, and every dominion is granted or revoked from His seat.

root.sense: advanced in days, aged, venerable (Aramaic)
days (Aramaic)

131.courtroomWord: A title of the presiding Judge — seniority as the ground of supreme jurisdiction.
131.itsRole: The highest court needs the highest standing, and standing here is age without beginning. The Ancient of Days sits, and when He sits, the session opens and the books are read. From this bench dominion is given — to the Son of man, an everlasting dominion (Daniel 7:14) — and from it dominion is taken away. Every contested authority is settled when this Judge takes His seat.

proofTexts.text: The Ancient of days did sit, whose garment was white as snow.
The judgment was set, and the books were opened.
There was given him dominion... an everlasting dominion.
proofTexts.note: The Son of man receives the grant from the Ancient of Days — given, not seized.

proofTexts.text: The Ancient of days came, and judgment was given to the saints.
proofTexts.note: The verdict issued for His people.

plainTerms: The Ancient of Days is the presiding Judge — the One older than every kingdom, who holds the highest court by right of being first. When He sits, the trial begins and the records are opened. He gives dominion and He takes it away.
bringItHome: Every power in the room is young next to the One at the bench — kingdoms rise and fall, and He was there before the first and will be there after the last. That is the Ancient of Days: seniority that is jurisdiction. When He finally sits, the books open, and the contest over who rules is over.

courtroomRoles.role: the Ancient of Days, the presiding Judge
courtroomRoles.does: holds the highest bench; opens the session; gives and takes dominion.
receives the everlasting dominion from His hand.
for whom judgment is given.

133.lead: Synagoge means a gathering — a body assembled. The word is neutral until the question every court asks is put to it: by what standing? A lawful assembly is convened by authority; a counterfeit one convenes itself and claims the bench. Scripture marks the difference sharply, naming a “synagogue of Satan” — those “which say they are... and are not” (Revelation 2:9; 3:9). The break is not the gathering; it is the claim to a standing that was never granted — a body seated to teach and judge on its own warrant.

root.sense: a gathering together, an assembly; from syn (together) + ago (to bring, lead)

133.courtroomWord: A standing term — an assembled body, and the question of whether its authority to teach and judge was granted or seized.
133.itsRole: Authority to teach and to render judgment is conferred, never assumed. In the break a synagoge claims the seat by its own vote — they say they are, and are not. The counterfeit assembly issues rulings, binds consciences, and casts out, on a warrant it manufactured. The mark of it is self-authorization: standing claimed, never conferred.

proofTexts.text: Them which say they are... and are not, but are the synagogue of Satan.
The synagogue of Satan, which say they are... and do lie.
proofTexts.note: The counterfeit body named for its false claim.

proofTexts.text: They cast him out.
proofTexts.note: The self-seated body exercising judgment against the man who confessed the truth.

proofTexts.text: They sit in Moses' seat... they bind heavy burdens.
proofTexts.note: Binding by a seat taken, not granted.

plainTerms: A synagogue is just an assembly — a group gathered. The word turns dark only when the group claims a seat it was never given: the right to teach as final, to judge, to cast out.
Scripture's test is blunt — they say they are, and are not. The gathering is not the problem; the stolen gavel is.
bringItHome: A room of people is only a room of people — until someone stands at the front, claims the bench, and begins handing down verdicts no one authorized. That is the break: an assembly that seats itself and rules. The true assembly is convened by Yahuah; the counterfeit convenes itself.

courtroomRoles.does: alone confers the standing to teach and to judge.
claims the seat it was never given.
judged by a court with no jurisdiction, for confessing the truth.

134.lead: Diabolos is built from dia (across) and ballo (to throw) — one who throws a charge across the room at the accused. It is the court word for the slanderer: not a witness stating what he saw, but a prosecutor manufacturing the case. Scripture names him “the accuser of our brethren... which accused them before our Elohim day and night” (Revelation 12:10). The diabolos does not prove; he alleges. His whole standing depends on a charge sticking — and the break is that the charge is a lie thrown, not a truth testified.

root.sense: slanderer, false accuser; from dia (across) + ballo (to throw)

134.courtroomWord: A prosecution term — the party who lodges the charge; in the break, a charge slandered rather than proven.
134.itsRole: A lawful court receives testimony and weighs it. The diabolos short-circuits that — he throws the accusation and lets it work before it is tested. In the break, accusation itself becomes the weapon: the case is the smear. But the accused has an answer in the same court — an Advocate (1 John 2:1), and a blood that speaks better things (Hebrews 12:24). When the true price is paid, the thrown charge finds nothing to land on, and the accuser is cast down.

proofTexts.text: The accuser of our brethren is cast down, which accused them... day and night.
proofTexts.note: The slanderer's charge thrown out of court.

proofTexts.text: Satan standing at his right hand to resist him.
proofTexts.note: The accuser positioned to prosecute the priest.

proofTexts.text: He is a liar, and the father of it.
proofTexts.note: The accuser's charges are fabricated, not testified.

proofTexts.text: We have an advocate with the Father.
proofTexts.note: The answer to the diabolos — counsel for the accused.

plainTerms: A diabolos is a slanderer — someone who throws an accusation instead of proving one. Scripture's accuser works day and night, lodging charges against the delivered.
The break is that the charge is a lie. And the answer is not to argue it but to have an Advocate and a paid account — then the thrown charge has nothing to stick to.
bringItHome: Picture a man in the dock while someone across the room hurls accusation after accusation, hoping one sticks — none proven, all thrown. That is the diabolos. But the accused has counsel who rises with a receipt: the debt is paid, the account is clear. The charges fall to the floor, and the accuser is put out of court.

courtroomRoles.does: throws the charge, prosecutes by slander.
counsel for the accused, answering the charge with a settled account.
before whom the charge is lodged, and who casts the accuser down.
charged day and night, cleared by the paid account.

135.lead: Two Hebrew verbs sit at opposite poles of the law. Badal is to divide, to distinguish, to set apart — the work Yahuah does from the first day, dividing light from darkness (Genesis 1:4), and the priest's charge “to put difference between holy and unholy, and between unclean and clean” (Leviticus 10:10). Balal is the opposite: to mingle, to confound — the root of Babel, where Yahuah “did there confound the language” (Genesis 11:9). The law runs on badal, on maintained distinctions. The break runs on balal — the deliberate blurring of the lines the law drew, until holy and common cannot be told apart.

root.sense: to divide, separate, distinguish, set apart
to mingle, mix, confound, confuse

135.courtroomWord: A distinction pair — badal, the lawful drawing of boundaries; balal, the unlawful erasing of them.
135.itsRole: The whole legal order depends on distinctions kept: holy from common, clean from unclean, light from darkness. Badal is the court maintaining its categories. In the break, balal dissolves them — the boundary erased not by relocation but by fog, until they “have put no difference between the holy and profane” (Ezekiel 22:26). Confusion is not neutral; it is the counterfeit's method, because a law whose lines are blurred cannot convict.

proofTexts.text: Put difference between holy and unholy, and between unclean and clean.
Elohim divided the light from the darkness.
proofTexts.note: Distinction as the first act of order.

proofTexts.text: They have put no difference between the holy and profane.
Because Yahuah did there confound the language.
proofTexts.note: Confusion named — balal, the root of Babel.

plainTerms: Badal means to separate and tell apart — holy from common, clean from unclean. Balal means to mix until you cannot tell them apart. The law lives on badal; every commandment draws a line.
The break works by balal — not erasing the line openly, but fogging it, until no one can say where holy ends and common begins. A blurred law cannot judge.
bringItHome: A surveyor's whole job is the line — this land is yours, that is your neighbor's. Move the stone and it is theft; but fog the whole field and no one can prove anything. Badal sets the stones; balal brings the fog. The break rarely tears the law down — it just mixes everything together until holy and common look the same, and a law you cannot read is a law you cannot keep.

courtroomRoles.does: divides, sets the categories, commands the difference kept.
charged to put difference between holy and common.
mingles the categories until none can be told apart.

136.lead: Parad is to part, to sever — to drive a wedge between what was joined. Where badal separates by lawful category, parad separates by injury: “a whisperer separateth chief friends” (Proverbs 16:28); “he that repeateth a matter separateth very friends” (Proverbs 17:9). It is severance produced by testimony thrown between — the slander that splits a bond, the report that parts brothers. In the court of the break, parad is the diabolos's work reaching the ground: the charge thrown becomes the friendship severed.

root.sense: to divide, separate, part, sever — often of relationships broken

136.courtroomWord: A severance term — division worked between parties by injurious testimony, not by lawful judgment.
136.itsRole: A lawful court parts the guilty from the innocent by verdict. The break parts brother from brother by whisper — parad is division engineered, the wedge driven by a report repeated. It is the diabolos operating at ground level: the thrown charge lands, and a bond that should have held is severed. The tell is the whisper — not testimony given openly and tested, but a matter repeated to part friends.

proofTexts.text: A whisperer separateth chief friends.
He that repeateth a matter separateth very friends.
proofTexts.note: The repeated report that parts a bond.

proofTexts.text: He that soweth discord among brethren.
proofTexts.note: Among the things Yahuah hates — the parad worker condemned.

proofTexts.text: Through desire a man, having separated himself, seeketh and intermeddleth.

plainTerms: Parad means to split apart — to sever a bond. In the break it is division on purpose: the whisper that turns friends against each other, the repeated story that parts brothers.
It is slander with a target — not just a lie told, but a bond broken by it. Scripture lists sowing discord among the brethren among the things Yahuah hates.
bringItHome: Two brothers stand together until a third keeps carrying words between them — a little here, a little there, each repeated at the right moment. Nothing is proven; everything is severed. That is parad: not a verdict that separates the guilty, but a whisper that separates friends. The break does not always attack the law head-on; sometimes it just parts the people who were keeping it together.

courtroomRoles.does: parts friends by testimony thrown between.
divided by a charge never proven.
who hates the sowing of discord and sees the wedge for what it is.

137.lead: Cheirographon is a handwritten certificate of debt — an IOU, a signed acknowledgment of what one owes. Paul says Yahushua blotted out “the handwriting of ordinances that was against us... and took it out of the way, nailing it to his cross” (Colossians 2:14). The word is precise, and so is the target: what was cancelled and nailed up was the record of debt standing against the guilty — the bond of charges — not the Torah itself. A cancelled IOU is a discharged debt, not an abolished law. The certificate that accused us was posted as paid; the standard that defined the debt still stands.

root.sense: a handwritten document; specifically a certificate or bond of debt

137.courtroomWord: A debt-instrument term — the signed certificate of what is owed, here cancelled and posted.
137.itsRole: A debt is recorded on a certificate, and the certificate is what a creditor holds against the debtor. Cheirographon is that instrument. At the cross it was blotted out and nailed — the ancient sign of a debt discharged, the bond posted as paid. This is the heart of the courtroom reading of Colossians 2: the charges against us were cancelled, the accusing record removed. It does not read ‘the law was abolished’; it reads ‘the debt was paid.’ The standard that measured the debt remains; the IOU is gone.

proofTexts.text: Blotting out the handwriting of ordinances that was against us... nailing it to his cross.
proofTexts.note: The certificate of debt cancelled and posted — not the law repealed.

proofTexts.text: Having forgiven you all trespasses.
proofTexts.note: The context: debts forgiven, charges cancelled.

proofTexts.text: Having slain the enmity thereby.
proofTexts.note: The barrier of hostility removed, the parties reconciled.

proofTexts.text: Where no law is, there is no transgression.
proofTexts.note: The standard must remain for the debt to have existed at all.

plainTerms: A cheirographon was a handwritten IOU — a signed record of what you owe. Colossians 2:14 says that record of debt was cancelled and nailed to the cross. That is a paid debt, not an abolished law.
The bill against us is gone; the standard that defined the bill still stands.
bringItHome: Picture a signed IOU pinned to a board with PAID stamped across it — the debt is discharged, the certificate void. That is what Colossians 2:14 describes: the record of charges against us, cancelled and posted at the cross. It does not say the law was torn up. It says the debt was paid — which only makes sense if the law that measured the debt is still there.

courtroomRoles.does: cancels the certificate of debt against the guilty.
by whom the debt is discharged and the bond posted paid.
the accusing certificate, blotted out and nailed up.
unrepealed — the measure by which the debt existed.

138.lead: A dogma is an enacted decree with legal force — a ruling laid down by authority that binds those under it. Caesar’s census goes out as a dogma (Luke 2:1); the Jerusalem council’s decisions are delivered as dogmata (Acts 16:4). The word names legislation, not opinion. This matters at Colossians 2:14, where the certificate of debt stood against us in its dogmata — its decrees. What is cancelled there is the binding force of the charges recorded against the guilty, the decrees that condemned them — a debt discharged by a higher ruling, not the Lawgiver’s own standard erased.

root.sense: a decree, ordinance, edict with binding legal force

138.courtroomWord: A decree term — an enacted ruling that binds those under it.
138.itsRole: Authority legislates by decree, and a dogma is a decree in force. In the courtroom reading of Colossians 2, the certificate ‘of dogmata’ is the record of binding charges against the guilty; its cancellation is the discharge of those charges by a higher ruling. Dogma is the legal weight behind a ruling — which is exactly why cancelling the debt-decree against us is a judicial act, not the abolition of Yahuah’s law.

proofTexts.text: The handwriting of ordinances that was against us.
There went out a decree from Caesar Augustus.
They delivered them the decrees for to keep.
The law of commandments contained in ordinances.
proofTexts.note: The dividing decrees between the parties, removed — the enmity, not the Lawgiver’s standard.

plainTerms: A dogma is a binding decree — a ruling with legal force, like Caesar’s census order. In Colossians 2, the ‘ordinances’ cancelled are the decrees of debt standing against the guilty. A higher ruling discharged the charges; it did not erase the Lawgiver’s own standard.
bringItHome: A dogma is a decree that carries the weight of law — when it goes out, people are bound. In Colossians 2 the decrees against us — the recorded charges of debt — are cancelled by a higher court’s ruling. The charges are discharged. The Lawgiver’s own standard is not what was struck.

courtroomRoles.does: lays down the binding decree.
bound by the dogma.
cancelled at the cross by a higher ruling.

139.lead: ‘Under the law’ — hupo nomon — is one of the most misread phrases in the New Testament. The church hears it as ‘obligated to keep the commandments,’ and concludes that to be freed from being under law is to be freed from obeying it. But the phrase is positional, and its position is the dock: to be hupo nomon is to be under the law’s jurisdiction as a defendant — under its sentence, held in custody by its verdict of guilt. “The scripture hath concluded all under sin” (Galatians 3:22) locks the prisoner up; to be delivered from under law is to be released from its condemnation, not from its commandments. The acquitted man leaves the dock — and then keeps the law he is no longer condemned by.

root.sense: under; beneath the authority or power of
law; here, the law as a jurisdiction and its sentence

139.courtroomWord: A jurisdiction phrase — to stand under the law’s sentence, as a defendant in custody.
139.itsRole: The whole weight of the phrase is positional: hupo nomon is where the guilty stand — under the law’s verdict, held by its condemnation. Paul’s argument is that all are shut up there until deliverance comes. To be brought out from under law is to be released from the sentence, not from the standard. This is the hinge the abolition case misses: leaving the dock is not the same as tearing up the statute. The freed defendant is precisely the one now free to keep the law without its condemnation hanging over him.

proofTexts.text: The scripture hath concluded all under sin.
proofTexts.note: The prisoner shut up under the verdict.

proofTexts.text: That... all the world may become guilty before Elohim.
proofTexts.note: The whole world in the dock, under the sentence.

proofTexts.text: Made under the law, to redeem them that were under the law.
proofTexts.note: Deliverance from the sentence, by One who entered it.

proofTexts.text: Ye are not under the law, but under grace. What then? shall we sin?... forbid.
proofTexts.note: Out from the condemnation, into favor — not out from the commandments.

plainTerms: ‘Under the law’ does not mean ‘obligated to obey.’ It means standing under the law’s sentence — in the dock as a guilty defendant. To be freed from being under law is to be released from its condemnation, not from its commandments.
The acquitted man walks out of court and still lives by the law he is no longer condemned by.
bringItHome: A convict is ‘under’ the law in the sense that matters: under its sentence, held in custody by its verdict. When he is pardoned, he is no longer under it that way — he walks out of the dock. But pardon does not repeal the statute, and it does not make him free to break it. He is now free to keep it without the sentence hanging over him. That is hupo nomon: the position of the condemned, and deliverance from it is release from the sentence, not from the standard.

courtroomRoles.does: under whose sentence the guilty are held.
shut up ‘under law,’ in the dock.
entered ‘under law’ to redeem those held under its sentence.
releases from the condemnation, the standard still standing.

142.lead: In one breath Yahushua forbids two titles of standing: “be not ye called Rabbi... neither be ye called masters: for one is your Master, even the Messiah” (Matthew 23:8,10). Didaskalos is the teacher, the one with authority to instruct; kathegetes is the leader, the guide men follow. Both name a standing over others — and both are withheld from men, reserved to One. The break is the taking of the title: a man seating himself as the teacher and guide whose word settles the matter, in a chair Yahushua said belongs to the Messiah alone.

root.sense: teacher, master, instructor
leader, guide, one who goes before

142.courtroomWord: Title terms — the standing to instruct and to lead, which Yahushua assigns to One and forbids to men.
142.itsRole: Standing to teach with finality and to lead as master belongs to the Messiah, appointed by Yahuah. In the break, men take the titles — Rabbi, Father, Master — and with them the authority to bind and to be followed as the final word. The forbidding is not against teaching; it is against the seizing of a rank Yahushua kept for Himself. “One is your Master” is a boundary stone around an office men keep trying to occupy.

proofTexts.text: Be not ye called Rabbi: for one is your Master... and all ye are brethren.
proofTexts.note: The title withheld; the assembly leveled to brethren.

proofTexts.text: Neither be ye called masters: for one is your Master, even the Messiah.
proofTexts.note: The standing reserved to One, the Messiah.

proofTexts.text: Call no man your father upon the earth: for one is your Father, which is in heaven.
proofTexts.note: The same boundary around another title — one Father, the Most High.

proofTexts.text: He that is greatest among you shall be your servant.
proofTexts.note: The standing inverted — service, not title.

plainTerms: Didaskalos is teacher; kathegetes is leader or master. Yahushua forbade His followers to take either title, because both belong to One — the Messiah, appointed by the Father.
The break is a man taking the chair: styling himself the teacher whose word is final and the master men follow. Teaching is fine; seizing the rank is the offense.
bringItHome: A room of brothers has one Teacher and one Guide — and every one of them is a brother, level with the rest. Then a man stands, takes the title, and asks to be called Master, his word final. Yahushua drew the line before it happened: one is your Master, even the Messiah; the rest of you are brethren. The break is the title taken — a chair occupied that was reserved for One.

courtroomRoles.does: holds the standing to teach and lead, as the One the Father appointed — not a second self-standing authority, but the Messiah given the office.
the source; one is your Father, which is in heaven.
takes the rank Yahushua forbade, seating himself as final.
leveled, all brothers, none the master of the rest.

93.lead: The husband is the covenant party holding lawful authority and answerable obligation within the marriage bond. When Yahuah says, “I was an husband unto them” (Jeremiah 31:32), He invokes a legal relationship complete with terms, not a romance without stipulation. The husband bore defined duties and defined rights under the marriage covenant. This frames Israel’s unfaithfulness as breach of contract rather than mere cooling of affection — a covenant party failing its obligations to the other. To call Yahuah husband is to place the relationship inside marriage law, where loyalty is owed, provision is due, and violation is actionable.

root.sense: lord, master, husband; the covenant head of the marriage
man, husband

93.courtroomWord: A covenant-party term — the husband bearing the marriage bond’s rights and duties.
93.itsRole: Marriage is a covenant, and the husband is a party to it with defined obligations — provision, protection, faithfulness — and defined rights the covenant secures. Yahuah as husband to Israel invokes this legal frame; her idolatry is breach of the marriage contract, not merely lost feeling. The word places the relationship under law, where duties are owed and violations are actionable.

proofTexts.text: Although I was an husband unto them, saith Yahuah.
Thy Maker is thine husband; Yahuah of hosts is his name.
Thou shalt call me Ishi.
Husbands, love your wives... as Messiah also loved the assembly.

plainTerms: A husband, in Scripture, is a covenant party — with duties (provision, protection, faithfulness) and rights secured by the marriage bond. When Yahuah calls Himself Israel’s husband, He is naming a legal relationship with terms, not a romance. Her unfaithfulness was breach of contract.
bringItHome: A husband is not merely a lover; he is a party to a covenant, bound to provide and protect, holding rights the bond secures. That is what Yahuah means calling Himself Israel’s husband: a legal relationship with obligations on both sides — and her idolatry was breaking it.

courtroomRoles.does: the covenant head, bound to provide and protect.
the covenant party owing faithfulness.
the terms defining the duties of both.

53.lead: To inherit is to receive title and take lawful possession of an allotment. “The meek... shall inherit the earth” (Matthew 5:5) is not a soft blessing but a grant of estate rights — legal possession conferred. The verb transfers property under law from one holder to another. To inherit the kingdom is to come into a lawful holding, entered as its rightful possessor. This is why inheritance can be lost, forfeited, or secured — it behaves like the legal title it is. The promises framed as inheritance are promises of property one will lawfully hold, not merely blessings one will enjoy.

root.sense: to take possession, to inherit
to receive by lot, to inherit

sharesRoot.note: The kleron- family: to inherit (kleronomeo) is to take the inheritance (kleronomia) as the heir (kleronomos).

53.courtroomWord: A conveyance term — the receiving of title and lawful possession of an estate.
53.itsRole: To inherit is to have property conveyed to one under law — title received, possession taken. It is not a wish granted but an estate entered. The kingdom, the land, the earth are all spoken of as inherited: lawful holdings received by right of standing. Because it is title, it can be secured or forfeited, which is why the inheritance is guarded and the unworthy are said not to inherit.

proofTexts.text: The meek... shall inherit the earth.
Inherit the kingdom prepared for you.
Shall not inherit the kingdom of Elohim.
An inheritance incorruptible... reserved in heaven for you.

plainTerms: To inherit is to receive title and take possession of an estate — by right, under law. ‘Inherit the earth’ or ‘inherit the kingdom’ means lawful holdings conferred, not vague blessings. And because it is title, it can be kept or lost.
bringItHome: To inherit is not to be handed a nice surprise — it is to have property legally conveyed to you and to take possession as its rightful owner. That is what the promises mean: the earth, the kingdom, entered as a lawful holding by right of your standing as a son.

courtroomRoles.does: conveys the estate to the heirs.
receives title and takes possession.
the lawful holding conveyed.

51.lead: An inheritance is an estate grant — heritable property allotted by law and protected against permanent loss. The land of Israel was distributed as nachalah, parcel by parcel, by lot, and hedged by the Jubilee so that no family’s estate could be alienated forever (Leviticus 25:23). Inheritance is title, not sentiment. So when believers are called heirs of an inheritance reserved in heaven (1 Peter 1:4), the language is estate-law: a lawful holding assigned, recorded, and secured. To inherit is not to be given a gift on a whim; it is to receive property to which one holds recognized legal claim.

root.sense: an inheritance, heritable estate
an inheritance, allotted possession

sharesRoot.note: The kleron- family: the inheritance (kleronomia) is received by inheriting (kleronomeo), taken by the heir (kleronomos).

51.courtroomWord: An estate term — the heritable property allotted and secured by law.
51.itsRole: An inheritance is legal property, assigned and protected: distributed by lot, guarded by the Jubilee against permanent loss, passed by right of standing. It is not a gift of the moment but a holding on the record. The believer’s inheritance, reserved in heaven, is spoken in this register — a lawful estate secured, to which the heir holds recognized claim.

proofTexts.text: The land shall not be sold for ever... the land is mine.
Unto these the land shall be divided for an inheritance.
An inheritance incorruptible... reserved in heaven for you.
The earnest of our inheritance.
proofTexts.note: The estate guaranteed by a pledge.

plainTerms: An inheritance is heritable property allotted and protected by law — title, not a whim. Israel’s land was divided as inheritance and guarded by the Jubilee. The believer’s inheritance is the same kind of thing: a lawful estate, secured and reserved.
bringItHome: An inheritance is not a present that might or might not come — it is an estate assigned to you by law, on the record, protected from being lost. Israel’s land worked that way, hedged by the Jubilee. The believer’s inheritance is reserved and secured the same way: yours by right.

courtroomRoles.does: allots and secures the inheritance.
holds recognized claim to the estate.
the heritable property protected by law.

118.lead: Innocent means acquitted — clean of the charge, free of blood-guilt. “The innocent and righteous slay thou not” (Exodus 23:7) treats innocence as a legal verdict of standing, not a comment on temperament. To be naqi is to leave the court unblamed, with no charge sustained. Pilate’s “I am innocent of the blood of this just person” (Matthew 27:24) is an attempted legal disclaimer of guilt. Innocence in Scripture is a finding, not a feeling — the state of one against whom the case has failed. To be declared innocent is to be released from the charge, the record showing no guilt assessed.

root.sense: clean, free from guilt, acquitted; innocent of a charge

118.courtroomWord: A verdict term — the finding that no guilt is sustained; acquittal.
118.itsRole: Innocence is a ruling: the charge examined and not sustained, the party released unblamed. It is the verdict opposite condemnation. Torah guards the innocent because a false finding of guilt is a grave wrong; the court must not slay the innocent. To be naqi is to have the case fail against you — a legal standing, not a self-assessment.

proofTexts.text: The innocent and righteous slay thou not.
proofTexts.note: Innocence guarded as a legal standing.

proofTexts.text: Cursed be he that taketh reward to slay an innocent person.
proofTexts.note: The wrong of condemning the acquitted.

proofTexts.text: I am innocent of the blood of this just person.
He that hath clean hands, and a pure heart.
proofTexts.note: The innocent standing before the bench.

plainTerms: Innocent means acquitted — the charge did not stand — not a comment on your personality. It is a verdict: the case failed, no guilt assessed. Torah fiercely protects the innocent because condemning the acquitted is a grave wrong.
bringItHome: To be innocent, in court, is not to feel good about yourself — it is to have the charge fail and walk out unblamed. That is naqi: the verdict that no guilt sticks. And the law treats slaying the innocent — condemning the acquitted — as one of the worst offenses a court can commit.

courtroomRoles.does: the charge against him not sustained.
guards the innocent and renders the acquittal.
examined and failed.

12.lead: Reduced to ‘praying for someone.’ The root paga means to meet, to reach, to encounter — and in its legal sense, to step in and plead on another’s behalf before authority. Isaiah 53:12 files the Servant’s work under it: “he bare the sin of many, and made intercession for the transgressors.” That is not a warm prayer at a distance; it is an intercessor placing himself between the guilty and the bench, absorbing the collision. Intercession happens in a courtroom, at the moment of sentencing, when someone with standing steps between the accused and the verdict.

root.sense: to meet, to reach, to encounter; to interpose, to plead for

12.courtroomWord: An interposition term — stepping between the accused and the verdict to plead for them.
12.itsRole: To intercede is to place oneself between the guilty and the sentence — to meet the collision on their behalf. It is not distant well-wishing but active interposition before the bench. The Servant intercedes by bearing the sin and standing between the transgressors and the verdict; the risen One ever lives to make intercession. Intercession is courtroom advocacy at the point of judgment.

proofTexts.text: He... made intercession for the transgressors.
proofTexts.note: The interposition on behalf of the guilty.

proofTexts.text: He ever liveth to make intercession for them.
Who also maketh intercession for us.
I sought for a man... that should stand in the gap before me.

plainTerms: To intercede is not just to pray at a distance — it is to step between the guilty and the sentence and plead for them. The word means to meet, to interpose. The Servant does it by bearing the sin and standing in the gap; the risen One does it as our standing advocate.
bringItHome: Picture someone stepping between the accused and the falling gavel — taking the collision, pleading the case at the last moment. That is intercession: not a prayer from afar, but interposition before the bench. The Servant made intercession for the transgressors by standing exactly there.

courtroomRoles.does: steps between the guilty and the verdict, and pleads for them.
on whose behalf He interposes.
before whom the intercession is made.

96.lead: Jealous is the rightful stance of the offended covenant party — not petty envy, but a spouse enforcing the exclusivity the contract grants. “I Yahuah thy Elohim am a jealous El” (Exodus 20:5) follows immediately upon the prohibition of other gods, because jealousy here is the enforcement of a covenant clause. A husband with exclusive claim is right to refuse a rival. Divine jealousy is therefore judicial, not emotional weakness: it is the covenant party insisting on the terms He is owed. To provoke Yahuah to jealousy (Deuteronomy 32:21) is to breach the exclusivity of the bond and invoke His rightful enforcement of it.

root.sense: jealous, zealous; the rightful jealousy of an exclusive claim

96.courtroomWord: An enforcement term — the covenant party insisting on the exclusivity clause He is owed.
96.itsRole: A covenant of marriage grants exclusivity, and jealousy is the enforcement of that clause. It is not insecurity but right: the offended party refusing a rival the contract forbids. Yahuah’s jealousy follows directly on the command against other gods — it is Him holding the covenant’s exclusivity. To provoke it is to breach the bond and invoke its rightful enforcement.

proofTexts.text: I Yahuah thy Elohim am a jealous El.
proofTexts.note: Jealousy as the enforcement of exclusivity.

proofTexts.text: Yahuah, whose name is Jealous, is a jealous El.
They have moved me to jealousy with that which is not El.
I am jealous over you with godly jealousy.
proofTexts.note: The rightful jealousy of the betrothing party.

plainTerms: Jealous, here, is not petty envy — it is the rightful stance of a spouse whose covenant grants exclusive claim. Yahuah is ‘jealous’ because the covenant forbids rivals, and He enforces that clause. To provoke His jealousy is to break the exclusivity of the bond.
bringItHome: A husband with a rightful, exclusive claim is not insecure when he refuses a rival — he is enforcing the covenant. That is Yahuah’s jealousy: it comes right after ‘no other gods,’ because it is Him holding the exclusivity clause of the bond. It is judicial, not petty.

courtroomRoles.does: enforces the covenant’s exclusivity.
owing exclusive loyalty by the bond.
the other god the covenant forbids.

22.lead: This is the one that should stop a ‘the-law-is-done-away’ preacher cold, because Jubilee is nothing but law — debt, property, and liberty statute (Leviticus 25). Every fiftieth year debts were cancelled, bond-servants walked free, and every parcel of land reverted to its original family by legal title. The word for the freedom proclaimed is deror (H1865) — a manumission term, the legal release of one bound. There is no ‘spiritual feeling’ in Jubilee; it is a property-records reset enforced by statute. And it is the framework Yahushua read off the scroll to announce His own ministry (Luke 4:18-19) — He launched the good news in the language of release law.

root.sense: the Jubilee; the ram’s-horn year of release, cancellation, and reversion

22.courtroomWord: A release-statute term — the fiftieth-year reset of debt, bondage, and property title.
22.itsRole: Jubilee is pure statute: on the fiftieth year debts cancel, bondservants go free, and land reverts to its original family by legal title. It is a scheduled reset of the property and debt records, enforced by law, not a sentiment. Yahushua opens His ministry by reading it (Luke 4) — announcing deliverance in the exact register of release law. The good news arrives as Jubilee: debts cleared, captives freed, estates restored.

proofTexts.text: Proclaim liberty throughout all the land... it shall be a jubile unto you.
Ye shall return every man unto his possession.
In the jubile it shall go out, and he shall return unto his possession.
To preach the acceptable year of the Lord.
proofTexts.note: The ministry announced in Jubilee terms.

plainTerms: Jubilee is nothing but law — debt, property, and freedom statute. Every fiftieth year, debts were cancelled, slaves freed, and land returned to its family. It is a legal reset, not a feeling. And Yahushua announced His whole ministry by reading it: good news as release law.
bringItHome: Imagine a law that, every fiftieth year, wipes every debt, frees every bondservant, and returns every family’s land — a total legal reset. That is Jubilee. Far from being done away, it is the very language Yahushua chose to launch His ministry: the acceptable year, the great release.

courtroomRoles.does: decrees the fiftieth-year release.
debts cancelled, freedom restored.
reverting to its family by legal title.

1.lead: The modern ear hears ‘judge’ and pictures disapproval — Yahuah frowning from a distance. But shaphat is an office, not a mood: the one who shaphats convenes the court, hears the case, weighs the evidence, and hands down a binding ruling that carries force. Abraham appeals to it directly — “Shall not the Judge of all the earth do right?” (Genesis 18:25) — expecting not sentiment but due process. The word seats Yahuah on a bench with a docket. To call Him Judge is not to call Him harsh; it is to say the universe has a court, and He presides over it.

root.sense: to judge, to govern, to render a ruling; the judicial office

sharesRoot.note: Mishpat (the ruling) is from shaphat (to judge): the Judge (shaphat) hands down the judgment (mishpat).

1.courtroomWord: An office term — the one who convenes the court and renders binding rulings.
1.itsRole: To judge is to hold an office: convene the case, weigh the evidence, render a ruling with force. It is not disapproval but adjudication. Yahuah as Judge presides over a real court with a real docket; Abraham appeals to His justice expecting due process. The judicial office is the seat from which the whole courtroom operates — and it is His.

proofTexts.text: Shall not the Judge of all the earth do right?
Elohim is judge himself.
Yahuah is our judge, Yahuah is our lawgiver, Yahuah is our king.
There is one lawgiver... who is able to save and to destroy.

plainTerms: To judge, in Scripture, is to hold an office — convening the court, weighing evidence, handing down a binding ruling — not to frown from a distance. Yahuah as Judge means the universe has a court with a docket, and He presides. Abraham appealed to that, expecting due process.
bringItHome: When Abraham said ‘Shall not the Judge of all the earth do right?’, he was not appealing to a mood — he was appealing to an office, expecting the bench to weigh the case justly. That is what ‘Judge’ means: the seat of the court. To call Yahuah Judge is to say the universe has a courtroom, and He is on the bench.

courtroomRoles.does: convenes the court and renders binding rulings.
whose case is weighed before Him.
the matters the Judge decides.

2.lead: Christians hear ‘judgment’ and brace for wrath. But mishpat is first the ruling a judge pronounces and then the accumulated body of case-law that guides him — the most common legal noun in the Hebrew Scriptures. When David prizes Yahuah’s mishpatim as more to be desired than gold (Psalm 19:9-10), he is not admiring a temperament; he is treasuring a code of just verdicts. To love the mishpatim of Yahuah is to love the way His court rules. Strip the legal sense and half the Psalms turn to sentiment; keep it and they read as a citizen’s delight in a righteous bench.

root.sense: a verdict, a legal decision; also the body of ordinances. From shaphat, to judge

sharesRoot.note: Mishpat is from shaphat: the Judge (shaphat) issues the judgment (mishpat), and the mishpatim are the case-law behind His rulings.

2.courtroomWord: A ruling term — the verdict pronounced, and the case-law that guides it.
2.itsRole: Mishpat is both the ruling and the code — the verdict a judge hands down and the accumulated ordinances that shape it. It is the most frequent legal noun in Scripture. To love Yahuah’s mishpatim is to treasure His just verdicts and the standard behind them. Judgment is not a mood of wrath but the rendering of a righteous ruling.

proofTexts.text: The judgments of Yahuah are true and righteous altogether.
All his ways are judgment: a Elohim of truth.
proofTexts.note: The just verdict as His way.

proofTexts.text: Seek judgment, relieve the oppressed.
proofTexts.note: Mishpat as the just ruling to be sought.

proofTexts.text: To do justly, and to love mercy.
proofTexts.note: The rendering of right judgment required.

plainTerms: Judgment, in Scripture, is first a verdict and then the body of just rulings behind it — not a mood of wrath. To love Yahuah’s ‘judgments’ is to treasure the way His court rules. It is the most common legal word in the Hebrew Scriptures.
bringItHome: When the Psalmist calls Yahuah’s judgments ‘more to be desired than gold,’ he is not admiring a temper — he is treasuring a body of just verdicts, a righteous bench that always rules true. That is mishpat: the ruling and the case-law behind it. Half the Psalms read as a citizen’s delight in a just court.

courtroomRoles.does: renders the judgment.
the just verdicts and the code behind them.
who love and seek His just judgment.

4.lead: Justification is the acquittal made formal — the standing a man walks out with once the verdict is read. A justified man leaves the court with no charge filed against his name. But the noun is empty air without a code behind it: there is nothing to be acquitted of where nothing was ever prohibited. Modern preaching wants the relief of justification while discarding the law that makes acquittal mean anything. It cannot have both. Remove the statute and ‘justified’ describes a trial with no charge, no evidence, and no verdict — a word left hanging over an empty bench.

root.sense: acquittal, justification; the act of being declared in the right

sharesRoot.note: Dikaiosis (the noun) comes from dikaioo (the verb): to justify (acquit) yields justification (the standing).

4.courtroomWord: A verdict-standing term — the acquittal made formal, the standing after the ruling.
4.itsRole: Justification is what the acquitted walk out with: a standing of no-charge, the verdict entered on the record. It presupposes a real court, a real charge, a real law — acquittal is meaningless without them. This is the flaw in wanting justification while discarding the standard: strip the law and there is nothing to be acquitted of, and the word collapses.

proofTexts.text: Raised again for our justification.
The free gift came upon all men unto justification of life.
The free gift is of many offences unto justification.
It is Yahuah that justifieth.
proofTexts.note: The acquittal rendered by the Judge.

plainTerms: Justification is the acquittal made official — the clean standing you walk out with when the verdict clears you. But it only means something against a real law and a real charge. Wanting justification while throwing out the standard leaves the word hanging over an empty court.
bringItHome: Justification is the moment the verdict is read and you walk out with no charge on your name — the acquittal made your standing. But an acquittal needs a charge, and a charge needs a law. Keep the standard, and justification is glorious. Discard it, and there was nothing to be acquitted of.

courtroomRoles.does: renders the acquittal that becomes the standing.
walks out with no charge on the record.
without which there is nothing to be acquitted of.

3.lead: The church has spiritualized this into a warm inner glow, but dikaioo never left the courtroom. It means to declare a defendant legally in the right — to acquit from the bench. It does not make a man righteous; it pronounces him so, the way a verdict of ‘not guilty’ changes a man’s standing without changing his chemistry. This is why justification is always something rendered, never something felt. And the word refuses to stay parked at the entry door: Scripture also says “the doers of the law shall be justified” (Romans 2:13), pointing the same verb forward. An acquittal presupposes a court, and a court presupposes a law.

root.sense: to declare righteous, to acquit; to pronounce in the right

sharesRoot.note: Dikaioo (the verb) yields dikaiosis (the noun): to justify (acquit) yields justification (the standing).

3.courtroomWord: A verdict verb — to declare a defendant in the right; to acquit from the bench.
3.itsRole: To justify is to pronounce, not to transform — the court declaring a defendant in the right. It is a verdict rendered, the standing changed by the ruling, not the chemistry changed by feeling. And the same verb points forward: the doers of the law shall be justified. Acquittal presupposes a bench and a code; where there is no law, there is nothing to be declared right against.

proofTexts.text: Being justified freely by his grace.
The doers of the law shall be justified.
It is Yahuah that justifieth.
proofTexts.note: The acquittal rendered from the bench.

proofTexts.text: This man went down to his house justified.

plainTerms: To justify is to declare someone legally in the right — to acquit — not to make them feel righteous. It is a verdict, like ‘not guilty,’ that changes your standing without changing your nature. And it needs a court and a law: no standard, nothing to acquit against.
bringItHome: When a judge says ‘not guilty,’ he does not change the defendant’s chemistry — he changes his standing, by a ruling. That is to justify: to declare in the right, from the bench. And an acquittal only means something where there was a real law and a real charge.

courtroomRoles.does: pronounces the defendant in the right.
acquitted, his standing changed by the ruling.
against which the acquittal is meaningful.

132.lead: Karath is the covenant death-sentence of severance — the penalty of being ‘cut off.’ “That soul shall be cut off from his people” (Genesis 17:14; Leviticus 20:3) is not a mere excommunication but a sentence of severance, the guilty party cut away from the covenant community and its life. It is the same verb by which a covenant is cut (karat) — the cutting that binds a covenant is the cutting that removes its breaker. Karath is the ultimate sanction of the covenant court: the transgressor severed, cut off from the people, the promise, and the life the covenant carried.

root.sense: to cut, to cut off; the karet penalty of covenant severance

sharesRoot.note: One root H3772: the covenant cut (Cut), the marriage bond cut (Divorce), and here the covenant-breaker cut off (karet).

132.courtroomWord: A severance-sentence term — the penalty of being cut off from the covenant people.
132.itsRole: The covenant that is cut into force can cut its breaker out: karath is that sentence. To be cut off is not a light expulsion but a severance from the covenant community, its promises, and its life. It is the gravest sanction of the covenant court — and it stands behind the reading of death itself as severance, the transgressor cut off from the life the covenant carried until the cutting is answered.

proofTexts.text: That soul shall be cut off from his people; he hath broken my covenant.
I will cut him off from among his people.
That soul shall be cut off from among his people.
Evildoers shall be cut off.
proofTexts.note: The sentence of severance on the wicked.

plainTerms: Karath is the sentence of being ‘cut off’ — severed from the covenant people, its promises, and its life. It is not a mild expulsion but the covenant court’s gravest penalty. And it is the same verb by which a covenant is ‘cut’: the cutting that makes a covenant is the cutting that removes its breaker.
bringItHome: The same word that makes a covenant — to ‘cut’ it — is the word for its ultimate penalty: to be ‘cut off.’ The covenant-breaker is severed, cut away from the people, the promise, and the life the covenant held. That is karath: the death-sentence of severance, the sharpest edge of the covenant court.

courtroomRoles.does: pronounces the sentence of severance.
cut off from the people and the life of the covenant.
whose breach the cutting-off answers.

33.lead: To engrave is to cut permanently into stone or metal — the ancient guarantee of an unalterable document. The commandments were “graven upon the tables” (Exodus 32:16), precisely because engraving cannot be quietly revised the way ink can. What is cut in stone is meant to outlast the hand that cut it. The imagery is deliberately legal: a code engraved is a code declared beyond amendment. This makes the promise to write the same law on tablets of the heart (2 Corinthians 3:3) all the more pointed — the terms are not softened in the transfer, only relocated; still engraved, now on flesh.

root.sense: to engrave, to cut in
to hew, to carve out

33.courtroomWord: A permanence term — cutting a document into stone so it cannot be revised.
33.itsRole: A law’s authority depends on its being fixed, and engraving fixes it. What is cut in stone cannot be edited without leaving the cut; it is the ancient seal of an unalterable text. The commandments were engraved for exactly this reason. And when the promise comes to write the law on the heart, the verb is not ‘soften’ but ‘engrave’ — the same fixed terms, relocated to flesh, still beyond amendment.

proofTexts.text: The writing... graven upon the tables.
proofTexts.note: The law cut in stone, unalterable.

proofTexts.text: Tables of stone, written with the finger of Elohim.
Graven upon the table of their heart.
proofTexts.note: Engraving as permanence, here of sin.

proofTexts.text: Written... in fleshy tables of the heart.
proofTexts.note: The same terms relocated, not softened.

plainTerms: To engrave is to cut a document permanently into stone — so it can’t be quietly changed. The commandments were engraved for that reason. And the new-covenant promise is to engrave the same law on the heart: relocated to flesh, not softened.
bringItHome: Ink can be erased; a cut in stone cannot. That is why the commandments were engraved — to declare them beyond amendment. So when Scripture promises the law written on the heart, notice the verb: not softened, engraved. Same fixed terms, new tablet.

courtroomRoles.does: engraves the terms beyond amendment.
the surface the law is cut into.
fixed by the engraving, relocated but not revised.

48.lead: To keep is to guard as a charge — to watch over and preserve something entrusted, the way a sentinel keeps a post. Shamar first appears with Adam set “to dress it and to keep it” (Genesis 2:15) — a custodial duty, not a suggestion. To keep the commandments is to stand guard over them, protecting them from breach as one guards a trust. This is far more than obeying when convenient; it is the active, vigilant custody of a charge one is answerable for. ‘Keep my commandments’ places the believer as watchman over the terms of the covenant, responsible to see they are not violated.

root.sense: to keep, guard, watch, preserve; to attend to a charge

48.courtroomWord: A custody term — the vigilant guarding of an entrusted charge.
48.itsRole: A charge entrusted must be guarded, and shamar is that guarding. To keep the commandments is to hold them as a trust, watching against their breach — an active custody, not passive compliance. Adam was to keep the garden; the priest keeps the charge of the sanctuary; the believer keeps the covenant terms. Keeping is the watchman’s duty over what he is answerable for.

proofTexts.text: To dress it and to keep it.
proofTexts.note: The custodial charge given to man.

proofTexts.text: Ye shall diligently keep the commandments of Yahuah.
proofTexts.note: The terms guarded as a trust.

proofTexts.text: Thy word have I hid in mine heart, that I might not sin.
proofTexts.note: The charge kept close, against breach.

proofTexts.text: If ye love me, keep my commandments.
proofTexts.note: Keeping as the proof of loyalty.

plainTerms: To keep is to guard something entrusted to you — to watch over it like a sentinel, not just obey when convenient. To keep the commandments is to stand guard over them, protecting them from breach. It is active custody of a charge you answer for.
bringItHome: A watchman does not ‘keep’ his post by agreeing with it — he guards it, alert against anything that would breach it. That is shamar. To keep the commandments is to be that watchman over the covenant terms: responsible, vigilant, answerable that they are not violated.

courtroomRoles.does: guards the charge entrusted to him.
gives the terms to be kept.
the trust to be guarded against breach.

73.lead: A king is the sovereign lawgiver — the one whose word is statute and whose throne is the source of binding rule. Kingship in Scripture is a legal office: the melek issues decrees, renders judgment, and holds the authority the whole realm answers to. “Yahuah is our king” (Isaiah 33:22) sits beside ‘Yahuah is our judge’ and ‘Yahuah is our lawgiver’ — three names for one seat of authority. To call Yahuah King is not to praise His grandeur but to locate the source of law: His will is the statute the court enforces. The King is where the law comes from, and the throne is where it is upheld.

root.sense: king, sovereign; the ruler who issues law and renders judgment

73.courtroomWord: A sovereignty term — the lawgiver whose word is binding statute.
73.itsRole: Law has a source, and the King is it. The melek issues the decrees the realm is bound by and renders the judgments the court enforces. In Scripture, King, Judge, and Lawgiver are joined in one seat — Yahuah. To call Him King is to name the origin of the standard: His will is the statute. The King’s word is law, and the throne is where that law is upheld.

proofTexts.text: Yahuah is our judge, Yahuah is our lawgiver, Yahuah is our king.
proofTexts.note: The offices joined in one seat.

proofTexts.text: For Elohim is the King of all the earth.
Thou art my King, O Elohim: command deliverances.
The King of kings, and Lord of lords.

plainTerms: A king, in Scripture, is the sovereign lawgiver — the one whose word is statute and whose throne is the source of binding rule. ‘Yahuah is our king’ names Him as the origin of the law, alongside Judge and Lawgiver. To call Him King is to say His will is the standard.
bringItHome: A king is not just a grand figure — he is the source of law: his word is statute, his throne the seat rule comes from. That is what ‘Yahuah is our King’ means: the standard the whole court enforces comes from His will. King, Judge, and Lawgiver are one seat, and it is His.

courtroomRoles.does: issues the statute and holds supreme authority.
bound by the King’s decrees.
where the King’s law is upheld.
