56.lead: The landmark was the boundary stone that fixed a family’s legal title to its inheritance — and moving it was a serious crime. “Thou shalt not remove thy neighbour’s landmark” (Deuteronomy 19:14), and “Cursed be he that removeth his neighbour’s landmark” (Deuteronomy 27:17) place property fraud under a curse. The landmark marked where one man’s estate ended and another’s began; to move it was to steal land by redrawing the record. It is legal-title language: the boundary of a lawful holding, protected by statute. To respect the landmark is to honor the fixed boundaries of the law’s allotments; to move it is quiet theft.

root.sense: a border, boundary; the marked limit of an inheritance

56.courtroomWord: A boundary term — the fixed marker of legal title to an estate.
56.itsRole: Property has boundaries, and the landmark fixes them. It marks where a lawful holding ends, protecting each family’s inheritance from encroachment. Moving it is theft by redrawing the record — which is why Torah puts it under a curse. The landmark stands for the fixed boundaries the law sets; to honor it is to honor the allotment, to move it is to steal by stealth.

proofTexts.text: Thou shalt not remove thy neighbour’s landmark.
Cursed be he that removeth his neighbour’s landmark.
Remove not the ancient landmark, which thy fathers have set.
Remove not the old landmark; and enter not into the fields of the fatherless.

plainTerms: A landmark was the boundary stone that marked a family’s legal title to its land. Moving it was theft — stealing land by redrawing the line — and Torah put it under a curse. To respect the landmark is to honor the fixed boundaries the law set.
bringItHome: The boundary stone told everyone where your land ended and your neighbour’s began. Slide it a few feet in the night and you have stolen his field without touching a plow. That is why ‘remove not the landmark’ carries a curse: it is quiet theft of a lawful holding.

courtroomRoles.does: whose inheritance the landmark protects.
steals by redrawing the boundary.
fixes the boundaries and curses their removal.

23.lead: Liberty is the legal release of the bound — a manumission term, not a mood of freedom. Deror is the specific word for the release proclaimed at Jubilee: “proclaim liberty throughout all the land unto all the inhabitants thereof” (Leviticus 25:10). It is the freeing of slaves, the cancelling of servitude, the return of the captive to his own — an act of law with a legal record. When Isaiah announces “liberty to the captives” (Isaiah 61:1), the word is release, the loosing of one held. Liberty in Scripture is not the absence of law but a provision of it: the law’s own mechanism for setting the bound free.

root.sense: liberty, release; the manumission of the bound

23.courtroomWord: A release term — the legal manumission of one held in bondage.
23.itsRole: Bondage has a lawful end, and liberty is it — the release of the captive, the cancelling of servitude, proclaimed by statute at Jubilee. Deror is a legal act, not a feeling: the bound set free by the law’s own provision. Isaiah’s ‘liberty to the captives’ is this release, and the good news announces it. Liberty is not freedom from law but the law freeing the bound.

proofTexts.text: Proclaim liberty throughout all the land unto all the inhabitants thereof.
To proclaim liberty to the captives.
To proclaim liberty unto them.
The liberty wherewith Messiah hath made us free.
proofTexts.note: The release into a standing to be held.

plainTerms: Liberty is a legal release — the freeing of the bound — not a vague feeling of freedom. Deror is the manumission word proclaimed at Jubilee: slaves freed, servitude cancelled, captives returned. It is the law’s own mechanism for setting people free.
bringItHome: When Jubilee ‘proclaimed liberty,’ slaves walked out free and debts were cleared — a legal release, enacted by statute. That is deror. And when Isaiah announced liberty to the captives, he used the same word: not freedom from the law, but the law itself loosing the bound.

courtroomRoles.does: proclaims the release by statute.
freed from servitude and captivity.
the mechanism by which liberty is granted.

84.lead: To ‘lift the face’ — nasa panim — is the courtroom idiom for partiality: to accept a person’s face, to be swayed by who stands before the bench rather than by the case. Torah forbids it flatly: the judge shall not “respect persons” — not lift the face — “neither take a gift” (Deuteronomy 16:19). Justice requires a blind bench, weighing the matter and not the man. This is why Yahuah is praised as the One who “regardeth not persons” (Deuteronomy 10:17): the perfect Judge lifts no one’s face. To lift the face is to corrupt judgment at its root, ruling by favor instead of fact.

root.sense: to lift the face; from nasa (to lift) + panim (face) — the idiom for partiality

sharesRoot.note: Nasa lifts a charge away (Forgive), bears one as liability (Bear Iniquity), or lifts an empty report and carries it (False Report); panim is the face one appears before (Face) or lifts in partiality here.

84.courtroomWord: A partiality idiom — to be swayed by the person rather than the case.
84.itsRole: A just verdict weighs the matter, not the man; to lift the face is to weigh the man. Torah forbids it in the judge and praises Yahuah for never doing it. The lifted face is judgment corrupted at the root — ruling by who stands there, by gift or status or fear, instead of by the evidence. The blind bench, lifting no one’s face, is the standard the law demands and Yahuah keeps.

proofTexts.text: Thou shalt not respect persons, neither take a gift.
Which regardeth not persons, nor taketh reward.
Thou shalt not respect the person of the poor, nor honour the person of the mighty.
proofTexts.note: No face lifted, high or low.

proofTexts.text: Elohim is no respecter of persons.

plainTerms: To ‘lift the face’ is Scripture’s idiom for partiality — being swayed by who is standing before you instead of by the facts. Torah forbids judges to do it and praises Yahuah for never doing it. It means ruling by favor instead of by evidence.
bringItHome: A corrupt judge ‘lifts the face’ — he looks at who is in front of him, their status, their gift, their power, and rules for them instead of for the truth. Torah bans it outright. The perfect Judge lifts no one’s face: He weighs the case, never the man.

courtroomRoles.does: forbidden to lift any face, high or low.
regards no person and takes no gift.
to be weighed by the case, not the face.

55.lead: The lot was a binding method of judicial allocation — a decision entrusted to Yahuah and accepted as final, without appeal. The land of Canaan was divided ‘by lot’ (Numbers 26:55), Achan was identified by lot (Joshua 7:14-18), and the apostles filled Judas’s place by lot (Acts 1:26). “The lot is cast into the lap; but the whole disposing thereof is of Yahuah” (Proverbs 16:33) — the outcome was received as His ruling. The lot was not gambling but adjudication: a legally binding allotment or verdict, settled by a means that removed human favoritism and left the decision to the Judge.

root.sense: a lot; a binding allotment or decision made by lot

55.courtroomWord: An allocation term — a binding judicial decision entrusted to Yahuah, without appeal.
55.itsRole: Some decisions were settled by lot — the division of the land, the identifying of the guilty, the filling of an office — and the result was binding, received as Yahuah’s ruling. It removed favoritism: no face could be lifted where the Judge disposed the outcome. The lot is judicial allocation, final and without appeal, its whole disposing His.

proofTexts.text: The lot is cast into the lap; but the whole disposing thereof is of Yahuah.
proofTexts.note: The outcome received as His ruling.

proofTexts.text: The land shall be divided by lot.
proofTexts.note: The binding allocation of the inheritance.

proofTexts.text: The tribe which Yahuah taketh shall come.
They gave forth their lots; and the lot fell upon Matthias.
proofTexts.note: An office filled by binding lot.

plainTerms: The lot was a binding way of deciding — dividing land, finding the guilty, filling an office — with the result received as Yahuah’s ruling, final and without appeal. It was not gambling; it was adjudication that left the decision to the Judge and removed human favoritism.
bringItHome: When Israel divided the land or filled an office ‘by lot,’ they were not rolling dice for fun — they were handing the decision to Yahuah and accepting the result as binding. ‘The whole disposing is of Yahuah’: the lot was a verdict, final, with no favoritism and no appeal.

courtroomRoles.does: disposes the outcome of the lot.
bound by the result without appeal.
the binding method of allocation.

97.lead: The modern West reads love as a feeling; Scripture reads it as covenant loyalty enacted — allegiance shown in deeds. “Thou shalt love Yahuah thy Elohim” (Deuteronomy 6:5) is a covenant command, and no one can command a feeling; what is commanded is loyalty, the wholehearted allegiance a covenant party owes. Love in this register is measurable by conduct: “if ye love me, keep my commandments” (John 14:15). It is the treaty word for the devotion a vassal owes his sovereign — fidelity in action, not warmth in the chest. To love Yahuah is to keep covenant with Him; the feeling may follow, but the love is the loyalty.

root.sense: to love; covenant loyalty
love as committed goodwill and allegiance

97.courtroomWord: A loyalty term — covenant allegiance shown in conduct.
97.itsRole: Love, in covenant, is loyalty, not feeling — which is why it can be commanded. To love Yahuah is to render the wholehearted allegiance the covenant requires, proven by keeping His terms. ‘If ye love me, keep my commandments’ ties love directly to conduct. It is the devotion a covenant party owes, measurable in action, the feeling secondary to the fidelity.

proofTexts.text: Thou shalt love Yahuah thy Elohim with all thine heart.
If ye love me, keep my commandments.
This is the love of Elohim, that we keep his commandments.
Keepeth covenant and mercy with them that love him.

plainTerms: Love, in Scripture, is covenant loyalty shown in action — not a feeling. You cannot command a feeling, but ‘love Yahuah’ is commanded, because it means allegiance: keeping His terms. ‘If ye love me, keep my commandments’ ties love to conduct. The feeling may come; the loyalty is the love.
bringItHome: You cannot order someone to feel something — yet ‘love Yahuah’ is a command. That is because love here is loyalty, the allegiance a covenant party owes, proven by keeping the terms. ‘If ye love me, keep my commandments’ is the definition: love is fidelity in action.

courtroomRoles.does: owes loyalty, shown by keeping the terms.
to whom the allegiance is owed.
by which love is measured.

106.lead: A measure is the fixed standard of judgment — the just weight or rule the law requires, and the standard by which one will be judged. Torah demands honest measures: “a perfect and just measure shalt thou have” (Deuteronomy 25:15), because a false measure is a lie built into the transaction. And the standard cuts both ways: “with what measure ye mete, it shall be measured to you again” (Matthew 7:2) — the rule you apply becomes the rule applied to you. A measure is not arbitrary; it is the fixed benchmark against which quantity, and conduct, are judged. To keep a just measure is to keep the law’s own standard of fairness.

root.sense: a measure, a measured standard; the rule by which a thing is judged

106.courtroomWord: A standard term — the fixed benchmark against which quantity and conduct are judged.
106.itsRole: Judgment needs a fixed standard, and the measure is it. Torah requires it just — a false measure defrauds — and warns that the measure one uses returns on one’s own head. The measure is the benchmark: quantity weighed by it, conduct judged by it. To keep a just measure is to keep the law’s standard; to falsify it is to build fraud into the very rule of judgment.

proofTexts.text: A perfect and just measure shalt thou have.
Ye shall do no unrighteousness in judgment, in meteyard, in weight, or in measure.
With what measure ye mete, it shall be measured to you again.
proofTexts.note: The standard returned on the one who sets it.

proofTexts.text: The bag of deceitful weights.

plainTerms: A measure is the fixed standard by which things are judged — a just weight, an honest rule. Torah demands it be true, because a false measure builds a lie into the deal. And the standard cuts both ways: the measure you use on others is the one used on you.
bringItHome: A crooked scale cheats every transaction it touches — which is why Torah demands ‘a perfect and just measure.’ A measure is the fixed standard judgment runs on. And there is a warning in it: the measure you apply to others becomes the measure applied to you.

courtroomRoles.does: requires the measure just, and applies it justly.
weighed by the fixed standard.
the benchmark of quantity and conduct.

11.lead: A mediator is the legally recognized go-between who stands between two parties to make a covenant hold — an office, not a friendly gesture. Moses served as mediator of the Sinai covenant, receiving the terms and standing between Yahuah and the people (Galatians 3:19). “There is one mediator between Yahuah and men, the man Messiah Yahushua” (1 Timothy 2:5) names the office precisely: one authorized party bridging the two sides so the covenant can stand. Note the framing — ‘the man’ — the mediator represents men before Yahuah, an appointed intermediary, not a third party equal to the One he mediates toward.

root.sense: a mediator, an arbitrator; the middle party who makes a covenant hold

11.courtroomWord: An office term — the authorized go-between who makes a covenant stand.
11.itsRole: A covenant between parties at distance needs a mediator — the recognized middle party who carries the terms and stands between the two. Moses did it at Sinai; the Messiah does it for the renewed covenant. The office is representative: the mediator stands for men before Yahuah, an appointed intermediary. ‘One mediator... the man Messiah Yahushua’ locates Him as the authorized bridge, not a co-equal to the One toward whom He mediates.

proofTexts.text: One mediator between Yahuah and men, the man Messiah Yahushua.
proofTexts.note: The office named — the mediator a man, for men.

proofTexts.text: Ordained by angels in the hand of a mediator.
He is the mediator of the new testament.
proofTexts.note: The office for the renewed covenant.

proofTexts.text: To Yahushua the mediator of the new covenant.
proofTexts.note: The go-between who makes it hold.

plainTerms: A mediator is the authorized go-between who stands between two parties to make a covenant hold — an office, not a favor. Moses did it at Sinai; the Messiah does it now. And note ‘the man Messiah Yahushua’: the mediator represents men before Yahuah, an appointed bridge, not a co-equal.
bringItHome: When two parties cannot come together directly, a recognized middle man carries the terms and makes the agreement stand. That is a mediator. Moses stood between Yahuah and Israel; Yahushua stands between Yahuah and men — ‘the man,’ the appointed go-between, representing us before the bench.

courtroomRoles.does: the appointed man who stands between Yahuah and men to make the covenant hold.
toward whom the mediator represents men.
whom the mediator represents.

36.lead: A memorial is a remembrance filed on the record — an act or object that keeps a matter formally before the court, and before Yahuah. The feast of Pesach is “a memorial” (Exodus 12:14); the stones from Jordan stand as a memorial (Joshua 4:7); the offering bears ‘the memorial thereof’ before Yahuah. A memorial is not mere nostalgia; it is a deliberate entry into the record, a marker set so that a thing is not forgotten but kept on file. Prayers and deeds can “come up for a memorial before Elohim” (Acts 10:4) — entered before the bench. The memorial is evidence deliberately preserved.

root.sense: a memorial, remembrance; from zakar, to remember — a record kept before

sharesRoot.note: Zikaron is from zakar (to remember): the memorial (zikaron) is the record that keeps a matter remembered (zakar) before the court.

36.courtroomWord: A record term — a remembrance deliberately entered and kept on file.
36.itsRole: A court keeps records so matters are not lost, and the memorial is a record set on purpose — a feast, a stone, an offering — to keep a thing before Yahuah. It is evidence preserved: the deed marked, the deliverance kept on file, the prayer entered ‘for a memorial.’ Far from nostalgia, a memorial is a deliberate entry into the record of the court.

proofTexts.text: This day shall be unto you for a memorial.
proofTexts.note: The deliverance kept on the record.

proofTexts.text: These stones shall be for a memorial.
proofTexts.note: A marker set to keep the matter remembered.

proofTexts.text: Thy prayers and thine alms are come up for a memorial before Elohim.
Burn the memorial of it upon the altar.

plainTerms: A memorial is a remembrance put on the record — a feast, a stone, an offering — set on purpose so a matter is kept before Yahuah, not forgotten. It is not nostalgia; it is evidence deliberately preserved. Prayers and deeds can come up ‘for a memorial’ before the bench.
bringItHome: A memorial is not a warm memory — it is a marker deliberately set so a thing stays on the record. Pesach keeps the deliverance on file; the Jordan stones keep the crossing remembered; a prayer comes up ‘for a memorial’ before Elohim. It is evidence, kept on purpose.

courtroomRoles.does: before whom the memorial is kept.
entering the matter into the record.
the remembrance preserved as evidence.

72.lead: Messiah — mashiach, ‘the anointed one’ — is a title of appointed office, not a name and not a claim to independent deity. To be the Messiah is to be the One Yahuah anointed and installed: invested with office by the Anointer, holding authority conferred, not seized. Kings and priests were each a mashiach in their measure; the Messiah is the anointed One in the fullest measure, appointed to reign and to judge by the Father’s own commission. The title itself is a hierarchy: there is One who anoints and one who is anointed. To confess Yahushua as Messiah is to confess Him as the appointed of Yahuah — given dominion, not sharing an eternal throne by nature.

root.sense: anointed, the anointed one; from mashach, to anoint into office

sharesRoot.note: Mashiach is from mashach (to anoint): the Messiah is the one the anointing produces, the office-holder installed by the Anointer.

72.courtroomWord: A title of appointed office — the One anointed and installed by Yahuah.
72.itsRole: The Messiah holds an office conferred, not a rank possessed by nature. Mashiach means anointed — installed by the Anointer — and the title itself names two parties: One who anoints, one who is anointed. Kings, priests, and prophets were anointed in their measure; the Messiah is the anointed One in full, given dominion and judgment by the Father’s commission. To confess the Messiah is to confess the appointed of Yahuah.

proofTexts.text: Against Yahuah, and against his anointed.
proofTexts.note: The Anointer and the anointed — two parties.

proofTexts.text: Unto the Messiah the Prince.
Yahuah hath made that same Yahushua... both Lord and Messiah.
Yahuah anointed Yahushua of Nazareth.
proofTexts.note: The Anointer and the anointed named.

plainTerms: Messiah means ‘anointed one’ — a title of appointed office, not a name and not a claim to be co-equal deity. To be the Messiah is to be the One Yahuah anointed and installed, given authority by the Anointer. The title itself has two parties: One who anoints, and one who is anointed.
bringItHome: ‘Messiah’ is not a surname — it is an office, ‘the anointed one.’ And an anointed one, by definition, was anointed by someone: there is an Anointer and an anointed. To confess Yahushua as Messiah is to confess Him as the One Yahuah appointed and installed — given dominion, not sharing a throne by nature.

courtroomRoles.does: anoints and installs the Messiah into office.
the anointed One, given authority to reign and judge.
the commission conferred, not seized.

87.lead: The mouth is where testimony and decree issue — the organ of legal utterance. “At the mouth of two witnesses... shall the matter be established” (Deuteronomy 19:15) counts mouths, not hearings: the case stands on independent testimony spoken. And “out of thine own mouth will I judge thee” (Luke 19:22) makes one’s own words evidence against oneself. The mouth is the point where a matter enters the record — by testimony, by confession, by oath, by decree. To establish a thing ‘at the mouth’ of witnesses is to require it spoken and corroborated; the mouth is where the word becomes legally binding.

root.sense: mouth; the organ of speech, testimony, and decree

87.courtroomWord: A testimony term — the point where a matter is spoken into the record.
87.itsRole: A court runs on what is spoken, and the mouth is where speech becomes legal. Testimony is counted ‘at the mouth’ of witnesses; confession, oath, and decree all issue from it; one’s own mouth can convict. The two-or-three-witness rule counts mouths precisely — independent sources of speech, corroborated. The mouth is where a word enters the record and becomes binding.

proofTexts.text: At the mouth of two witnesses... shall the matter be established.
At the mouth of two witnesses, or three witnesses, shall he... be put to death.
Out of thine own mouth will I judge thee.
In the mouth of two or three witnesses every word may be established.

plainTerms: The mouth is where legal words are spoken — testimony, confession, oath, decree. ‘At the mouth of two witnesses’ counts mouths, not hearings: a matter stands on independent testimony. And your own mouth can convict you. The mouth is where a word enters the record and becomes binding.
bringItHome: A matter was established ‘at the mouth’ of two or three witnesses — the count was of mouths, of independent voices, not one story repeated. The mouth is where words become legal: testimony given, oaths sworn, and sometimes a man’s own words used to judge him.

courtroomRoles.does: whose independent testimony establishes the matter.
whose own mouth can convict him.
establishes the matter at the mouth of witnesses.

38.lead: A name in Scripture is legal identity and authority — not a mere label but the standing a person holds and the authority he acts under. To act ‘in the name’ of another is to act with delegated legal authority (1 Samuel 17:45); to have one’s name ‘cut off’ is to lose standing and inheritance (Deuteronomy 25:6). The name carries reputation, right, and legal identity together. This is why blotting out a name is a judicial act and why the Name of Yahuah is treated with such weight — to invoke it is to invoke His authority. A name is who you are before the law and what you are empowered to do.

root.sense: name; legal identity, reputation, and delegated authority

38.courtroomWord: An identity term — legal standing and the authority one acts under.
38.itsRole: A name is the person’s legal identity: his standing, his reputation, and the authority attached to him. To act in a name is to act with that authority delegated; to blot out a name is to remove a standing. The Name of Yahuah carries His authority, which is why it is invoked in oath, in blessing, and in judgment. A name is who one is before the court and what one is empowered to do.

proofTexts.text: I come to thee in the name of Yahuah of hosts.
That his name be not put out of Israel.
proofTexts.note: The name as standing and inheritance.

proofTexts.text: This is my name for ever.
proofTexts.note: The Name that carries His authority.

proofTexts.text: A good name is rather to be chosen than great riches.
proofTexts.note: The name as reputation and standing.

plainTerms: A name, in Scripture, is your legal identity and the authority you act under — not just a label. To act ‘in the name’ of another is to act with their authority; to have a name ‘blotted out’ is to lose standing. The Name of Yahuah carries His authority.
bringItHome: David came against Goliath ‘in the name of Yahuah’ — not invoking a word, but acting under an authority. That is what a name is: your standing before the law and the power you are empowered to wield. To blot out a name is to erase a legal identity.

courtroomRoles.does: whose Name carries His power to those who act in it.
whose name is his standing and identity.
the legal standing and delegated authority.

122.lead: Nasa avon means ‘to bear iniquity’ — to carry the legal liability of an offense. Nasa is to lift and carry; avon is guilt, the crookedness of a wrong and the penalty it incurs. To bear iniquity is to shoulder the charge and its consequence: sometimes the guilty carry their own (“that soul shall bear his iniquity,” Leviticus 5:1), and sometimes a substitute carries it for them. This is the exact language of the Servant: “he shall bear their iniquities” (Isaiah 53:11). Nasa avon is the mechanism of substitution stated in legal terms — the liability lifted from one party and carried by another, the charge borne rather than merely forgiven.

root.sense: to lift, carry, bear
iniquity, guilt, the liability of a wrong

sharesRoot.note: Nasa lifts a charge off the record (Forgive), lifts a face in partiality (Lift the face), lifts an empty report and carries it (False Report), and here bears the charge as liability.

122.courtroomWord: A liability-bearing term — to carry the charge and penalty of an offense.
122.itsRole: A charge, once entered, must be borne by someone. Nasa avon is the bearing — the guilty carrying their own liability, or a substitute carrying it for them. The same verb that lifts a charge in forgiveness (nasa) here shoulders it as a burden. The Servant bears the iniquity of many: the liability lifted from the guilty and carried by another. It is substitution in the law’s own vocabulary — the charge borne, not waved away.

proofTexts.text: If he do not utter it, then he shall bear his iniquity.
proofTexts.note: The guilty bearing their own liability.

proofTexts.text: He shall bear their iniquities.
proofTexts.note: The Servant carrying the charge of others.

proofTexts.text: The goat shall bear upon him all their iniquities.
proofTexts.note: The liability carried away by a substitute.

proofTexts.text: Ye shall bear your iniquities.

plainTerms: Nasa avon means ‘to bear iniquity’ — to carry the legal liability of a wrong. Sometimes the guilty carry it themselves; sometimes a substitute carries it for them. The Servant ‘bears the iniquities of many’: the charge lifted off the guilty and shouldered by another. It is substitution in legal terms.
bringItHome: Every wrong leaves a liability that someone has to carry. Nasa avon is that carrying. The guilty can bear their own — or a substitute can shoulder it. Isaiah says the Servant ‘bears the iniquities of many’: the same verb that lifts a charge in forgiveness, here carrying it away on His own back.

courtroomRoles.does: whose iniquity is a liability to be borne.
bears the iniquity of many, carrying the charge away.
lays the liability where the covering provides.

104.lead: To number is to enroll on the official roll — an act of legal registration, not mere counting. When Israel was ‘numbered,’ each person was entered on the census with standing, obligation, and a ransom price paid for being counted (Exodus 30:12). To be numbered among a people is to hold recognized membership; to be numbered with the transgressors (Isaiah 53:12) is to be legally reckoned in their company. The word carries enrollment and reckoning together. To have one’s days numbered, or one’s name numbered in a roll, is to be entered on a record that has legal weight. Numbering is registration, and registration is standing.

root.sense: a number, a reckoning
to count, to number, to appoint

104.courtroomWord: A registration term — enrollment on an official roll, with standing and obligation.
104.itsRole: To number is to register — to enter a person on the official roll with the standing and duties membership carries. Israel’s census enrolled each soul, with a ransom for being counted. To be numbered among a people is recognized membership; to be numbered with the transgressors is to be reckoned in their legal company. Numbering is enrollment on a record of weight, and the record confers standing.

proofTexts.text: When thou takest the sum... then shall they give every man a ransom.
proofTexts.note: Numbering as registration with a price.

proofTexts.text: He was numbered with the transgressors.
So teach us to number our days.
Your names are written in heaven.
proofTexts.note: Enrollment on the roll that counts.

plainTerms: To number is to enroll someone on an official roll — registration, not just counting. Israel’s census entered each person with standing and a ransom paid. To be ‘numbered with the transgressors’ is to be legally reckoned in their company. Numbering is enrollment, and enrollment is standing.
bringItHome: When Israel was ‘numbered,’ it was not a headcount for curiosity — it was a legal registration, each soul entered on the roll with a ransom paid for being counted. To be numbered among a people is recognized membership. And Isaiah’s Servant was ‘numbered with the transgressors’: reckoned, on the record, in their company.

courtroomRoles.does: enrolls the people on His roll.
entered with standing and obligation.
the register that confers membership.

141.lead: Orthotomeo means to cut straight — to handle a matter accurately, along its true lines. “Rightly dividing the word of truth” (2 Timothy 2:15) is a single Greek word, orthotomeo: to cut a straight path, as a mason cuts a stone true or a builder lays a straight road. Crucially, it is not ‘dividing’ the word into parts to be discarded — it is the accurate, straight handling of the whole record. The abolition reading turns this verb into a license to partition Scripture and cut pieces away; the word means the opposite: to keep the line straight, handling the testimony without warping or slicing it. Right division is accuracy, not amputation.

root.sense: to cut straight; to handle rightly, along true lines. From orthos (straight) + temno (to cut)

141.courtroomWord: A handling term — the accurate, straight handling of the record.
141.itsRole: The record must be handled truly, and orthotomeo is that handling — cutting a straight line through the testimony, not warping or partitioning it. The word pictures a craftsman cutting straight: the workman that needeth not to be ashamed handles the truth accurately. It is not permission to divide the word and discard sections; it is the demand to keep the line straight. Right division is faithful accuracy, the opposite of slicing the law away.

proofTexts.text: Rightly dividing the word of truth.
proofTexts.note: The straight, accurate handling of the record.

proofTexts.text: A workman that needeth not to be ashamed.
He shall direct thy paths.
proofTexts.note: The straight way — the same picture.

proofTexts.text: I esteem all thy precepts concerning all things to be right.
proofTexts.note: The whole record handled as true.

plainTerms: Orthotomeo means ‘to cut straight’ — to handle the word accurately, along its true lines, like a mason cutting a stone true. ‘Rightly dividing the word of truth’ is not slicing Scripture into keep-and-discard piles; it is handling the whole record straight and accurate. Right division is accuracy, not amputation.
bringItHome: A stonemason ‘cuts straight’ — true to the line, or the whole wall is crooked. That is orthotomeo: handling the word of truth accurately, along its real lines. It does not mean carving Scripture into parts to throw away. It means keeping the cut straight — the opposite of slicing the law off.

courtroomRoles.does: cuts the record straight, handling it accurately.
to be handled true, not warped or partitioned.
whose testimony is kept straight by right handling.

124.rootLine: exo tes paremboles / exo tes pules — Greek
124.lead: ‘Outside the camp’ is the place of the legally condemned — where the sentence was executed and the unclean were put. The blasphemer was taken “without the camp” and stoned (Leviticus 24:14); the sin-offering’s body was burned “without the camp” (Leviticus 4:12); the leper dwelt outside it (Leviticus 13:46). To be put outside the camp was to be removed from the covenant community and its presence — a legal expulsion, the location of judgment executed. This is why Hebrews marks it deliberately: “Yahushua also, that he might sanctify the people with his own blood, suffered without the gate” (Hebrews 13:12). He was executed in the very place the condemned were put — taking the location of the sentence.

root.sense: outside the camp; also exo tes pules (G4439), without the gate — the place of the condemned and unclean

124.courtroomWord: A place term — the location outside the community where the sentence was executed.
124.itsRole: A sentence needs a place of execution, and ‘outside the camp’ is it — where the condemned were stoned, the sin-offering burned, the unclean removed. To be put there was legal expulsion from the covenant community and its presence. Hebrews marks the location on purpose: Yahushua suffered without the gate, executed in the place of the condemned. He took not only the sentence but its location — borne outside, where the guilty were put.

proofTexts.text: Bring forth him that hath cursed without the camp... and let all the congregation stone him.
The whole bullock shall he carry forth without the camp... and burn him.
Yahushua also... suffered without the gate.
proofTexts.note: Executed in the place of the condemned.

proofTexts.text: Let us go forth therefore unto him without the camp, bearing his reproach.
proofTexts.note: Joining Him in the place of reproach.

plainTerms: ‘Outside the camp’ was where the condemned were put — where the guilty were stoned, the sin-offering burned, the unclean sent. It was legal expulsion from the community. And Hebrews notes it on purpose: Yahushua ‘suffered without the gate,’ executed in the very place the condemned were put.
bringItHome: The camp was the place of the living community; outside it was the place of the condemned — execution, burning, banishment. So when Hebrews says Yahushua ‘suffered without the gate,’ it is placing Him exactly where the guilty were sent. He took not just the sentence but its address: outside, with the condemned.

courtroomRoles.does: whose sentence is executed outside the camp.
suffered without the gate, in the place of the guilty.
from which the condemned are removed.

37.lead: A pillar was a standing stone set up as a legal witness — a monument that testified to a covenant or a boundary. Jacob set up a pillar and called it “a witness between me and thee” (Genesis 31:48-52); Joshua set a great stone “for a witness... it hath heard all the words” (Joshua 24:27). The pillar stood as silent, permanent testimony, entered into the record of the land. It is evidence made monumental: a stone that holds the memory of an agreement so it cannot be denied later. To raise a pillar was to file a witness in stone — a testimony that would outlast the parties who made it.

root.sense: a standing pillar, a monument set up as a witness

37.courtroomWord: A witness term — a standing stone set as permanent testimony.
37.itsRole: Testimony can be set in stone, and the pillar is that testimony — a monument witnessing to a covenant or boundary, entered into the record of the land. Jacob’s heap and Joshua’s stone stand ‘for a witness,’ silent and permanent. The pillar is evidence made to outlast the parties: a stone that holds the memory of the agreement so it cannot later be denied. To raise it is to file a witness that endures.

proofTexts.text: This heap is a witness between me and thee this day.
This stone shall be a witness unto us... it hath heard all the words.
Jacob... set it up for a pillar.
Twelve pillars, according to the twelve tribes of Israel.

plainTerms: A pillar was a standing stone set up as a legal witness — a monument testifying to a covenant or boundary. Jacob’s stone was ‘a witness between me and thee’; Joshua’s had ‘heard all the words.’ The pillar is evidence made permanent: a stone that holds the memory of an agreement so it cannot be denied.
bringItHome: When Jacob and Laban made their covenant, they piled up stones and said, ‘this heap is a witness between us.’ The pillar was testimony you could not argue with later — a witness set in stone, standing long after the handshake. To raise a pillar was to file evidence that would outlast everyone present.

courtroomRoles.does: set the pillar as their witness.
the standing stone testifying to the agreement.
before whom the pillar stands as witness.

115.lead: To plead is to bring and argue a lawsuit — to contend a case before the bench, not merely to beg. “Plead my cause, O Yahuah, with them that strive with me” (Psalm 35:1) asks the Judge to take up a legal contest and press it. Rib is the verb of litigation: to enter a controversy, argue it, and seek a ruling. When Yahuah says “Come now, and let us reason together” (Isaiah 1:18), the setting is a courtroom, the parties contending toward a verdict. To plead is to prosecute or defend a real case — which is why Yahuah is asked to plead the cause of the widow and the poor: to take their suit and argue it to judgment.

root.sense: to contend, to conduct a lawsuit, to plead a case

sharesRoot.note: Rib as verb (to plead) and rib as noun (the cause, the case) share the root: to plead is to argue the cause.

115.courtroomWord: A litigation term — to bring and argue a lawsuit before the bench.
115.itsRole: A case must be argued, and to plead is the arguing — contending a controversy before the court toward a ruling. It is not begging but litigation: entering the suit and pressing it. Yahuah is asked to plead the cause of the defenseless — to take their case and argue it to a verdict. He also pleads His own controversy with His people. To plead is to prosecute or defend a real matter at law.

proofTexts.text: Plead my cause, O Yahuah, with them that strive with me.
proofTexts.note: The Judge asked to argue the case.

proofTexts.text: Come now, and let us reason together.
proofTexts.note: The courtroom contest toward a verdict.

proofTexts.text: Yahuah hath a controversy with his people... he will plead with Israel.
He shall plead their cause with thee.
proofTexts.note: The case argued for the defenseless.

plainTerms: To plead is to bring and argue a lawsuit — to contend a case in court — not just to beg. ‘Plead my cause’ asks Yahuah to take up a legal contest and press it to a ruling. He is asked to plead for the widow and the poor: to argue their case to judgment. And He pleads His own controversy with His people.
bringItHome: To ‘plead’ is what a lawyer does — not plead for mercy, but argue the case, contend the matter, press it to a verdict. When the Psalmist cries ‘plead my cause,’ he wants the Judge to enter the fight and argue it. And Yahuah pleads for the defenseless the same way: taking their suit and arguing it to judgment.

courtroomRoles.does: argues the cause of the defenseless, and His own controversy.
whose case is argued before the bench.
the controversy pleaded toward a verdict.

54.lead: A portion is the assigned legal share — the part of an estate allotted to a party by right. The Levites received “no portion” of land because “Yahuah is their portion” (Deuteronomy 10:9); each tribe received its portion of the inheritance by allotment. Cheleq is a share fixed by law, not distributed by whim. To have a portion is to hold a defined claim on the estate; to say “Yahuah is my portion” (Psalm 73:26) is to claim Him as one’s assigned inheritance, using estate language deliberately. A portion is what the law apportions to you — your legal share, entered and secured.

root.sense: a portion, share, allotment; the legally assigned part

54.courtroomWord: A share term — the legally assigned part of an estate.
54.itsRole: An estate is divided into shares, and the portion is one’s assigned part — fixed by law, not by favor. The tribes received their portions by allotment; the Levites’ portion was Yahuah Himself. To hold a portion is to hold a defined, secured claim on the inheritance. ‘Yahuah is my portion’ claims Him as one’s allotted share — estate language, chosen on purpose. The portion is what the law apportions, entered and held by right.

proofTexts.text: The Levites have no part nor inheritance... Yahuah is his inheritance.
proofTexts.note: The portion assigned — here Yahuah Himself.

proofTexts.text: Elohim is... my portion for ever.
proofTexts.note: Claiming Him as one’s allotted share.

proofTexts.text: I am thy part and thine inheritance among the children of Israel.
Yahuah is the portion of mine inheritance.
proofTexts.note: The assigned share held by right.

plainTerms: A portion is your assigned legal share of an estate — fixed by law, not handed out on a whim. The tribes got their portions by allotment; the Levites’ portion was Yahuah Himself. To say ‘Yahuah is my portion’ is to claim Him as your assigned inheritance, using estate language on purpose.
bringItHome: When an estate is divided, each heir gets a portion — a defined share, secured by law. That is cheleq. And the deepest use turns it personal: the Levites held no land because ‘Yahuah is their portion.’ To say that is to claim Him as your assigned inheritance — the share the law apportions to you.

courtroomRoles.does: assigns each party its portion; is Himself the Levite’s portion.
holds the assigned share by right.

57.lead: To possess is to take and hold as legal owner — to enter into lawful ownership, often by dispossessing a prior holder. “Go up and possess it” (Deuteronomy 1:21) is a command to take legal title to the land, driving out those who held it without right. Yarash carries both taking possession and holding it: seizure ripening into ownership. To possess the inheritance is to come into full legal ownership of the estate, not merely to occupy it. This is why possession is spoken of as secured or lost — it is title, held or forfeited. To possess is to own by right, entered on the record as the lawful holder.

root.sense: to take possession, to inherit, to dispossess; to seize and hold as owner

57.courtroomWord: An ownership term — taking and holding lawful title to an estate.
57.itsRole: To possess is to hold legal title — to take ownership and keep it, sometimes by dispossessing a prior holder without right. Israel was to possess the land: enter into lawful ownership of the inheritance. Possession is title held, which is why it can be secured or forfeited. To possess the estate is to own it by right, entered on the record as the lawful holder, not merely to occupy the ground.

proofTexts.text: Go up and possess it, as Yahuah... hath said.
proofTexts.note: The command to take legal title.

proofTexts.text: Thou shalt possess it.
To give thee this land to inherit it.
His seed shall inherit the earth.

plainTerms: To possess is to take and hold legal ownership — to come into title, sometimes by removing a holder who had no right. ‘Go up and possess the land’ means take lawful ownership of it, not just walk on it. Possession is title, held or forfeited.
bringItHome: To possess is more than to occupy — it is to hold legal title, to own by right. When Israel was told to ‘possess the land,’ they were to enter into lawful ownership of the inheritance. Possession is a deed in hand, not just feet on the ground — and like any title, it can be kept or lost.

courtroomRoles.does: gives the estate to be possessed.
takes and holds lawful title.
possessed as owned property.

77.lead: The priest is an officer of the court who teaches the law and renders rulings on it — far more than a man who offers sacrifices. “The priest’s lips should keep knowledge, and they should seek the law at his mouth” (Malachi 2:7); hard cases were brought “unto the priests the Levites, and unto the judge” for a binding decision (Deuteronomy 17:9). The kohen mediated between Yahuah and the people, taught the distinctions of clean and unclean, and pronounced legal findings. He is a judicial and teaching officer, standing in the court of the sanctuary. To hold the priesthood was to hold an office of instruction and adjudication in the law of Yahuah.

root.sense: a priest; an officer who ministers, teaches the law, and renders rulings

77.courtroomWord: An office term — the officer who teaches the law and renders rulings on it.
77.itsRole: The priest is a court officer: he mediates, teaches the law, and pronounces findings — clean or unclean, guilty or clear. Hard cases came to the priests for a binding ruling. His lips keep knowledge, and the people seek the law at his mouth. The priesthood is a teaching and judicial office in the sanctuary’s court, not merely a sacrificial role. To be a priest is to instruct and adjudicate in the law.

proofTexts.text: The priest’s lips should keep knowledge, and they should seek the law at his mouth.
Thou shalt come unto the priests the Levites, and unto the judge... and they shall shew thee the sentence of judgment.
That ye may teach the children of Israel all the statutes.
proofTexts.note: The priest as teacher of the law.

proofTexts.text: The priest shall look on him, and pronounce him unclean.

plainTerms: A priest was an officer of the court — he taught the law, mediated, and rendered rulings (clean or unclean, and more) — not just a man at an altar. Hard cases came to the priests for a binding decision. ‘Seek the law at his mouth’: the priesthood was a teaching and judicial office.
bringItHome: The priest was not merely a sacrifice-offerer — he was the man you went to for a ruling: is this clean or unclean, guilty or clear, what does the law require here? ‘Seek the law at his mouth.’ He taught the statutes and pronounced findings. The priesthood was an office of the court, standing in the sanctuary.

courtroomRoles.does: teaches the law and renders rulings on it.
who seek the law at his mouth.
whose law the priest teaches and applies.

70.lead: To profane is to breach a holy boundary — to treat as common what the law set apart, a legal violation of the sacred. Chalal is the opposite of sanctify: to sanctify sets a thing apart into holy status; to profane drags it back into common use, breaking the boundary. To “profane the sabbath” (Exodus 31:14) or “profane the name” (Leviticus 22:32) is not a mood but an act — the violation of a set-apart status. The priest who profaned his office, the man who profaned the holy things, incurred real legal consequence. To profane is to cross a line the law drew around the holy, collapsing the distinction between sacred and common.

root.sense: to profane, to defile, to treat as common; to breach a holy boundary

70.courtroomWord: A violation term — the breaching of a set-apart, holy status.
70.itsRole: The law draws boundaries around the holy, and to profane is to breach them — to treat as common what was set apart. It is the reverse of sanctifying: sanctify moves a thing into holy status, profane drags it back to common. Profaning the sabbath, the name, or the holy things is an act with legal consequence, not a feeling. To profane is to collapse the distinction the law established between sacred and common.

proofTexts.text: Every one that defileth it shall surely be put to death.
proofTexts.note: Profaning the sabbath — a capital breach.

proofTexts.text: Neither shall ye profane my holy name.
proofTexts.note: The breach of the holy Name.

proofTexts.text: They have profaned mine holy things... they have put no difference between the holy and profane.
Judah... hath profaned the holiness of Yahuah.

plainTerms: To profane is to breach a holy boundary — to treat as common what the law set apart. It is the opposite of sanctifying. To ‘profane the sabbath’ or ‘profane the name’ is a real legal violation, not a mood: crossing the line the law drew around the holy and collapsing the difference between sacred and common.
bringItHome: To sanctify is to set a thing apart as holy; to profane is to drag it back into common use, breaking the boundary. Profaning the sabbath or the Name was not a bad attitude — it was an act that crossed a line the law had drawn, with real consequence. It collapses the distinction the law worked to keep.

courtroomRoles.does: sets the boundaries around the holy.
breaches the boundary, treating the holy as common.
the sabbath, the Name, the sanctuary — violated.

44.lead: A promise is a binding pledge that confers a legal claim on the one who receives it — not a hopeful intention but an enforceable commitment. When Scripture speaks of “the promise” made to Abraham (Galatians 3:16), it means a covenant grant that created a right, guaranteed by the character and oath of the Promiser. An epaggelia is a legal undertaking: the party who gives it is bound, and the party who holds it has standing to claim it. This is why the promises are called ‘yea and amen’ — confirmed, signed, sure. To hold a promise of Yahuah is to hold an enforceable claim, secured by the One who cannot lie.

root.sense: a promise, a pledge; a binding legal undertaking

44.courtroomWord: A pledge term — a binding commitment that confers an enforceable claim.
44.itsRole: A promise binds the one who gives it and grants a claim to the one who receives it. The promise to Abraham created a right, secured by oath. It is not intention but undertaking: the Promiser is bound, the holder has standing. Yahuah confirms His promises by oath so that the heirs might have strong consolation — an enforceable guarantee. To hold His promise is to hold a legal claim, sure because the Promiser cannot lie.

proofTexts.text: To Abraham and his seed were the promises made.
proofTexts.note: The covenant grant that created a right.

proofTexts.text: It was impossible for Elohim to lie.
All the promises of Elohim in him are yea, and in him Amen.
What he had promised, he was able also to perform.

plainTerms: A promise is a binding pledge that gives you a legal claim — not a hopeful ‘I’ll try,’ but an enforceable commitment. The promise to Abraham created a right, guaranteed by oath. The Promiser is bound; the one who holds it has standing to claim it. Yahuah’s promises are ‘yea and amen’: confirmed, signed, sure.
bringItHome: A promise from Yahuah is not a wish — it is a binding undertaking that gives you an enforceable claim, secured by His oath and His character. He even swore an oath ‘that we might have strong consolation.’ To hold His promise is to hold a legal guarantee, sure because the One who gave it cannot lie.

courtroomRoles.does: binds Himself by the pledge, confirmed by oath.
has standing to claim the promise.
the enforceable commitment secured by the Promiser.

125.lead: Kategoros is the prosecutor — the party who stands before the bench and presses the charge against the accused. It is the noun behind the verb ‘to accuse’ (kategoreo): the one who lodges the indictment and argues for the defendant’s guilt. Revelation names the great kategoros, “the accuser of our brethren... which accused them before our Elohim day and night” (Revelation 12:10). The prosecutor’s whole function depends on a live charge under a real law; where the account is answered, he has nothing to prosecute. To face a kategoros is to face a formal case pressed against you — and to have an Advocate is to have that case answered.

root.sense: an accuser, a prosecutor; the party who brings the charge in court

sharesRoot.note: Kategoros (the prosecutor) and kategoreo (to accuse) share the kateg- root: the party, and the act of pressing the charge.

125.courtroomWord: A prosecution term — the party who presses the charge before the bench.
125.itsRole: Every trial has a prosecutor, and the kategoros is it — the party who lodges the charge and argues the defendant’s guilt. The great accuser prosecutes the brethren without rest, but his case stands only while the charge is live and unanswered. Against the covered, the Advocate answers it and the prosecutor is cast down. The kategoros holds no power beyond an open charge.

proofTexts.text: The accuser of our brethren... accused them before our Elohim day and night.
Where are those thine accusers?
proofTexts.note: The prosecutors withdrawn, no case pressed.

proofTexts.text: Gave commandment to his accusers... to say before thee.
proofTexts.note: Accusers bringing their charge to the bench.

proofTexts.text: Have the accusers face to face, and have licence to answer.
proofTexts.note: The prosecutor faced, the defense allowed.

plainTerms: A kategoros is a prosecutor — the party who presses the charge against you in court. It is the noun for ‘accuser.’ The great one prosecutes the brethren day and night, but only while the charge is open. Answer the account, and the prosecutor has nothing to press.
bringItHome: Picture the prosecutor at his table, indictment in hand, arguing your guilt to the judge. That is the kategoros. He works relentlessly — but the moment your Advocate lays a paid receipt on the bench, the charge is answered and the prosecutor is dismissed. His power was only ever a live case.

courtroomRoles.does: presses the charge against the accused.
answers the charge for the defense.
before whom the case is lodged, and who dismisses it.

126.lead: Qerev is to draw near, to approach; haqrev, its causative, is to be brought near — formally presented before authority. In Daniel’s vision, one “like the Son of man... came to the Ancient of days, and they brought him near before him” (Daniel 7:13). This is not a casual approach but a legal presentation: escorted into the presence of the court to receive what the bench confers. The same root governs the bringing near of offerings and of persons before Yahuah. To be brought near is to be presented before the bench — and in Daniel 7, the One presented receives dominion, glory, and a kingdom from the Ancient of Days.

root.sense: to draw near, approach; causative, to be brought near, presented before (Aramaic)

126.courtroomWord: A presentation term — to be formally brought near before the bench.
126.itsRole: To come before the court is to be presented, and haqrev is that presentation — escorted into the presence of authority to receive what it confers. In Daniel 7 the Son of man is brought near before the Ancient of Days and given an everlasting dominion. The bringing-near is legal, not casual: a party presented before the bench, receiving from it. Approach to Yahuah, of offerings and of persons, runs on this same root.

proofTexts.text: They brought him near before him.
proofTexts.note: The Son of man presented before the Ancient of Days.

proofTexts.text: There was given him dominion, and glory, and a kingdom.
proofTexts.note: What the presented One receives from the bench — given, not seized.

proofTexts.text: Ye shall bring your offering.
proofTexts.note: The bringing-near of what is presented before Yahuah.

proofTexts.text: Moses brought their cause before Yahuah.
proofTexts.note: A matter presented before the court.

plainTerms: Qerev means to draw near; haqrev means to be brought near — formally presented before authority. In Daniel 7, the Son of man is ‘brought near’ before the Ancient of Days: escorted into the court to receive dominion. It is a legal presentation, not a casual approach.
bringItHome: In Daniel 7, the Son of man does not simply walk up — He is ‘brought near,’ presented before the Ancient of Days like a party escorted before the bench. And there He receives dominion, glory, and a kingdom — given by the court, not seized. To be brought near is to be presented to receive.

courtroomRoles.does: before whom the presentation is made, and who confers dominion.
brought near, presented, and given the kingdom.
who present the party before the bench.

15.lead: A ransom is the price that answers a forfeited life — the payment that lawfully releases one whose life is otherwise required. Kopher is the sum accepted in place of a life owed: “then he shall give for the ransom of his life whatsoever is laid upon him” (Exodus 21:30). Lutron, in the Greek, is the price of release: the Son of man came “to give his life a ransom for many” (Matthew 20:28). A ransom presupposes a real debt of life — a claim the law has filed that must be satisfied. It is not a symbol of rescue but the legal price that discharges the claim, releasing the one whose life was forfeit.

root.sense: a ransom, the price of a life
the price of release

sharesRoot.note: Kopher (ransom) and kaphar (atonement) share the k-p-r root: the ransom is the price the atonement covers with.

15.courtroomWord: A price term — the payment that lawfully releases a forfeited life.
15.itsRole: When a life is forfeit, the law may accept a ransom in its place — the price that discharges the claim. Kopher is that price; lutron is the release it buys. The ransom presupposes a real debt of life the court has filed. The Son of man gives His life a ransom for many: the price that answers the forfeit and releases the bound. It is a legal transaction, not a picture — the claim satisfied, the captive freed.

proofTexts.text: Then he shall give for the ransom of his life whatsoever is laid upon him.
proofTexts.note: The price accepted for a life owed.

proofTexts.text: To give his life a ransom for many.
Deliver him from going down to the pit: I have found a ransom.
proofTexts.note: The ransom that releases the condemned.

proofTexts.text: Who gave himself a ransom for all.

plainTerms: A ransom is the price that answers a forfeited life — the payment that lawfully releases someone whose life is otherwise required. It assumes a real debt of life the court has filed. The Son of man gave His life ‘a ransom for many’: the price that discharged the claim and freed the bound.
bringItHome: When a life was forfeit under the law, a ransom — an accepted price — could be paid in its place, and the condemned went free. That is what ‘a ransom for many’ means: not a poetic rescue, but the legal price that answered the claim on forfeited lives. The debt of life was real, and the price satisfied it.

courtroomRoles.does: His life the price that releases the forfeited.
who accepts the ransom and releases the bound.
whose lives were required, now released by the price.

101.lead: To reckon is to credit or debit an account — to enter a value on the ledger, formally and with consequence. “Abraham believed Yahuah, and it was counted unto him for righteousness” (Genesis 15:6) is accounting language: a value entered to his account. Logizomai, the Greek, is a bookkeeping verb — to calculate, to impute, to post to a ledger. To be reckoned righteous is to have righteousness credited to one’s account, entered on the books. And sin can be reckoned or not reckoned (Romans 4:8) — debited or left off the ledger. Reckoning is not sentiment; it is the formal entry that determines the balance.

root.sense: to reckon, account, impute
to calculate, to credit or debit an account

101.courtroomWord: A ledger term — to credit or debit a value to an account.
101.itsRole: The books must be posted, and to reckon is the posting — crediting or debiting a value to a party’s account. Abraham’s belief was reckoned for righteousness: a value entered on his ledger. Sin can be not reckoned: left off the books. Reckoning determines the balance a party stands at before the court. It is formal accounting, not feeling — the entry that fixes what one is credited or charged.

proofTexts.text: He believed Yahuah; and he counted it to him for righteousness.
proofTexts.note: A value credited to the account.

proofTexts.text: Blessed is the man to whom Yahuah will not impute sin.
proofTexts.note: The charge left off the ledger.

proofTexts.text: The reward... reckoned of debt.
proofTexts.note: The accounting of debit and credit.

proofTexts.text: Not imputing their trespasses unto them.
proofTexts.note: The debt not posted to the account.

plainTerms: To reckon is to credit or debit an account — to enter a value on the ledger. Abraham’s belief was ‘reckoned for righteousness’: credited to his books. Sin can be ‘not reckoned’: left off. It is accounting, not sentiment — the formal entry that determines the balance you stand at.
bringItHome: A bookkeeper ‘reckons’ — posts a credit or a debit to your account, and the balance changes. That is what happened with Abraham: his belief was reckoned to him as righteousness, entered on his ledger. And the mercy is that sin can be ‘not reckoned’ — the charge left off the books entirely.

courtroomRoles.does: credits and debits each account.
whose balance the reckoning fixes.
where the value is entered.

29.lead: To reconcile is to bring estranged parties back into a settled legal relationship — the ledger brought to zero, the enmity removed, peace restored between them. Katallasso is a relational-legal term: “we were reconciled to Yahuah by the death of his Son” (Romans 5:10). It presupposes a real breach — parties at law, a standing hostility — that is formally ended. Reconciliation is not a warm feeling but a change of legal standing: the two parties, once opposed, brought back into accord, the account settled between them. To be reconciled is to have the dispute resolved and the relationship restored, on the record.

root.sense: to reconcile, to change from enmity to accord; to settle a relationship

29.courtroomWord: A settlement term — the restoring of estranged parties to accord, the account cleared.
29.itsRole: A breach between parties must be settled, and reconciliation is the settling — the enmity removed, the account brought to zero, the relationship restored. It assumes a real dispute at law. Reconciled to Yahuah means the standing hostility is ended and the parties brought back into accord. It is a change of legal standing, not a mood: the case between them closed, peace on the record.

proofTexts.text: We were reconciled to Yahuah by the death of his Son.
Yahuah was in Messiah, reconciling the world unto himself.
Hath reconciled us to himself... and hath given to us the ministry of reconciliation.
proofTexts.note: The settled relationship and its proclamation.

proofTexts.text: Having made peace through the blood of his cross.

plainTerms: To reconcile is to bring estranged parties back into accord — the enmity removed, the account cleared, the relationship restored. It assumes a real breach, parties at law. ‘Reconciled to Yahuah’ means the hostility is ended and the two brought back together, on the record. It is a change of standing, not a feeling.
bringItHome: When two parties are at law, reconciliation is the settlement — the dispute resolved, the account zeroed, the enmity ended, and the relationship restored. That is what ‘reconciled to Yahuah’ means: not a softened mood, but a real breach formally closed, peace made through the price paid.

courtroomRoles.does: who reconciles the world to Himself.
by whose death the breach is settled.
brought back into accord, the account cleared.

13.lead: To redeem is to buy back under the kinsman law — to recover a person or property from bondage or forfeiture by paying the price, exercised by the one with the right to do so. The goel, the kinsman-redeemer, had both the right and the duty to buy back a relative’s forfeited land or freedom (Leviticus 25:25, 48-49). Padah is the parallel: to ransom, to release by payment. Redemption is a family-law transaction — the near kinsman stepping in to recover what was lost, at cost to himself. To be redeemed is to be bought back into the family and the inheritance by one who held the legal right of redemption.

root.sense: to redeem, to act as kinsman-redeemer
to ransom, to release by payment

sharesRoot.note: Gaal is the root of both the redeemer (goel) who buys back and the avenger (goel ha-dam) who requires blood — the same kinsman-office, its two duties.

13.courtroomWord: A kinsman-law term — to buy back a forfeited person or estate by the right of redemption.
13.itsRole: Under the kinsman law, what is lost can be recovered by the one with the right to redeem it — the goel, who pays the price to buy back a relative’s land or freedom. Redemption is this family-law act: the near kinsman stepping in, at his own cost, to recover the forfeited. To be redeemed is to be bought back into the family and inheritance by the one holding the legal right — the Redeemer who pays what recovery requires.

proofTexts.text: Then shall his kinsman come to redeem it.
proofTexts.note: The goel buying back forfeited land.

proofTexts.text: One of his brethren may redeem him.
proofTexts.note: The kinsman recovering a relative from bondage.

proofTexts.text: I know that my redeemer liveth.
Messiah hath redeemed us from the curse of the law.
proofTexts.note: The price paid to buy back.

plainTerms: To redeem is to buy back — to recover a person or property from bondage or forfeiture by paying the price, done by the one with the right to do it. The goel, the kinsman-redeemer, bought back a relative’s lost land or freedom at his own cost. To be redeemed is to be bought back into the family and the inheritance.
bringItHome: Under the kinsman law, when a family member lost his land or freedom, the near kinsman — the goel — had the right to step in and buy it back, at cost to himself. That is redemption: not a rescue in general, but a family-law transaction. The Redeemer pays the price to recover His own into the inheritance.

courtroomRoles.does: the kinsman who buys back the forfeited at His own cost.
recovered from bondage into the family and inheritance.
what redemption lawfully requires.

14.lead: Redemption is the release secured by a price — the completed act of buying back, and the freedom it obtains. Geulah is the right and the result of the kinsman’s recovery (Leviticus 25:24); apolutrosis, in the Greek, is the release-on-payment, the deliverance a ransom buys (Ephesians 1:7). Redemption is not merely rescue; it is lawful recovery: a price paid, a claim satisfied, a captive released, a title restored. “In whom we have redemption through his blood, the forgiveness of sins” (Ephesians 1:7) names the price and the result together. To have redemption is to hold the secured release — the transaction completed, the freedom obtained by payment.

root.sense: the right or act of redemption
release secured by a ransom

sharesRoot.note: Geulah is the noun of gaal (to redeem): the act of the kinsman-redeemer and the release it secures.

14.courtroomWord: A release term — the completed buying-back, and the freedom it secures.
14.itsRole: Redemption is the recovery completed — the price paid, the claim satisfied, the release secured. Geulah is the kinsman’s right and result; apolutrosis is the freedom the ransom buys. It is lawful recovery, not mere rescue: a title restored, a captive freed, the transaction on the record. Redemption through his blood names the price and the freedom together. To have redemption is to hold the release, secured and complete.

proofTexts.text: In whom we have redemption through his blood, the forgiveness of sins.
proofTexts.note: The price and the release named together.

proofTexts.text: Ye shall grant a redemption for the land.
The redemption that is in Messiah Yahushua.
Having obtained eternal redemption for us.

plainTerms: Redemption is the release a price secures — the completed buying-back and the freedom it obtains. It is lawful recovery: the price paid, the claim satisfied, the captive freed, the title restored. ‘Redemption through his blood’ names the price and the result together. To have redemption is to hold the secured release.
bringItHome: Redemption is the whole transaction done: the price paid, the claim answered, and the captive walking free with his title restored. Not a rescue in the abstract, but a lawful recovery completed. ‘Redemption through his blood’ is the price and the freedom in one phrase — the buying-back finished.

courtroomRoles.does: by whose blood the redemption is secured.
recovered, freed, title restored.
whose claim the redemption satisfies.

113.lead: The city of refuge was a place of legal asylum with due process — a provision that protected the accused killer until his case could be tried. “Ye shall appoint you cities of refuge... that the slayer may flee thither, which killeth any person at unawares” (Numbers 35:11). The refuge did not excuse guilt; it guaranteed a trial: the manslayer was safe there from the avenger of blood “until he stand before the congregation in judgment” (Numbers 35:12). It is one of Torah’s due-process safeguards — protection from summary vengeance, a fair hearing before any execution. To flee to the refuge was to claim legal asylum, the right to be tried before being condemned.

root.sense: a refuge, asylum; the city that protected the accused until trial

113.courtroomWord: An asylum term — legal protection of the accused until his case is tried.
113.itsRole: The accused killer needed protection from summary vengeance, and the refuge provided it — asylum until trial. It did not excuse guilt; it guaranteed due process: safe from the avenger until judged by the congregation. The refuge is Torah’s safeguard against vengeance outrunning verdict — a fair hearing before any execution. To reach it was to claim the right to be tried, not lynched.

proofTexts.text: Cities of refuge... that the slayer may flee thither.
A refuge from the avenger; that the manslayer die not, until he stand before the congregation in judgment.
Prepare thee a way... that every slayer may flee thither.
Until he stand before the congregation for judgment.

plainTerms: The city of refuge was legal asylum — it protected the accused killer from the avenger of blood until his case could be tried. It did not excuse guilt; it guaranteed a fair trial before any execution. It is one of Torah’s due-process safeguards: a hearing before condemnation.
bringItHome: A man who killed by accident could be run down by the victim’s kinsman before anyone judged whether it was murder or mishap. The city of refuge stopped that: flee there, and you were safe until the congregation tried your case. Not an escape from justice — a guarantee of it: trial before vengeance.

courtroomRoles.does: flees to the refuge, claiming asylum until trial.
held off until judgment is rendered.
which tries the case before any execution.
provides the refuge as due process.

24.lead: Release is the sabbatical cancelling of debt — a scheduled legal discharge, enacted by statute. Every seventh year was ‘the Lord’s release’: “every creditor that lendeth ought unto his neighbour shall release it... because it is called Yahuah’s release” (Deuteronomy 15:1-2). Shemittah is a letting-drop: the debt is not merely paused but released, the obligation discharged by law on a fixed cycle. It is the same release-logic that flowers into the Jubilee. Release is not the creditor’s whim but the law’s provision — a built-in mechanism that keeps debt from becoming permanent bondage, the ledger cleared by statute at the appointed time.

root.sense: a release, a letting-drop; the sabbatical remission of debt

24.courtroomWord: A discharge term — the scheduled, statutory cancelling of debt.
24.itsRole: Debt could become permanent bondage, and the release prevents it — a scheduled discharge, enacted by law every seventh year. Shemittah lets the debt drop: the obligation cancelled, not merely paused, on a fixed cycle. It is the law’s own mechanism, Yahuah’s release, flowering into the Jubilee. Release is statutory mercy: the ledger cleared at the appointed time, so no man is crushed under a debt forever.

proofTexts.text: At the end of every seven years thou shalt make a release.
Every creditor... shall release it... it is called Yahuah’s release.
The year of release, is at hand.
In the seventh year shall be a sabbath of rest unto the land.
proofTexts.note: The sabbatical release of the land.

plainTerms: Release is the seventh-year cancelling of debt — a scheduled legal discharge, ‘Yahuah’s release.’ The debt is not paused but dropped: the obligation cancelled by statute on a fixed cycle. It is the law’s own way of keeping debt from becoming permanent bondage — the ledger cleared at the appointed time.
bringItHome: Every seventh year, the law simply cancelled debts — ‘Yahuah’s release.’ Not the creditor being generous, but the statute letting the debt drop. It kept a bad year from turning into lifelong bondage. And it grows into the Jubilee: release built into the calendar, mercy written as law.

courtroomRoles.does: decrees the release on the fixed cycle.
who lets the debt drop by statute.
whose obligation is cancelled at the appointed time.

45.lead: To remember, in Torah, is to act on a standing obligation — not merely to recall a fact, but to bring it to mind in order to do it. “Remember the sabbath day, to keep it holy” (Exodus 20:8) commands action, not nostalgia: to remember is to observe. When Yahuah ‘remembers’ His covenant (Exodus 2:24), He acts on it — He moves to fulfill His obligations. Zakar joins memory to deed. To remember the commandments is to carry them out; to forget is to neglect the duty. Remembering is covenant faithfulness in motion — calling the obligation to mind precisely so that it is kept.

root.sense: to remember, to bring to mind; to act upon a standing obligation

sharesRoot.note: Zikaron (the memorial) is from zakar (to remember): the record set so a matter is remembered, and the remembering that acts on it.

45.courtroomWord: An obligation term — to bring a duty to mind in order to perform it.
45.itsRole: In covenant, to remember is to act — to call an obligation to mind so that it is kept. ‘Remember the sabbath’ commands observance, not recollection. When Yahuah remembers His covenant, He moves to fulfill it. Zakar binds memory to deed: remembering the commandments is doing them; forgetting is neglect. It is covenant faithfulness in motion, the duty brought to mind precisely to be performed.

proofTexts.text: Remember the sabbath day, to keep it holy.
Elohim... remembered his covenant.
That ye may... remember all the commandments of Yahuah, and do them.
Thou shalt remember all the way which Yahuah... led thee.
proofTexts.note: The standing obligation kept in mind.

plainTerms: To remember, in Torah, is to act on an obligation — not just recall a fact. ‘Remember the sabbath’ means keep it, not merely think of it. When Yahuah ‘remembers’ His covenant, He moves to fulfill it. Remembering joins memory to deed: to remember the commandments is to do them.
bringItHome: ‘Remember the sabbath’ is not asking you to recall that it exists — it is commanding you to keep it. That is how Torah uses ‘remember’: memory that acts. When Yahuah remembered His covenant with Israel, He did not merely think of it — He moved to deliver them. Remembering is obligation in motion.

courtroomRoles.does: who remembers His covenant and acts on it.
who remembers the commandments in order to do them.
brought to mind precisely to be kept.

25.lead: Rest, in Torah, is secured possession of the inheritance — the settled enjoyment of what was promised, not mere cessation of labor. “Yahuah your Elohim... hath given you rest, and hath given you this land” (Joshua 1:13) joins rest to the secured estate: rest is the settled state of a people safe in their possession. Menuchah is a resting-place, a settled inheritance. This is why Hebrews can speak of a rest that “remaineth” (Hebrews 4:9) — an inheritance yet to be entered. The sabbath rest points to it: not idleness, but the secured enjoyment of the promise, the estate possessed and at peace.

root.sense: to rest, to settle
a resting-place, a settled inheritance

25.courtroomWord: A possession term — the settled, secured enjoyment of the inheritance.
25.itsRole: Rest is not the mere stopping of work but the settled possession of the estate — a people safe and at peace in their inheritance. Joshua joins rest to the land given; menuchah is the resting-place secured. The sabbath enacts it weekly; Hebrews points to a rest that remaineth — an inheritance still to be entered. To enter rest is to come into settled possession of the promise, the estate held and at peace.

proofTexts.text: Yahuah your Elohim hath given you rest, and hath given you this land.
proofTexts.note: Rest joined to the secured estate.

proofTexts.text: Ye are not as yet come to the rest and to the inheritance.
proofTexts.note: Rest as the inheritance to be entered.

proofTexts.text: There remaineth therefore a rest to the people of Elohim.
And rested the seventh day.
proofTexts.note: The sabbath rest that points to it.

plainTerms: Rest, in Torah, is the secured possession of the inheritance — a people settled and at peace in what was promised — not just a break from work. Joshua ties rest to the land given. Hebrews speaks of a rest that ‘remaineth’: an inheritance still to be entered. The sabbath points to it: the estate possessed and at peace.
bringItHome: When Israel came into ‘rest,’ it did not mean they stopped working — it meant they were settled, safe, in possession of the land promised them. That is rest: the inheritance secured and at peace. The sabbath rehearses it weekly, and Hebrews says a fuller rest still ‘remaineth’ — an estate yet to be entered.

courtroomRoles.does: who gives rest with the inheritance.
settled and at peace in the estate.
the secured enjoyment of the promise.

27.lead: Restitution is the wrong repaid in full — the legal restoration of what was taken, often with a penalty added. Torah requires it precisely: the thief “shall restore double” or fourfold, and “if he have nothing, then he shall be sold for his theft” (Exodus 22:1-3). Shalam, the root, means to make whole, to complete, to pay in full — the same root as shalom (peace) and recompense. Restitution makes the injured party whole: the loss restored, the balance settled, and more. It is not mere apology but repayment — the concrete squaring of an account, the wrong undone by paying back what it cost, so that peace (shalom) is restored between the parties.

root.sense: to make whole, to complete, to repay in full; to make restitution

sharesRoot.note: All from shalam: the wrong repaid (Restitution), the account settled (Recompense), and the peace that results (Shalom). One root, three faces.

27.courtroomWord: A repayment term — the full restoration of a loss, with penalty, that makes the injured whole.
27.itsRole: A wrong leaves a party out of pocket, and restitution repays it — in full, often with a penalty added, so the injured is made whole. Shalam means to complete, to pay in full: restitution squares the account concretely, not with apology but with repayment. And its root is shalom: the loss restored and the penalty paid, peace is restored between the parties. Restitution is the making-whole the law requires.

proofTexts.text: He shall restore five oxen for an ox, and four sheep for a sheep.
He should make full restitution.
He shall... restore it in the principal, and shall add the fifth part more.
If I have taken any thing from any man... I restore him fourfold.

plainTerms: Restitution is repaying a wrong in full — restoring what was taken, often with a penalty added, so the injured party is made whole.
