Its root, shalam, means to make whole, and it is the same root as shalom (peace): the loss restored and the balance settled, peace is restored between the parties. It is repayment, not apology.
bringItHome: A thief did not just say sorry — he paid back what he took, and then some: double, fourfold, or fivefold. That is restitution: the wrong undone by concrete repayment, the injured made whole. And its root is peace — shalom — because when the account is squared in full, the breach between the parties is healed.

courtroomRoles.does: repays the loss in full, with penalty.
made whole by the restitution.
who requires the wrong repaid so peace is restored.

30.lead: To restore is to return what was lost to its rightful place or owner — property, standing, or estate given back by law. “He shall restore that which he took violently away” (Leviticus 6:4); “restore the years that the locust hath eaten” (Joel 2:25). Shuv is to bring back, to return — and in the legal sense, to reinstate a party to what was his. Restoration is not a vague renewal but a lawful reinstatement: the dispossessed returned to his inheritance, the wronged made whole, the standing given back. To be restored is to be returned to one’s rightful place on the record — the loss reversed, the estate re-entered.

root.sense: to turn back, to return, to restore; to reinstate to a former place

30.courtroomWord: A reinstatement term — the returning of property or standing to its rightful owner.
30.itsRole: What was lost or taken can be returned by law, and restoration is that return — the dispossessed reinstated, the wronged made whole, the standing given back. It is lawful reinstatement, not mere renewal: the party returned to his rightful place, the estate re-entered on the record. To restore is to reverse the loss and reinstate the owner — the years given back, the possession returned, the standing recovered.

proofTexts.text: He shall restore that which he took violently away.
I will restore to you the years that the locust hath eaten.
He restoreth my soul.
Wilt thou at this time restore again the kingdom to Israel?
proofTexts.note: The estate returned to its owner.

plainTerms: To restore is to return what was lost to its rightful place or owner — property, standing, or estate given back by law. It is lawful reinstatement: the dispossessed returned to his inheritance, the wronged made whole. To be restored is to be put back on the record where you belong, the loss reversed.
bringItHome: Restoration is not a fresh start from nothing — it is being returned to what was rightfully yours: the stolen thing given back, the lost years repaid, the standing recovered. ‘He restoreth my soul’ is that reinstatement. To be restored is to be put back in your place, the record corrected, the estate re-entered.

courtroomRoles.does: returns the lost to its rightful place.
returned to inheritance and standing.
given back, re-entered on the record.

108.lead: A reward is the due paid to the faithful — the legal wage earned and owed, handed down at the verdict. “Behold, I come quickly; and my reward is with me, to give every man according as his work shall be” (Revelation 22:12) is a payout, rendered by the Judge according to the record. Sakar and misthos both mean wage, hire, the pay due for labor. A reward is not a whimsical gift but a due: what the faithful have earned and the court owes them. This is why it is paid ‘according to works’ — the reward is calibrated to the record, the wage assessed and rendered at the bench. To be rewarded is to be paid what one is owed.

root.sense: wages, hire, reward
wage, pay, the due for labor

sharesRoot.note: The same wage-word covers the pay owed to the faithful (Reward) and the pay earned by labor (Wages).

108.courtroomWord: A due-payment term — the wage owed to the faithful, rendered at the verdict.
108.itsRole: The faithful earn a due, and the reward is its payment — the wage owed, handed down at the verdict according to works. It is not a gift of whim but a due assessed against the record. The Judge comes to render every man’s reward according to his work: the payout calibrated to the ledger. To be rewarded is to be paid what one is owed, the wage rendered at the bench.

proofTexts.text: My reward is with me, to give every man according as his work shall be.
proofTexts.note: The payout rendered at the verdict.

proofTexts.text: I am thy shield, and thy exceeding great reward.
proofTexts.note: The reward as the due secured.

proofTexts.text: A rewarder of them that diligently seek him.
proofTexts.note: The due paid to the faithful.

proofTexts.text: He shall receive a reward.
proofTexts.note: The wage rendered for the work.

plainTerms: A reward is the due paid to the faithful — the wage earned and owed, handed down at the verdict ‘according to works.’ It is not a whimsical gift but a due the court owes. The Judge comes to pay every man according to his record. To be rewarded is to be paid what you are owed.
bringItHome: A reward, in Scripture, is a wage — the pay owed to the faithful for their work, rendered at the verdict. ‘My reward is with me, to give every man according as his work shall be.’ It is not a lottery prize; it is a due, calibrated to the record and paid at the bench.

courtroomRoles.does: renders every man’s reward according to his work.
who are owed the wage they earned.
by which the reward is assessed.

82.lead: The right hand is the seat of delegated authority — the place of highest honor and executive power beside the sovereign. “Sit thou at my right hand, until I make thine enemies thy footstool” (Psalm 110:1) seats one in the position of conferred rule: to be at the right hand is to wield the sovereign’s authority by appointment. It is a legal position, not mere proximity. The right hand acts for the throne; the one placed there exercises power delegated from it. This is why the Messiah is said to be seated ‘at the right hand’ of Yahuah — given executive authority to rule and to judge, the position conferred by the One on the throne.

root.sense: the right hand; the place of authority, honor, and executive power

82.courtroomWord: A delegated-authority term — the seat of conferred executive power beside the sovereign.
82.itsRole: Beside the throne is a seat of power, and the right hand is it — the position of delegated authority, wielding the sovereign’s rule by appointment. ‘Sit at my right hand’ confers executive power, not mere nearness. The one placed there acts for the throne. The Messiah at the right hand of Yahuah holds authority to rule and judge — conferred by the One on the throne, exercised on His behalf. It is position and power, granted.

proofTexts.text: Sit thou at my right hand, until I make thine enemies thy footstool.
By the right hand of Yahuah exalted.
Set him at his own right hand in the heavenly places.
Sat down on the right hand of the Majesty on high.

plainTerms: The right hand is the seat of delegated authority — the highest place of honor and power beside the sovereign. ‘Sit at my right hand’ confers executive rule, not just nearness. The Messiah at Yahuah’s right hand holds authority to rule and judge — power conferred by the One on the throne, exercised on His behalf.
bringItHome: To be seated ‘at the right hand’ of a king was to hold his authority — to act for the throne, wielding power delegated from it. That is where the Messiah is placed: at the right hand of Yahuah, given executive authority to rule and judge. Not equal to the throne — seated beside it, exercising power the One on it conferred.

courtroomRoles.does: confers the right-hand authority.
wields delegated executive power to rule and judge.
made a footstool under the conferred rule.

6.lead: Righteousness is conformity to the standard — rightness measured against the law, the quality of what aligns with the just norm. Tsedeq is not a warm inner glow but a legal rectitude: right weights and measures are ‘just’ (tsedeq), a right verdict is righteous, a righteous man is one who conforms to the covenant standard. “The righteous Yahuah loveth righteousness” (Psalm 11:7). Because righteousness is measured against a standard, it presupposes the standard: there is no rightness where there is no norm to be right by. To be righteous is to align with the law’s requirement; the word itself is anchored to the code it conforms to.

root.sense: rightness, justice, conformity to the standard
righteousness, righteous conduct

6.courtroomWord: A conformity term — rightness measured against the standard of the law.
6.itsRole: Righteousness is measured, not felt — conformity to the just standard the law sets. A right weight, a right verdict, a right man: each is tsedeq because each aligns with the norm. It presupposes the standard it conforms to; strip the law and ‘righteous’ has nothing to be right by. Yahuah is righteous because His every act aligns with His own perfect standard. To be righteous is to conform to the code — the word anchored to the law it measures against.

proofTexts.text: The righteous Yahuah loveth righteousness.
proofTexts.note: Rightness as His nature and delight.

proofTexts.text: Just balances, just weights... shall ye have.
proofTexts.note: Righteousness as conformity to the standard.

proofTexts.text: It shall be our righteousness, if we observe to do all these commandments.
proofTexts.note: Righteousness tied to keeping the law.

proofTexts.text: My righteousness shall not be abolished.

plainTerms: Righteousness is conformity to the standard — rightness measured against the law, not a warm feeling. A just weight, a right verdict, a righteous man: each aligns with the norm. And it presupposes the norm: there is no ‘right’ without a standard to be right by. To be righteous is to conform to the law’s requirement.
bringItHome: Righteousness is like a true measure — it is ‘right’ because it matches the standard. A just scale, a just verdict, a just man: all are tsedeq because all conform to the norm. Which means righteousness cannot float free of the law: strip the standard, and there is nothing left for ‘righteous’ to mean.

courtroomRoles.does: righteous in every act, the norm righteousness conforms to.
whose rightness aligns with the law.
the standard against which righteousness is measured.

21.lead: The Sabbath is the covenant sign, kept — a perpetual mark of the bond between Yahuah and His people, and a command to be observed. “It is a sign between me and you throughout your generations” (Exodus 31:13); “the sabbath... for a perpetual covenant” (Exodus 31:16). Shabbat is to cease, to rest — the seventh-day cessation set apart at creation and written into the covenant terms. It is not a suggestion but a sign one keeps, marking whose people one is. To keep the Sabbath is to bear the covenant sign; to profane it was a grave breach. The Sabbath is the observed mark of the covenant, the seventh day set apart and kept.

root.sense: the Sabbath, the seventh day; from shabat, to cease, to rest

21.courtroomWord: A covenant-sign term — the observed seventh-day mark of the bond.
21.itsRole: A covenant has its sign, and the Sabbath is Israel’s — the seventh-day cessation set apart at creation and written into the covenant as ‘a sign... a perpetual covenant.’ It is kept, not merely admired: the mark one bears to show whose people one is. Profaning it was a grave breach; keeping it is bearing the sign. The Sabbath is the observed covenant mark, the seventh day ceased and set apart.

proofTexts.text: It is a sign between me and you throughout your generations.
The sabbath... for a perpetual covenant.
proofTexts.note: The sign written into the terms.

proofTexts.text: Remember the sabbath day, to keep it holy.
Elohim blessed the seventh day, and sanctified it.
proofTexts.note: The day set apart at creation.

plainTerms: The Sabbath is the covenant sign, kept — the seventh-day rest set apart at creation and written into the covenant as ‘a sign between me and you.’ It is observed, not just admired: the mark you bear to show whose people you are. To keep it is to bear the sign of the bond.
bringItHome: The Sabbath is Israel’s covenant sign — like a seal you carry, marking whose you are. ‘A sign between me and you... a perpetual covenant.’ It was set apart at creation and written into the terms, to be kept. To keep the Sabbath is to bear the mark of the bond with Yahuah.

courtroomRoles.does: who set the Sabbath as the sign of the bond.
who keep the Sabbath as the mark of the covenant.
the seventh day set apart and observed.

69.lead: To sanctify is to set apart into holy status — a legal act of consecration that moves a person or thing from common to holy. Qadash is to declare and make holy: the seventh day was sanctified (Genesis 2:3), the firstborn sanctified to Yahuah (Exodus 13:2), the priests sanctified for office. It is a change of status conferred, not a feeling generated: what is sanctified is transferred into the holy category and thereby subject to holy use and holy rules. To sanctify is the opposite of to profane: one moves a thing into holy standing, the other drags it back to common. Sanctification is set-apart status, legally conferred.

root.sense: to set apart, to consecrate, to make or declare holy

69.courtroomWord: A consecration term — the setting-apart of a person or thing into holy status.
69.itsRole: The holy is a category, and to sanctify is to move something into it — a legal consecration, conferring set-apart status. The day, the firstborn, the priests, the vessels are each sanctified: transferred from common to holy, subject thereafter to holy use. It is the reverse of profaning: sanctify moves into holy standing, profane drags back to common. Sanctification is a change of status conferred by the One who makes holy.

proofTexts.text: Elohim blessed the seventh day, and sanctified it.
proofTexts.note: The day set apart into holy status.

proofTexts.text: Sanctify unto me all the firstborn.
I am Yahuah which sanctify you.
proofTexts.note: The One who confers holy status.

proofTexts.text: Ye shall be unto me... an holy nation.

plainTerms: To sanctify is to set apart into holy status — a legal act of consecration that moves a person or thing from common to holy. The day, the firstborn, the priests were each sanctified: transferred into the holy category. It is the opposite of profaning: sanctify moves into holy standing, profane drags back to common.
bringItHome: To sanctify is to move something into the holy category — set apart, consecrated, dedicated to Yahuah’s use. The seventh day, the firstborn, the priests: each was sanctified, transferred from common to holy. It is a change of standing, conferred by the One who makes holy — and the exact reverse of profaning.

courtroomRoles.does: confers holy status.
moved from common into holy standing.
the standing into which the sanctified is placed.

105.lead: The scales are the balance of just measure — the instrument by which weight, and by extension judgment, is rendered fairly. Torah demands them honest: “a just balance and scales are Yahuah’s” (Proverbs 16:11); “thou shalt not have in thy bag divers weights” (Deuteronomy 25:13). A false balance is “abomination to Yahuah” (Proverbs 11:1). The scales are also the image of judgment itself — a matter weighed, as Belshazzar was “weighed in the balances, and... found wanting” (Daniel 5:27). To weigh in the scales is to render a fair assessment; the just balance is the emblem of judgment done true.

root.sense: scales, a balance; the instrument of just weighing

105.courtroomWord: A weighing term — the balance by which weight and judgment are rendered fairly.
105.itsRole: Fair judgment is weighed, not guessed, and the scales are the instrument — demanded honest by the law, since a false balance defrauds. They are also the image of judgment itself: a matter set in the balance and assessed. Belshazzar was weighed and found wanting. The just scales stand for judgment done true — the assessment rendered by an honest measure, the verdict weighed rather than felt.

proofTexts.text: A just weight and balance are Yahuah’s.
Thou shalt not have in thy bag divers weights, a great and a small.
A false balance is abomination to Yahuah.
Thou art weighed in the balances, and art found wanting.

plainTerms: The scales are the balance of just measure — the instrument of fair weighing, demanded honest by the law. A false balance is an abomination. And the scales are the picture of judgment itself: a matter weighed and assessed, as Belshazzar was ‘weighed... and found wanting.’ The just balance is judgment done true.
bringItHome: An honest set of scales renders a fair weight; a crooked one cheats every measure. Torah demands them true — a false balance is an abomination. And the scales are also the image of the verdict itself: your matter set in the balance and weighed. Belshazzar was ‘weighed... and found wanting.’

courtroomRoles.does: whose are the just balance and weights; who weighs every matter true.
whose matters are set in the balance and assessed.
the just measure by which judgment is rendered.

75.lead: The scepter is the emblem of jurisdiction — the rod that marks the right to rule and to judge. “The sceptre shall not depart from Judah... until Shiloh come” (Genesis 49:10) is a prophecy of retained sovereign authority; “a sceptre of righteousness is the sceptre of thy kingdom” (Psalm 45:6) names the rule the scepter represents. Shebet is a rod, a staff — and the ruler’s scepter is the sign of his lawful dominion. To hold the scepter is to hold jurisdiction: the authority to command, to judge, and to enforce. It is the visible mark of the right to rule, held by the one to whom rule belongs.

root.sense: a rod, staff, scepter; the emblem of ruling authority

75.courtroomWord: A jurisdiction emblem — the rod marking the right to rule and judge.
75.itsRole: Authority to rule has a sign, and the scepter is it — the rod that marks lawful dominion, the right to command and to judge. Judah’s scepter would not depart until Shiloh came: sovereign authority retained. A scepter of righteousness is a kingdom ruled by the just standard. To hold the scepter is to hold jurisdiction, the visible emblem of the right to rule, borne by the one to whom rule belongs.

proofTexts.text: The sceptre shall not depart from Judah... until Shiloh come.
The sceptre of thy kingdom is a right sceptre.
A Sceptre shall rise out of Israel.
The king held out to Esther the golden sceptre.
proofTexts.note: The scepter extended as the sign of favor and authority.

plainTerms: The scepter is the emblem of the right to rule — the rod that marks lawful authority to command and to judge. ‘The sceptre shall not depart from Judah’ means sovereign authority retained. To hold the scepter is to hold jurisdiction: the visible sign that rule belongs to you.
bringItHome: A king’s scepter is not decoration — it is the emblem of his authority to rule and judge, the visible sign that jurisdiction is his. ‘The sceptre shall not depart from Judah’ is a promise that the right to rule stays in the line until the One it points to comes. To hold the scepter is to hold the right to rule.

courtroomRoles.does: holds the scepter as the sign of his right to rule.
who confers the scepter of righteousness.
the mark of lawful jurisdiction.

34.lead: A seal is an authenticating mark of ownership and authority — the impression that certifies a document genuine and a possession claimed. In the ancient world a seal made a matter official: a sealed document was authenticated and secured (Jeremiah 32:10), and to seal a thing was to mark it as one’s own and beyond tampering. “Ye were sealed with that holy Spirit of promise” (Ephesians 1:13) uses this legal image: marked as owned, authenticated, secured until redemption. To be sealed is to bear the owner’s mark — certified as belonging to Him, the possession authenticated and protected on the record.

root.sense: a seal, signet; the mark that authenticates and claims ownership

34.courtroomWord: An authentication term — the mark that certifies genuine and claims ownership.
34.itsRole: A document is made official by a seal, and a possession is claimed by one — the impression that authenticates and marks ownership, securing against tampering. A sealed deed is genuine and binding; a sealed thing is owned and protected. To be sealed with the Spirit is to bear the owner’s mark: authenticated as His, secured until redemption. The seal is the legal sign of genuine ownership, entered on the record.

proofTexts.text: I subscribed the evidence, and sealed it.
Ye were sealed with that holy Spirit of promise.
The Lord knoweth them that are his.
proofTexts.note: The seal of ownership and its mark.

proofTexts.text: Set me as a seal upon thine heart.
proofTexts.note: The seal as the claim of belonging.

plainTerms: A seal is an authenticating mark of ownership and authority — the impression that certifies a document genuine and claims a possession as one’s own. To be ‘sealed with the Spirit’ is to bear the owner’s mark: authenticated as His, secured until redemption. It is a legal sign of genuine ownership.
bringItHome: In the ancient world, a seal made it official — a sealed document was certified genuine, a sealed possession was marked as owned and safe from tampering. To be ‘sealed with the Spirit’ is to carry the owner’s stamp: certified as belonging to Yahuah, authenticated and secured on the record.

courtroomRoles.does: who seals His own, marking and securing them.
authenticated as His, secured until redemption.
the impression that certifies genuine and claims ownership.

121.lead: Two seats, two jurisdictions. A seat — kathedra, or moshab — is a derived judicial bench, the place of one who administers the law he was given: “the scribes and the Pharisees sit in Moses’ seat” (Matthew 23:2), holding a delegated teaching authority. A throne — thronos, or kisse — is the sovereign seat of the lawgiver himself, the source of rule, not its administrator. The distinction is legal, not decorative: the one on the seat applies a law he did not make; the One on the throne is where the law comes from. To confuse them is to confuse an appointed magistrate with the Sovereign — a delegated bench with the seat of ultimate authority.

root.sense: a seat, a derived judicial bench
a throne, the sovereign seat of the lawgiver

121.courtroomWord: A contrast of jurisdictions — the derived bench (seat) versus the sovereign seat of the lawgiver (throne).
121.itsRole: Not every seat is a throne. A seat is a delegated bench — the magistrate administering a law he was given, like those who sit in Moses’ seat. A throne is the source of law, the sovereign’s own seat. The distinction guards against confusing an appointed administrator with the Lawgiver Himself. The One on the throne makes the law; the one on the seat applies it. Rule flows from the throne; the seat only administers what the throne decrees.

proofTexts.text: The scribes and the Pharisees sit in Moses’ seat.
Elohim sitteth upon the throne of his holiness.
proofTexts.note: The sovereign seat of the Lawgiver.

proofTexts.text: The heaven is my throne.
proofTexts.note: The throne as the source of rule.

proofTexts.text: There are set thrones of judgment.
proofTexts.note: The seats of adjudication under the sovereign.

plainTerms: A seat and a throne are two different jurisdictions. A seat (like ‘Moses’ seat’) is a delegated bench — a magistrate applying a law he was given. A throne is the sovereign’s own seat — the source of the law, not its administrator. To confuse them is to mistake an appointed judge for the Lawgiver Himself.
bringItHome: ‘Moses’ seat’ was a real thing — a delegated bench, where teachers applied the law Moses received. But a seat is not a throne. The throne is where the law comes from, the sovereign’s own seat. One administers; the other originates. The distinction keeps a magistrate from being mistaken for the Sovereign.

courtroomRoles.does: the Lawgiver, the source of rule.
administers a law he was given, not made.
derived bench versus sovereign throne.

128.lead: ‘The books were opened’ — sifrin pethichu — is the entry of the evidentiary record into the court. When Daniel’s court convenes, “the judgment was set, and the books were opened” (Daniel 7:10): the trial cannot proceed until the records are brought forward and read. The opening of the books is a formal legal act — the evidence entered, the deeds of every party laid before the bench. Revelation echoes it: “the books were opened... and the dead were judged out of those things which were written in the books” (Revelation 20:12). The verdict is rendered from the record. To open the books is to enter the evidence on which the court will rule.

root.sense: the books were opened (Aramaic); the evidentiary record brought forward and read

128.courtroomWord: An evidence term — the opening of the record before the bench.
128.itsRole: A court rules from the record, and the opening of the books is its entry — the evidence brought forward and read before judgment. Daniel’s court sits and the books were opened: the deeds of every party laid before the bench. Revelation shows the same — the dead judged out of those things which were written in the books. The verdict follows the record. To open the books is to enter the evidence on which the court decides.

proofTexts.text: The judgment was set, and the books were opened.
proofTexts.note: The record entered as the court convenes.

proofTexts.text: The books were opened... and the dead were judged out of those things which were written in the books.
proofTexts.note: The verdict rendered from the record.

proofTexts.text: A book of remembrance was written before him.
proofTexts.note: The record kept for the court.

proofTexts.text: The Ancient of days did sit.
proofTexts.note: The bench and the record together.

plainTerms: ‘The books were opened’ is the entry of the evidence into the court. When Daniel’s court convened, ‘the judgment was set, and the books were opened’: the records brought forward and read before any verdict. Revelation shows the same — the dead ‘judged out of those things written in the books.’ The verdict follows the record.
bringItHome: A trial cannot rule until the evidence is before the bench. That is what ‘the books were opened’ means: the records brought forward and read. In Daniel 7 the court sits and the books open; in Revelation the dead are judged ‘out of the things written.’ The verdict is rendered from the record — and the record is opened for all to see.

courtroomRoles.does: before whom the books are opened.
the evidence entered and read.
whose deeds, written in the books, the verdict follows.

63.lead: A servant is one under a regulated bond of service — a legal status with defined rights and duties, not mere drudgery. Torah hedged the servant with protections: release in the seventh year, rest on the Sabbath, redress for injury (Exodus 21:2-6, 26-27). The ebed held a recognized standing, and the master’s authority over him was bounded by law. To be Yahuah’s servant is a title of honor and standing — Moses, David, and the prophets are called ‘servant of Yahuah,’ a position of trusted, regulated service. The word names a legal relationship with obligations flowing both ways: service owed, and the servant’s rights protected by statute.

root.sense: a servant, bondservant; one under a regulated bond of service

63.courtroomWord: A status term — the regulated bond of service, with defined rights and duties.
63.itsRole: Service in Torah is a legal relationship, not lawless labor — the servant holds a defined standing, protected by statute: release in the seventh year, Sabbath rest, redress for harm. The master’s authority is bounded by law. ‘Servant of Yahuah’ is a title of honor — Moses, David, the prophets — trusted, regulated service. The bond runs both ways: service owed, and the servant’s rights guaranteed. To be a servant is to hold a regulated legal status.

proofTexts.text: In the seventh year he shall go out free for nothing.
He shall let him go free for his eye’s sake.
That thy manservant and thy maidservant may rest as well as thou.
Moses the servant of Yahuah.
proofTexts.note: The title of honored, regulated service.

plainTerms: A servant is one under a regulated bond of service — a legal status with defined rights and duties, not just drudgery. Torah protected the servant: seventh-year release, Sabbath rest, redress for injury. ‘Servant of Yahuah’ is a title of honor. The bond runs both ways: service owed, and the servant’s rights guaranteed by law.
bringItHome: A servant in Torah was not a rightless laborer — he held a legal standing, hedged with protections: freed in the seventh year, rested on the Sabbath, compensated for injury. And ‘servant of Yahuah’ was a title of honor, borne by Moses and David. The bond had obligations both ways: service owed, rights protected.

courtroomRoles.does: owes regulated service, holds protected rights.
whose authority is bounded by law.
who regulates the bond and protects the servant.

140.lead: Katargeo is the word behind ‘done away’ and ‘abolished’ in the abolition texts — and it does not mean destroyed or erased. It means to render inoperative, to make idle, to put out of working effect. A fallow field is katargeo-ed — not destroyed, but not producing (Luke 13:7). When Paul says the veil is “done away in Messiah” (2 Corinthians 3:14), or the ministry of death was “to be done away” (2 Corinthians 3:7), the sense is a function suspended, an effect brought to nothing — not a statute struck from the books. The abolition case leans hard on this verb; the verb will not bear the weight. To render an instrument inoperative is not to strike it from the record.

root.sense: to render inoperative, to make idle or ineffective; not to destroy

140.courtroomWord: An effect term — to bring a function to nothing, not to erase the thing itself.
140.itsRole: The abolition reading needs ‘done away’ to mean ‘abolished, gone.’ Katargeo will not carry it. The word suspends an effect, renders a function idle — the veil’s blinding effect ended, the condemning ministry’s power brought to nothing — while the underlying thing may stand. To render inoperative is a change of operation, not of existence. Where katargeo is used, the question is always ‘what effect ceased?’ — not ‘what was erased from the code?’

proofTexts.text: The vail is done away in Messiah.
proofTexts.note: An effect — the veil’s blinding — suspended, not the text destroyed.

proofTexts.text: Why cumbereth it the ground?
Do we then make void the law through faith? Elohim forbid: yea, we establish the law.
proofTexts.note: The very verb explicitly denied of the law.

proofTexts.text: She is loosed from the law of her husband.
proofTexts.note: A bond’s effect ended by a death — the law itself standing.

plainTerms: Katargeo is the ‘done away’ word — and it does not mean destroyed. It means to render inoperative, to put out of working effect, like a fallow field that isn’t producing. So ‘done away in Messiah’ is a function suspended, not a statute erased.
And Romans 3:31 uses the very same verb to say faith does not ‘make void’ the law — it establishes it.
bringItHome: When a field lies fallow, it is katargeo-ed — not plowed under and destroyed, just not producing. That is the force of ‘done away’: an effect suspended, a function brought to nothing. So the abolition texts, read on the verb’s actual meaning, speak of effects ended — the veil’s blindness, condemnation’s power — not the law struck from the books. Paul settles it himself: faith does not katargeo the law; it establishes it.

courtroomRoles.does: rendered inoperative in its effect, not erased.
the operation suspended or brought to nothing.
whose law faith establishes, not makes void (Romans 3:31).

26.lead: Shalom is not merely peace-as-calm but the account paid, the books at zero — wholeness because nothing is outstanding. From the root shalam (to make whole, to pay in full), shalom is the state of a settled account: no debt owed, no breach open, all restored. “The chastisement of our peace was upon him” (Isaiah 53:5) ties peace directly to a price paid — our shalom is the result of a settlement. Shalom shares its root with restitution (the wrong repaid) and recompense (the account settled): peace is what remains when the ledger is squared. To have shalom is to stand with nothing outstanding against you.

root.sense: peace, wholeness, completeness; from shalam, to make whole, to pay in full

sharesRoot.note: All from shalam: the account settled (Recompense), the wrong repaid (Restitution), and the peace that results (Shalom). One root, three faces.

26.courtroomWord: A settlement term — the wholeness of an account paid, nothing outstanding.
26.itsRole: Peace, in Scripture, is a settled state — the account paid, the breach closed, nothing owed. Shalom is what remains when the ledger is squared: from shalam, to pay in full. ‘The chastisement of our peace was upon him’ makes it explicit — our shalom is the result of a price paid. It is not the absence of conflict as a mood but the presence of a settlement. To have shalom is to have nothing outstanding against you.

proofTexts.text: The chastisement of our peace was upon him.
proofTexts.note: Peace as the result of a price paid.

proofTexts.text: Yahuah lift up his countenance upon thee, and give thee peace.
proofTexts.note: Shalom conferred as the settled state.

proofTexts.text: Righteousness and peace have kissed each other.
proofTexts.note: The standard met and peace resulting.

proofTexts.text: We have peace with Yahuah through our Lord Yahushua Messiah.

plainTerms: Shalom is not just calm — it is wholeness because the account is paid, nothing outstanding. From shalam (to pay in full), it is the state of a settled ledger: no debt, no open breach. ‘The chastisement of our peace was upon him’ ties peace to a price paid. To have shalom is to stand with nothing owed against you.
bringItHome: Shalom is the quiet that comes when the account is squared — not the absence of noise, but the absence of anything outstanding. Its root means ‘paid in full.’ ‘The chastisement of our peace was upon him’: our shalom is the result of a settlement. Peace is what remains when the ledger reads zero.

courtroomRoles.does: confers shalom as the settled state.
by whose chastisement our peace was bought.
stands with nothing outstanding, in shalom.

35.lead: A sign is a token that proves and marks a covenant — an appointed mark that identifies a bond and testifies to it. The rainbow is “the token of the covenant” with Noah (Genesis 9:12-13); circumcision is “a token of the covenant” with Abraham (Genesis 17:11); the Sabbath is “a sign between me and you” (Exodus 31:13). An oth is not decoration but legal marking: it certifies the covenant and identifies its parties, like a seal on a contract. To bear the sign is to be marked as a party to the bond. Signs are the covenant’s identifying marks — the tokens that prove the agreement and name whose it is.

root.sense: a sign, token, mark; the appointed token of a covenant

35.courtroomWord: A token term — the appointed mark that proves and identifies a covenant.
35.itsRole: A covenant is marked by its sign — the token that certifies it and identifies its parties. The rainbow, circumcision, the Sabbath are each an oth: a legal mark, not an ornament, testifying to the bond and naming whose it is. To bear the sign is to be identified as a party to the covenant. Signs are the covenant’s proof and identification — the tokens that say the agreement stands and this one belongs to it.

proofTexts.text: I do set my bow in the cloud, and it shall be for a token of a covenant.
proofTexts.note: The sign that certifies the bond.

proofTexts.text: It shall be a token of the covenant betwixt me and you.
The sabbath... is a sign between me and you.
It shall be for a sign unto thee upon thine hand.

plainTerms: A sign is a token that proves and marks a covenant — an appointed mark identifying a bond. The rainbow, circumcision, the Sabbath are each a ‘sign’: a legal mark testifying to the covenant and naming its parties, like a seal on a contract. To bear the sign is to be marked as belonging to the bond.
bringItHome: A sign, in covenant terms, is like the seal on a contract — the token that proves the agreement and identifies who is party to it. The rainbow marks Noah’s covenant; the Sabbath marks Israel’s. To bear the sign is to be identified as belonging to the bond it certifies.

courtroomRoles.does: appoints the sign of the bond.
marked and identified by the token.
certifies the covenant and names its parties.

86.lead: To sit, in the courtroom sense, is to convene as judge — to take the bench and hold session. When the judge ‘sits,’ the court is in session and rulings issue: “the Ancient of days did sit... the judgment was set” (Daniel 7:9-10). To ‘sit in the gate’ is to hold court (Ruth 4:1-2); to ‘sit on the throne’ is to reign and judge. Yashab, to sit, is thus an act of authority — the one seated is the one who decides. This is why enthronement is described as sitting, and why the Messiah’s session ‘at the right hand’ is a position of rule. To sit is to take up the seat of judgment and preside.

root.sense: to sit, to dwell, to remain; to take the seat of authority, to convene as judge

86.courtroomWord: A session term — to take the bench and hold court.
86.itsRole: A court is in session when the judge sits, and yashab is that sitting — taking the seat of authority to decide. The Ancient of Days did sit and the judgment was set; the elders sit in the gate to try cases; the king sits on the throne to reign. To sit is to preside, to hold session, to be the one who rules. Enthronement and judgment are both described as sitting — the seat is authority taken up.

proofTexts.text: The Ancient of days did sit.
He took ten men... and said, Sit ye down. And they sat down.
proofTexts.note: The court convened at the gate.

proofTexts.text: Thou satest in the throne judging right.
Sit thou at my right hand.

plainTerms: To sit, in the courtroom sense, is to convene as judge — to take the bench and hold session. When the Ancient of Days ‘did sit,’ the court was in session. To ‘sit in the gate’ is to hold court; to ‘sit on the throne’ is to reign and judge. Sitting is an act of authority: the one seated is the one who decides.
bringItHome: When a judge ‘sits,’ court is in session and rulings follow. That is the force of it in Scripture: ‘the Ancient of days did sit, and the judgment was set.’ To sit in the gate was to hold court; to sit on the throne was to rule. The seat is authority — the one who sits is the one who decides.

courtroomRoles.does: takes the bench; when He sits, the court is in session.
who sit to judge and to rule.
convened when the judge sits.

65.lead: The sojourner is the resident alien — a legal class with a defined and protected status under Torah. The ger was not a citizen by birth but held real standing: the same law for the home-born and the stranger (Numbers 15:16), protection from oppression, a share in the gleanings, rest on the Sabbath. “Love ye therefore the stranger... for ye were strangers in the land of Egypt” (Deuteronomy 10:19). The sojourner’s status is legally recognized and legally guarded, a class the law names and protects. To be a sojourner is to hold the standing of a protected resident alien — not without rights, but with rights the covenant secures.

root.sense: a sojourner, resident alien, stranger; a protected legal class

65.courtroomWord: A status term — the resident alien’s protected legal standing.
65.itsRole: The law names its classes and protects them, and the sojourner is one — the resident alien with recognized standing: one law for stranger and home-born, protection from oppression, a share in the harvest, Sabbath rest. The ger is not rightless but hedged by statute. ‘One law’ for the stranger is a repeated refrain. To be a sojourner is to hold a protected status the covenant secures — an alien by birth, a protected party by law.

proofTexts.text: One law and one manner shall be for you, and for the stranger that sojourneth with you.
Love ye therefore the stranger.
proofTexts.note: The sojourner protected and cared for.

proofTexts.text: The stranger... shall be unto you as one born among you.
Thou shalt neither vex a stranger, nor oppress him.

plainTerms: The sojourner is the resident alien — a legal class with a defined, protected status under Torah. The ger wasn’t a citizen by birth but held real standing: one law for stranger and home-born, protection from oppression, a share in the gleanings, Sabbath rest. To be a sojourner is to hold a status the covenant names and guards.
bringItHome: A sojourner in Israel was a resident alien — not born to the people, but far from rightless. The law named the class and protected it: ‘one law’ for stranger and citizen alike, protection from oppression, a share in the harvest. To be a ger was to hold a real, guarded standing under the covenant.

courtroomRoles.does: holds a protected legal standing.
names the class and guards its rights.
bound to the same law toward the stranger.

62.lead: Sonship is the legal status that carries the inheritance — the standing of a son, which by law entitles one to the estate. It is not merely a warm relationship but a legal position: “if a son, then an heir of Yahuah through Messiah” (Galatians 4:7). The son’s status is what confers the claim on the inheritance; sonship and heirship travel together. Under the law, the son held rights the servant did not — standing, name, and estate. To be granted sonship is to be granted the legal position from which the inheritance is claimed. It is status with an estate attached, conferred by the Father.

root.sense: son; the legal status of a son
son; standing that carries the inheritance

sharesRoot.note: Huiothesia (adoption, the placing-as-son) is built on huios: adoption confers the sonship that carries the estate.

62.courtroomWord: A status term — the standing of a son, entitling to the inheritance.
62.itsRole: The son’s standing is a legal position, and it carries the estate: ‘if a son, then an heir.’ Sonship is what confers the claim on the inheritance — the servant does not hold it, the son does. It is status with rights: name, standing, and estate. To be granted sonship (by adoption) is to be placed in the position from which the inheritance is lawfully claimed. Sonship and heirship are one legal package, conferred by the Father.

proofTexts.text: If a son, then an heir of Yahuah through Messiah.
The children of Yahuah: and if children, then heirs.
Power to become the sons of Yahuah.
Ye are all the children of Yahuah by faith in Messiah Yahushua.

plainTerms: Sonship is the legal status that carries the inheritance — the standing of a son, which entitles you to the estate. ‘If a son, then an heir.’ It is not just a warm relationship but a legal position: the son holds rights the servant does not — name, standing, and estate. To be granted sonship is to be given the position from which the inheritance is claimed.
bringItHome: A son held what a servant did not: a name, a standing, and a claim on the estate. That is sonship — a legal position, not just affection. ‘If a son, then an heir.’ To be granted sonship is to be placed where the inheritance can be claimed by right. The status and the estate come together.

courtroomRoles.does: confers the status of son and its inheritance.
holds the standing that carries the estate.
which sonship entitles the son to claim.

80.lead: To stand, in the courtroom, is to hold legal standing before the bench — to have the recognized right to appear and to remain in the court’s presence. “Who shall stand in his holy place?” (Psalm 24:3); “the ungodly shall not stand in the judgment” (Psalm 1:5). To stand is to have standing: the position of one entitled to appear, whose case is admitted. To be unable to stand is to be cast out, denied a place before the court. Amad, to stand, is thus a legal posture — the one who stands is the one with the right to be there. To stand in the judgment is to hold a place before the bench that the verdict has not overturned.

root.sense: to stand, to take one’s stand, to remain; to hold standing before authority

80.courtroomWord: A standing term — the recognized right to appear and remain before the bench.
80.itsRole: To appear before the court, one must have standing, and to stand is to hold it — the right to be in the court’s presence, admitted and not cast out. ‘Who shall stand?’ asks who has the standing to remain before the Judge. ‘The ungodly shall not stand in the judgment’: their standing fails, they are removed. To stand is the posture of the party whose place before the bench is secure — admitted, remaining, not overturned.

proofTexts.text: Who shall stand in his holy place?
proofTexts.note: Who holds the standing to appear.

proofTexts.text: The ungodly shall not stand in the judgment.
proofTexts.note: Standing that fails at the bench.

proofTexts.text: And having done all, to stand.
proofTexts.note: To hold one’s ground before the court.

proofTexts.text: He shall be holden up: for Yahuah is able to make him stand.

plainTerms: To stand, in the courtroom, is to hold legal standing — the recognized right to appear and remain before the Judge. ‘Who shall stand in his holy place?’ asks who has that standing. ‘The ungodly shall not stand in the judgment’: their place fails. To stand is to be admitted before the bench; to fall is to be cast out.
bringItHome: In court, to ‘stand’ is to have standing — the right to be there, to appear, to remain. ‘Who shall stand in his holy place?’ is asking who is admitted before the Judge. And ‘the ungodly shall not stand in the judgment’ means their standing collapses — they are removed. To stand is to hold your place before the bench.

courtroomRoles.does: holds the standing to appear before the bench.
before whom one stands, who makes His own stand.
in which standing is held or fails.

109.lead: A steward is a trustee placed over another’s property and household — entrusted with management, and answerable for it. The oikonomos ran the estate on the owner’s behalf, with real authority but full accountability: “it is required in stewards, that a man be found faithful” (1 Corinthians 4:2). The steward does not own; he administers, and the day comes to “give an account of thy stewardship” (Luke 16:2). It is a position of trust with a reckoning attached. To be a steward is to be entrusted with what is not one’s own, empowered to manage it, and bound to answer for it at the audit.

root.sense: a household manager, steward; a trustee over another’s property

109.courtroomWord: A trustee term — one entrusted with management and answerable for it.
109.itsRole: Property is often placed in a trustee’s hands, and the steward is that trustee — entrusted with the estate, empowered to manage, and bound to account. He does not own; he administers on the owner’s behalf. The reckoning is built in: ‘give an account of thy stewardship.’ Faithfulness is the standard required of him. To be a steward is to hold a trust with an audit attached — authority to manage, and liability to answer.

proofTexts.text: It is required in stewards, that a man be found faithful.
Give an account of thy stewardship.
Who then is that faithful and wise steward?
As good stewards of the manifold grace of Yahuah.
proofTexts.note: The trust to be managed faithfully.

plainTerms: A steward is a trustee placed over someone else’s property and household — entrusted to manage it, and answerable for it. He doesn’t own; he administers, and the day comes to ‘give an account of thy stewardship.’ It is a position of trust with a reckoning attached: authority to manage, and liability to answer at the audit.
bringItHome: A steward runs the owner’s estate — with real authority, but always answerable. He manages what is not his, and one day the owner says: ‘give an account of thy stewardship.’ That is the steward: entrusted, empowered, and audited. Faithfulness with what belongs to another is the whole of the job.

courtroomRoles.does: manages the owner’s property, answerable for it.
entrusts the estate and requires the account.
the reckoning the steward must render.

120.lead: A surety is the pledge who guarantees another’s obligation — the one who legally stands good for a debt or a bond, liable if the other defaults. Judah becomes surety for Benjamin: “I will be surety for him; of my hand shalt thou require him” (Genesis 43:9). A surety does not merely encourage; he assumes the liability, pledging himself against the outcome. “Yahushua made a surety of a better testament” (Hebrews 7:22) names Him the guarantee of the covenant: the One who stands good for it, whose own person secures that it will hold. To be a surety is to pledge oneself as the guarantee — liable for the obligation of another.

root.sense: to pledge, to give surety, to become responsible for
a guarantor, surety

120.courtroomWord: A guarantee term — the one who pledges himself as security for another’s obligation.
120.itsRole: An obligation may be secured by a surety — one who stands good for it, liable if the party defaults. It is not encouragement but assumed liability: the surety pledges his own person against the outcome. Judah stood surety for Benjamin; Yahushua is ‘surety of a better testament,’ the guarantee that the covenant will hold. To be a surety is to pledge oneself as security — the guarantee that the obligation is met, liable in the debtor’s place.

proofTexts.text: I will be surety for him; of my hand shalt thou require him.
Was Yahushua made a surety of a better testament.
He that is surety for a stranger shall smart for it.
proofTexts.note: The real liability a surety takes on.

proofTexts.text: Be not thou one of them... that are sureties for debts.
proofTexts.note: The weight of standing good for another.

plainTerms: A surety is the one who guarantees another’s obligation — who legally stands good for a debt, liable if the other fails. Judah became surety for Benjamin: ‘of my hand shalt thou require him.’ Yahushua is ‘surety of a better testament’: the guarantee the covenant will hold. To be a surety is to pledge yourself as security for another.
bringItHome: A surety is not a cheerleader — he is the one who signs to guarantee your debt, and pays if you can’t. Judah pledged himself for Benjamin’s safe return: ‘of my hand shalt thou require him.’ Yahushua is called the ‘surety’ of the covenant: the guarantee, in His own person, that it will stand.

courtroomRoles.does: pledges Himself as the guarantee of the covenant.
whose obligation the surety stands good for.
to whom the guarantee is given.

42.lead: To swear is to bind oneself by oath — to invoke a higher witness and place oneself under penalty for breach. An oath was legally binding in the gravest way: “if a man swear an oath to bind his soul with a bond... he shall not break his word” (Numbers 30:2). Shaba is to bind by a solemn declaration, calling Yahuah to witness. When Yahuah swears “by himself” (Genesis 22:16; Hebrews 6:13), He binds His own word irrevocably. To swear is not casual speech but self-binding at law: the one who swears stakes himself on the truth or the performance of what he says, under sanction if he fails.

root.sense: to swear, to take an oath; to bind oneself by solemn declaration

42.courtroomWord: An oath term — to bind oneself under penalty by solemn sworn declaration.
42.itsRole: An oath binds the one who swears — self-binding at law, invoking a higher witness and accepting penalty for breach. ‘He shall not break his word’: the sworn oath is irrevocable. Yahuah swears by Himself to bind His own promise beyond doubt. To swear is to stake oneself on the truth or performance of what is said, under sanction. It is the most solemn form of legal commitment — the word made binding by oath.

proofTexts.text: If a man... swear an oath to bind his soul with a bond; he shall not break his word.
By myself have I sworn, saith Yahuah.
He sware by himself.
proofTexts.note: The oath that secures the promise.

proofTexts.text: Thou shalt fear Yahuah... and shalt swear by his name.
proofTexts.note: The oath sworn under the proper witness.

plainTerms: To swear is to bind yourself by oath — to invoke a higher witness and accept penalty if you break it. ‘He shall not break his word’: a sworn oath was irrevocable. When Yahuah ‘swears by Himself,’ He binds His own word beyond doubt. To swear is self-binding at law, staking yourself on what you say.
bringItHome: To swear an oath was to stake yourself on your word — calling Yahuah to witness, accepting the penalty if you failed. ‘He shall not break his word.’ And when Yahuah swore ‘by Himself,’ He bound His own promise irrevocably — there was no one greater to swear by. An oath is a word made binding under sanction.

courtroomRoles.does: binds himself under penalty for breach.
invoked to witness the oath; who swears by Himself.
the self-binding declaration, irrevocable.

8.lead: The testimony is the deposited terms of the covenant — the witnessed record placed on file, and by extension the tablets and the law themselves. The tablets are “the tables of testimony” (Exodus 31:18); the ark is “the ark of the testimony” (Exodus 25:22), because it held the covenant terms deposited as a permanent witness. Eduth, from the root for witness, is the covenant’s own testimony to itself: the terms recorded, witnessed, and preserved. To keep the testimony is to keep the deposited terms. The testimony is not vague inspiration but the documentary core of the covenant — the law placed on file as a standing witness.

root.sense: testimony, witness; the deposited covenant terms. From ed, a witness

sharesRoot.note: Eduth (the testimony) is from ed (a witness): the deposited terms are the covenant’s standing witness to itself.

8.courtroomWord: A deposited-record term — the witnessed covenant terms placed on file.
8.itsRole: A covenant deposits its terms as a witness, and the testimony is that deposit — the tablets, the law, placed on file in the ark. Eduth is from ‘witness’: the covenant’s own testimony to itself, recorded and preserved. To keep the testimony is to keep the deposited terms. It is the documentary core of the covenant, the standing witness against any breach — not inspiration but the recorded law itself.

proofTexts.text: Two tables of testimony, tables of stone.
Thou shalt put into the ark the testimony which I shall give thee.
proofTexts.note: The covenant terms placed on file.

proofTexts.text: The testimony of Yahuah is sure, making wise the simple.
proofTexts.note: The deposited terms as reliable witness.

proofTexts.text: Blessed are they that keep his testimonies.

plainTerms: The testimony is the deposited terms of the covenant — the witnessed record on file, and by extension the tablets and the law. The tablets are ‘the tables of testimony’; the ark held ‘the testimony.’ From the word for ‘witness,’ it is the covenant’s own record of itself. To keep the testimony is to keep the deposited terms.
bringItHome: The ‘testimony’ was the covenant’s terms, written and deposited in the ark as a standing witness — ‘the tables of testimony.’ The word comes from ‘witness,’ because the deposited law testifies to the agreement and against any breach. To keep His testimonies is to keep the recorded terms of the covenant.

courtroomRoles.does: gives the testimony to be deposited.
the witnessed law placed on file.
who keep the testimony as the covenant terms.

74.lead: The throne is the judgment seat itself — the sovereign seat from which rule and verdict issue. Not a chair of honor merely, but the seat of authority: “I saw Yahuah sitting upon his throne” (1 Kings 22:19); “a great white throne, and him that sat on it... and the dead were judged” (Revelation 20:11-12). The throne is where the King reigns and the Judge rules — the two offices meeting in one seat. To occupy the throne is to hold supreme authority; to approach it is to come before the highest court. The throne is the source-seat of law and judgment, distinct from every derived bench beneath it.

root.sense: a throne, the royal and judicial seat
a throne, the seat of the sovereign

74.courtroomWord: A sovereign-seat term — the judgment seat from which rule and verdict issue.
74.itsRole: Rule and judgment issue from a seat, and the throne is that seat — the sovereign’s own, where King and Judge meet. ‘I saw Yahuah sitting upon his throne’; ‘a great white throne... and the dead were judged.’ To sit on the throne is to hold supreme authority; to come before it is to stand before the highest court. The throne is the source-seat of law and verdict, above every delegated bench — the place from which the final ruling comes.

proofTexts.text: I saw Yahuah sitting on his throne.
A great white throne, and him that sat on it.
Justice and judgment are the habitation of thy throne.
He hath prepared his throne for judgment.
proofTexts.note: The throne as the seat of the verdict.

plainTerms: The throne is the judgment seat itself — the sovereign seat from which rule and verdict issue. Not just a chair of honor, but the seat of authority where King and Judge meet: ‘him that sat on it... and the dead were judged.’ To occupy the throne is to hold supreme authority; to approach it is to come before the highest court.
bringItHome: The throne is not decoration — it is the seat rule and judgment come from. ‘I saw Yahuah sitting upon his throne’; ‘a great white throne... and the dead were judged.’ King and Judge meet in that one seat. To come before the throne is to stand before the highest court there is.

courtroomRoles.does: reigns and judges from the sovereign seat.
the source of rule and verdict.
who come before the highest court.

88.lead: The tongue is evidence that justifies or condemns — the instrument of testimony whose words are entered on the record and weighed. “Death and life are in the power of the tongue” (Proverbs 18:21); “by thy words thou shalt be justified, and by thy words thou shalt be condemned” (Matthew 12:37). The tongue’s speech is legal testimony: what it declares can acquit or convict, bless or curse, and it is held accountable. A ‘lying tongue’ is a false witness (Proverbs 6:17), an abomination because it corrupts the evidence. To bridle the tongue is to guard one’s testimony; what the tongue speaks is entered as evidence, and by it one is judged.

root.sense: the tongue; the instrument of speech and testimony

88.courtroomWord: A testimony term — speech entered as evidence that acquits or condemns.
88.itsRole: What the tongue speaks is evidence, weighed and held accountable. ‘By thy words thou shalt be justified... condemned’: the tongue’s testimony can acquit or convict. A lying tongue is a false witness, corrupting the record; a faithful tongue testifies true. Death and life are in its power because its words are entered as evidence. To guard the tongue is to guard one’s testimony — for by it the verdict is shaped.

proofTexts.text: Death and life are in the power of the tongue.
By thy words thou shalt be justified, and by thy words thou shalt be condemned.
proofTexts.note: Speech as evidence for the verdict.

proofTexts.text: A lying tongue... doth Yahuah hate.
The tongue is a fire.

plainTerms: The tongue is evidence that justifies or condemns — the instrument of testimony whose words are entered on the record. ‘By thy words thou shalt be justified... condemned.’ A lying tongue is a false witness. What the tongue speaks can acquit or convict, and it is held accountable. To guard your tongue is to guard your testimony.
bringItHome: What you say is entered as evidence. ‘By thy words thou shalt be justified, and by thy words thou shalt be condemned’ — the tongue’s speech is testimony, weighed at the bench. A lying tongue is a false witness, an abomination. ‘Death and life are in the power of the tongue’ because its words go on the record, and by them you are judged.

courtroomRoles.does: whose tongue enters testimony on the record.
whose words acquit or condemn.
who weighs the words as evidence.

19.lead: Transgression is a specific, defined breach of a known statute — the crossing of a line the law drew, chargeable because the line existed. Pesha is rebellion, a breaking of covenant; parabasis, in the Greek, is literally a stepping-across — a violation of a boundary set. “Where no law is, there is no transgression” (Romans 4:15) states the principle exactly: transgression requires a standard to transgress. To transgress is not vague wrongdoing but the breach of a particular command — the boundary crossed, the statute violated. This is why transgression presupposes the law: no line, no crossing; no command, no transgression. The charge exists only because the standard does.

root.sense: rebellion, transgression, covenant breach
a stepping-across, a violation of a boundary

19.courtroomWord: A breach term — the crossing of a defined line the law drew.
19.itsRole: A boundary must exist before it can be crossed, and transgression is the crossing — the breach of a specific, known statute. Pesha is covenant rebellion; parabasis is stepping across a set line. ‘Where no law is, there is no transgression’: the charge depends on the standard. To transgress is to violate a particular command, the boundary breached. Transgression is the law’s own evidence that a line was there to cross — no command, no transgression.

proofTexts.text: Where no law is, there is no transgression.
Blot out my transgressions.
proofTexts.note: The specific breaches charged and removed.

proofTexts.text: Sin is the transgression of the law.
proofTexts.note: Sin defined as crossing the law’s line.

proofTexts.text: It was added because of transgressions.

plainTerms: Transgression is a specific breach of a known law — the crossing of a line the law drew. ‘Where no law is, there is no transgression’: you can’t cross a line that isn’t there. To transgress is to violate a particular command, not just do vague wrong. The charge exists only because the standard does.
bringItHome: You cannot step across a line that was never drawn. That is the logic of transgression: it is the crossing of a boundary the law set. ‘Where no law is, there is no transgression.’ So every charge of transgression is proof the standard was there — no command, nothing to transgress.

courtroomRoles.does: crosses the line the law drew.
the standard whose crossing is the transgression.
set the line and charges its breach.

110.lead: Trust is reliance placed on the reliable — resting one’s case on another’s faithfulness, the confidence that stakes an outcome on the one relied upon. Batach is to take refuge, to lean the full weight on: “trust in Yahuah with all thine heart” (Proverbs 3:5). It is not vague optimism but a directed reliance — the trusting party commits his cause to another and rests on that party’s ability and faithfulness to carry it. In the courtroom, to trust is to entrust one’s standing to an advocate, to rest on the surety who guarantees. Trust is the confidence that leans wholly on the reliable one, staking the outcome on him.

root.sense: to trust, to rely on, to take refuge; to lean the full weight upon

110.courtroomWord: A reliance term — resting one’s case wholly on the faithfulness of another.
110.itsRole: To rest a case on another is to trust, and batach is that resting — the full weight leaned on the reliable one. It is directed reliance, not vague hope: the trusting party commits his cause and stakes the outcome on the one relied upon. In the court, to trust is to entrust one’s standing to the advocate and the surety who stand good for it. Trust is confidence placed where it is warranted — the whole weight on the faithful one.

proofTexts.text: Trust in Yahuah with all thine heart.
Commit thy way unto Yahuah; trust also in him.
proofTexts.note: Committing the cause to the reliable one.

proofTexts.text: They that know thy name will put their trust in thee.
Thou wilt keep him in perfect peace... because he trusteth in thee.
proofTexts.note: The settled reliance that rests secure.

plainTerms: Trust is reliance placed on the reliable — leaning your full weight on another’s faithfulness, staking the outcome on them. ‘Trust in Yahuah with all thine heart.’ It is not vague optimism but directed reliance: committing your cause to one who can and will carry it. In court, to trust is to rest your standing on the advocate and surety who stand good for it.
bringItHome: Trust is leaning your whole weight on someone who can bear it — committing your case to them and resting on their faithfulness. ‘Trust in Yahuah with all thine heart.’ It is not a hopeful guess; it is a directed reliance, staking the outcome on the one who is proven able. In the court, you entrust your standing to the one who stands good for you.

courtroomRoles.does: rests his cause and standing on the reliable one.
the faithful one on whom the full weight is leaned.
to whom the standing is entrusted.

40.lead: Truth is not merely accuracy but reliability — firmness, faithfulness, that which is established and can be leaned on. Emet, from the root aman (to be firm, to confirm), is the quality of what stands: a true witness is a reliable one, a true word is one that holds. This is why truth and faithfulness are one word-family in Hebrew: “abundant in goodness and truth” (Exodus 34:6) means abounding in reliable faithfulness. In the courtroom, truth is the reliability of testimony that will not fail under examination. To speak truth is to speak what is firm and can be established; the same root gives us ‘amen’ — it is firm, it is established.

root.sense: truth, firmness, faithfulness; from aman, to be firm, established, reliable

sharesRoot.note: All from aman: truth (emet) is what is firm, amen affirms it is established, faithfulness (emunah) is the reliability itself. One root, one quality of firmness.

40.courtroomWord: A reliability term — the firmness of what is established and can be leaned on.
40.itsRole: Truth, in Scripture, is reliability — the firmness of what stands, not bare accuracy. From aman (to be firm), emet is the quality of the testimony that holds under examination, the word that will not fail. It shares its root with ‘amen’ (it is established) and ‘faithful’ (reliable). To speak truth is to speak what is firm and can be confirmed. In the court, truth is testimony that stands — established, reliable, leaned upon.

proofTexts.text: Abundant in goodness and truth.
Thy word is true from the beginning.
Thy word is truth.
Lead me in thy truth, and teach me.

plainTerms: Truth is not just accuracy but reliability — firmness, faithfulness, what stands and can be leaned on. From aman (to be firm), it shares a root with ‘amen’ (it is established) and ‘faithful.’ A true witness is a reliable one. To speak truth is to speak what will hold under examination. Truth is testimony that stands.
bringItHome: In Hebrew, truth and faithfulness are the same family of words — because truth is what is firm, what holds, what you can lean on. ‘Abundant in goodness and truth’ means abounding in reliable faithfulness. The same root gives ‘amen’: it is established. Truth is not just correct — it is testimony that stands under examination.

courtroomRoles.does: whose word is firm and reliable, established forever.
whose testimony stands under examination.
true because it is firm and can be confirmed.

68.lead: Unclean is a legal-ritual status, not a statement about hygiene or morality — a condition of ceremonial disqualification that barred one from the holy until it was resolved. Tame is a status one could contract (by contact with death, disease, or discharge) and from which one was cleansed by prescribed means. It is not the same as sinful: a woman after childbirth, a man who buried the dead, were ‘unclean’ without having done any wrong. The unclean was disqualified from the sanctuary until purified. To be unclean is to hold a status the law defines and the law removes — a ritual disqualification, addressed by the ritual remedy, not a verdict of guilt.

root.sense: unclean, ceremonially impure; a status of ritual disqualification

68.courtroomWord: A status term — ceremonial disqualification from the holy, until cleansed.
68.itsRole: Cleanness is access to the holy, and uncleanness is its suspension — a ritual status barring one from the sanctuary until resolved. Tame is contracted and cleansed by prescribed means; it is not sin. The one who buried the dead was unclean without wrongdoing. To be unclean is to hold a legally defined status of disqualification, addressed by the law’s own remedy. It is about ritual access, not moral guilt — a status the law names and the law removes.

proofTexts.text: To make a difference between the unclean and the clean.
The priest... shall pronounce him unclean.
proofTexts.note: The legal finding of the status.

proofTexts.text: He that toucheth the dead body... shall be unclean seven days.
proofTexts.note: A status contracted, not a sin.

proofTexts.text: Thus shall ye separate the children of Israel from their uncleanness.

plainTerms: Unclean is a legal-ritual status, not hygiene or sin — a ceremonial disqualification that barred one from the holy until cleansed. You could become unclean by contact with death or by childbirth, having done nothing wrong. To be unclean is to hold a status the law defines and the law removes: about ritual access, not moral guilt.
bringItHome: ‘Unclean’ did not mean dirty or wicked — it was a ritual status. A man who buried his father was unclean, though he had done a good and needed thing. It simply meant disqualified from the sanctuary until cleansed by the prescribed means. It is about access to the holy, not a verdict of guilt.

courtroomRoles.does: holds the ritual status of uncleanness.
pronounces and oversees the status and its cleansing.
defines the status and provides its remedy.

112.lead: Vengeance is judicial retribution reserved to the rightful authority — not private revenge, but the lawful requital that belongs to the one with standing to render it. “To me belongeth vengeance, and recompence” (Deuteronomy 32:35); “Vengeance is mine; I will repay, saith Yahuah” (Romans 12:19). Naqam is the just penalty exacted for wrong — and Scripture removes it from private hands precisely because it is a judicial act, reserved to Yahuah as Judge. To take vengeance is to render the wrong its due requital; that this belongs to Yahuah means the injured are not left to retaliate but may commit the matter to the One with authority to judge. Vengeance is the court’s requital, not the victim’s.

root.sense: vengeance, requital; the just retribution reserved to the rightful authority

112.courtroomWord: A retribution term — lawful requital reserved to the authority with standing to render it.
112.itsRole: Wrong requires requital, and vengeance is it — but reserved to the rightful judge, not seized by the wronged. ‘Vengeance is mine; I will repay.’ Naqam is judicial retribution, removed from private hands because it is a court’s act. That it belongs to Yahuah frees the injured from retaliation: they commit the matter to the One with authority to judge. Vengeance is lawful requital rendered by the bench — the wrong repaid by the One with standing to repay it.

proofTexts.text: To me belongeth vengeance, and recompence.
Vengeance is mine; I will repay, saith Yahuah.
Yahuah revengeth, and is furious.
O Yahuah, to whom vengeance belongeth.
proofTexts.note: Vengeance as the court’s, not the victim’s.

plainTerms: Vengeance is judicial retribution reserved to the rightful authority — not private revenge. ‘Vengeance is mine; I will repay, saith Yahuah.’ It is the just penalty for wrong, removed from private hands because it is a court’s act. That it belongs to Yahuah means the injured need not retaliate — they can commit the matter to the Judge.
bringItHome: ‘Vengeance is mine; I will repay, saith Yahuah’ is not a threat so much as a relief: the wrong done to you is not yours to avenge — it belongs to the One with authority to judge. Naqam is judicial requital, reserved to the bench. You can hand the matter to the Judge instead of taking it into your own hands.

courtroomRoles.does: to whom vengeance belongs; who renders the just requital.
commit the matter to the Judge rather than retaliate.
receives the lawful requital from the bench.

103.lead: To visit, in the legal sense, is to conduct an official inspection — to come and examine, muster, or audit, with consequences following the finding. Paqad means to attend to, to inspect, to reckon — and a divine ‘visitation’ is an official review that results in reward or reckoning. “In the day when I visit I will visit their sin upon them” (Exodus 32:34); “Yahuah visited Sarah as he had said” (Genesis 21:1). To be visited is to be inspected and dealt with according to the finding — blessed or charged. It is not a casual call but an audit: the record examined, and the appropriate consequence rendered. Visitation is the court coming to inspect and to act on what it finds.

root.sense: to visit, to attend to, to inspect, to muster, to reckon

103.courtroomWord: An inspection term — an official review, with consequence following the finding.
103.itsRole: An audit comes to examine and then to act, and to visit is that audit — the official inspection that results in reward or reckoning. Paqad attends to, inspects, musters. A ‘visitation’ reviews the record and renders the finding: Sarah visited with the promised son, sin visited upon the guilty. To be visited is to be inspected and dealt with accordingly. It is the court coming to examine, and acting on what it finds.

proofTexts.text: In the day when I visit I will visit their sin upon them.
Yahuah visited Sarah as he had said.
Thou knewest not the time of thy visitation.
Glorify Elohim in the day of visitation.
proofTexts.note: The day of inspection and reckoning.

plainTerms: To visit, in the legal sense, is to conduct an official inspection — to come, examine, and act on the finding. Paqad means to attend to, inspect, reckon. A ‘visitation’ reviews the record and renders the result: Sarah visited with a son, sin visited on the guilty. To be visited is to be inspected and dealt with accordingly — an audit, not a casual call.
bringItHome: A ‘visitation’ from Yahuah is an audit — He comes to inspect and to act on what He finds. It cuts both ways: He ‘visited Sarah’ with the promised son, and He would ‘visit their sin upon them.’ To be visited is to be examined and dealt with by the finding — the court arriving to review the record.

courtroomRoles.does: visits to examine and render the finding.
inspected and dealt with according to the record.
blessing or reckoning, following the inspection.

43.lead: A vow is a self-imposed binding obligation — a promise voluntarily undertaken that, once made, the law holds one to. “When thou shalt vow a vow unto Yahuah thy Elohim, thou shalt not slack to pay it” (Deuteronomy 23:21); “when thou vowest a vow... defer not to pay it” (Ecclesiastes 5:4). A neder is not a casual wish but a legally binding pledge one places on oneself: better not to vow than to vow and not pay (Ecclesiastes 5:5). The vow creates a real obligation the court will enforce. To make a vow is to bind oneself voluntarily; to break it is to default on a debt one freely incurred. Vows are self-created obligations the law takes seriously.

root.sense: a vow; a self-imposed binding obligation, voluntarily undertaken

43.courtroomWord: An obligation term — a binding pledge one voluntarily places on oneself.
43.itsRole: An obligation can be self-imposed, and a vow is that — a pledge freely undertaken that the law then holds one to. Neder is no casual wish: once made, it must be paid, and it is better not to vow than to default. The vow creates a real, enforceable obligation. To vow is to bind oneself voluntarily; to break it is to default on a debt freely incurred. The law honors the freedom to vow and enforces the obligation it creates.

proofTexts.text: When thou shalt vow a vow unto Yahuah... thou shalt not slack to pay it.
When thou vowest a vow unto Elohim, defer not to pay it.
proofTexts.note: The vow that must be paid.

proofTexts.text: Better is it that thou shouldest not vow, than that thou shouldest vow and not pay.
proofTexts.note: The weight of the self-imposed pledge.

proofTexts.text: If a man vow a vow... he shall not break his word.
proofTexts.note: The vow as an unbreakable bond.

plainTerms: A vow is a self-imposed binding obligation — a promise you freely make that the law then holds you to. ‘Thou shalt not slack to pay it.’ It is no casual wish: once vowed, it must be paid, and better not to vow than to vow and default. The vow creates a real, enforceable obligation you placed on yourself.
bringItHome: A vow is a promise you put on yourself — no one made you, but once you vow, the law holds you to it. ‘Better not to vow than to vow and not pay.’ It creates a real obligation, a debt you freely incurred. To break a vow is to default on something you bound yourself to with your own word.

courtroomRoles.does: binds himself voluntarily to the obligation.

courtroomRoles.role: the One to whom the vow is made
courtroomRoles.does: holds the vower to his word.
the self-imposed pledge the law enforces.

107.lead: Wages are the pay earned and owed — the due rendered for what one has done, whether the reward of the faithful or the payoff of sin. “The wages of sin is death” (Romans 6:23) is precise legal accounting: death is the earned pay, the due owed for the work of sin. Opsonion is a soldier’s pay; sakar is hire, wage. Wages are not arbitrary; they are what the labor earned, rendered according to the record. This is why sin’s wage is death — not an arbitrary penalty but the due the work incurs. Wages are owed, calculated, and paid: the exact return on what one has done, good or ill.

root.sense: hire, wages, the pay for labor
a soldier’s pay, wages

sharesRoot.note: The same wage-word covers the pay earned by labor (Wages) and the due paid to the faithful (Reward).

107.courtroomWord: A due-payment term — the pay earned and owed for what one has done.
107.itsRole: Labor earns a due, and wages are its payment — rendered according to the record, good or ill. ‘The wages of sin is death’: death is the earned pay for sin’s work, precise accounting, not arbitrary penalty. Opsonion and sakar are the pay owed for service. Wages are calculated and paid: the exact return on what one has done. What sin earns, it is paid; what faithfulness earns is the reward.

proofTexts.text: The wages of sin is death; but the gift of Elohim is eternal life.
proofTexts.note: The earned pay contrasted with the free gift.

proofTexts.text: The wages of him that is hired shall not abide with thee all night.
proofTexts.note: The wage owed and due promptly.

proofTexts.text: The hire of the labourers... which is of you kept back by fraud.
That useth his neighbour’s service without wages.

plainTerms: Wages are the pay earned and owed — the due rendered for what you have done. ‘The wages of sin is death’ is exact accounting: death is the pay sin’s work earns, not an arbitrary penalty. Wages are calculated and owed, the return on the labor. What sin earns, it is paid; the faithful, by contrast, receive the reward.
